We derive labels from the subsequent trajectories of outlier documents, distinguishing those that anticipate new topics from those that reinforce existing topics or remain isolated, and estimate label confidence through agreement across multiple embedding models. On two French news corpora, anticipatory outliers prove predictable at publication time. Under cross-validation, $F_1$ rises from about 0.77 over the full eligible population to above 0.90 on high-consensus subsets, and remains at 0.76-0.80 under a strictly chronological evaluation. Predictive performance is driven mainly by geometric features capturing each outlier's position in embedding space.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that documents which later become central to new topics (anticipatory outliers) can be predicted already at publication time using their position in embedding space.
AI.motivation: In embedding-based topic models, some documents are initially treated as noise but later emerge as key early instances of new topics. At publication time these anticipatory documents are hard to distinguish from genuine noise, yet identifying them early would be valuable for tracking emerging themes, forecasting information trends, and improving topic modeling. The paper is motivated by the need to detect such forward-looking, topic-creating documents prospectively, using only information available when they first appear.
AI.method: The authors (1) track the temporal trajectories of documents that are outliers in embedding space when they appear; (2) retrospectively label these outliers into three categories: those that anticipate new topics, those that reinforce existing topics, and those that remain isolated noise; (3) estimate label confidence via agreement across multiple embedding models; (4) build predictive models that, at publication time, classify an outlier into these categories using features derived from the document’s geometric position in the embedding space (and possibly other attributes); and (5) evaluate performance on two French news corpora using cross-validation and strictly chronological splits to mimic real-time prediction.
AI.result: On two French news datasets, anticipatory outliers are shown to be prospectively predictable. For the full set of eligible documents, the predictive model attains F1 scores around 0.77. When restricted to high-consensus subsets—where multiple embedding models agree on labels—F1 exceeds 0.90, indicating very reliable prediction for those cases. Under a strictly chronological evaluation, which is more realistic for deployment, F1 remains strong at 0.76–0.80. Analysis indicates that features encoding the geometric configuration of each outlier in embedding space contribute most to the predictive performance.
AI.conclusion: Documents that initially look like noisy outliers in embedding-based topic models but later become central to emerging topics can be identified with high accuracy at publication time. Reliable prediction is possible using only information available at first appearance, especially geometric features describing a document’s embedding-space position. This suggests that embedding geometry contains early signals of emerging topics and that topic modeling and trend-detection systems can be enhanced by explicitly modeling and classifying such anticipatory outliers.

title: EAGER: Enhancing Generative Event Extraction via Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
summary: End-to-end event extraction remains challenging for large language models as it requires simultaneous identification of event triggers, classification of event types, and extraction of schema-grounded argument spans. We present EAGER, a reinforcement learning framework for generative event extraction that combines fine-grained verifiable rewards with Schema-Contrastive Advantage Estimation to alleviate advantage collapse under sparse binary rewards. Our reward design explicitly targets structural validity, extraction accuracy, groundedness, coverage, over-generation, and span precision. Experiments across seven benchmark datasets show that EAGER consistently outperforms prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and prior reinforcement learning baselines, achieving a substantial improvement over the strongest prior method. Results demonstrate that task-aligned verifiable rewards and contrastive advantage estimation substantially improve structured extraction.

AI.tldr: EAGER is a reinforcement learning framework that improves end-to-end event extraction by using fine-grained verifiable rewards and a schema-contrastive advantage estimation method to stabilize learning under sparse rewards.
AI.motivation: End-to-end event extraction with large language models is difficult because it requires jointly detecting triggers, classifying event types, and extracting schema-grounded arguments, and existing prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and RL methods still underperform due to sparse, coarse rewards and structural errors.
AI.method: The paper introduces EAGER, a generative event extraction framework cast as a reinforcement learning problem. It defines multiple fine-grained verifiable rewards targeting structural validity, extraction accuracy, groundedness, coverage, over-generation, and span precision. It further proposes Schema-Contrastive Advantage Estimation to address advantage collapse under sparse binary rewards, improving training stability and performance.
AI.result: Across seven benchmark datasets, EAGER consistently outperforms strong baselines, including prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and previous RL-based approaches, with substantial gains over the strongest prior method in end-to-end event extraction metrics.
AI.conclusion: Task-aligned verifiable rewards combined with schema-contrastive advantage estimation significantly enhance structured event extraction performance of large language models, indicating that careful reward design and contrastive credit assignment are key to effective RL-based generative IE systems.

title: Learned Cross-Task Relationships in Multi-Task Models
comment: Accepted to the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys 2026). 10 pages, 6 figures
summary: We propose a framework that learns cross-task relationships in multi-task models by approximating the joint distribution of task labels through targeted pairwise relationships. This approach improves performance via transfer learning and enhances information extraction without the intractable complexity of modeling the full joint space. Although our framework applies to any multi-task system, we demonstrate its efficacy within YouTube's production recommendation systems. Experiments across the Notifications, Homepage, and Watch Next surfaces show improvements in both accuracy and user satisfaction metrics. Finally, we propose a workflow template to facilitate broader future implementation.

AI.tldr: Framework for learning cross-task relationships in multi-task models via pairwise label relationships, improving recommendation performance without modeling full joint label space.
AI.motivation: Modeling full joint distributions of multiple task labels in multi-task learning is computationally intractable, yet capturing dependencies between tasks is crucial for effective transfer learning and performance gains in large-scale systems like YouTube recommendations.
AI.method: Approximate the joint distribution of task labels using targeted pairwise task relationships within a general multi-task learning framework. Implement this framework in YouTube’s production recommendation systems across several surfaces (Notifications, Homepage, Watch Next), leveraging pairwise label relationships for improved transfer and information sharing.
AI.result: Empirical experiments on YouTube recommendation surfaces show improved accuracy metrics and user satisfaction when using the proposed cross-task relationship framework compared to baselines without such explicit pairwise modeling.
AI.conclusion: Targeted pairwise approximation of task-label joint distributions offers a practical and effective way to capture cross-task relationships in multi-task systems, yielding measurable gains in large-scale production recommenders and providing a reusable workflow template for broader adoption.

title: Post-Training Leaves Behavioral Shadows on Unrelated Decisions
summary: We find that language models can transfer capabilities through task-unrelated text. Post-training typically improves language models using task-specific data. Prior work on subliminal learning shows that information about these updates can pass through unrelated generations, but has largely focused on traits or preferences using extensive teacher outputs. We introduce Active Taskless Distillation (ATD), which achieves capability transfer using only a single word from the teacher per prompt. ATD probes the behavioral shadow of post-training by selecting prompts where the teacher and student's shared public ancestor is nearly indifferent between two ordinary words. A student initialized from this ancestor learns solely from the resulting prompt-word pairs, without target-task examples, teacher logits, or teacher parameters. In the primary coding experiment with Qwen2.5-1.5B, 5,664nses yield a 5.34 pp gain on HumanEval+ over an exact nuisance-matched control thadisrupts prompt-resperiments showtransfer in scientific knowledge, commonsense reasoning, and reading comprehensins across additional model generations, sizes, and families. Functional analyses show that the learned sid composable, andthat its strength tracks the teacher's update strength.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that language model capabilities can be transferred using task-unrelated text via a method called Active Taskless Distillation (ATD).
AI.motivation: Explore whether and how post-training improvements in language models can be transferred without task-specific data, logits, or parameters, going beyond prior subliminal learning work that needs extensive teacher outputs and focuses on traits/preferences rather than capabilities.
AI.method: Introduce ATD, which selects prompts where a teacher and a student’s common ancestor model is nearly indifferent between two ordinary words. The teacher provides only a single chosen word per prompt. A student model, initialized from the ancestor, is trained solely on these prompt–single-word pairs, without target-task examples or access to teacher logits/parameters. Experiments are run primarily on coding tasks with Qwen2.5-1.5B and extended to other tasks and model families.
AI.result: Using 5,664 ATD training instances in a coding setup yields a 5.34 percentage point gain on HumanEval+ over a nuisance-matched control that disrupts the prompt–response structure. Additional experiments demonstrate successful transfer in scientific knowledge, commonsense reasoning, and reading comprehension across different model generations, sizes, and families. Functional analysis reveals that the learned signal is composable and its effect size scales with the strength of the teacher’s own post-training update.
AI.conclusion: Language model capability improvements can be distilled through highly compressed, task-unrelated signals: a single word per prompt. ATD effectively transfers skills without direct exposure to target-task data, teacher logits, or weights, suggesting that post-training leaves a behavioral “shadow” that can be probed and harvested in a data-efficient, model-agnostic way.

title: No More Free Lunch: Corpus Task Complexity Matters as Corpora Grow
summary: Given a large corpus, the questions one might ask can vary -- from "When was the first human heart transplant?" to "What are all the contradictory claims in this literature?" -- but what makes some questions more challenging than others? In this work, we define a notion of Corpus Task Complexity (CTC) that characterizes tasks by how their difficulty grows with corpus size; for instance, a retrieval query only requires a single linear pass over a corpus, while finding contradictions requires checking a quadratically growing set of claim pairs. Observing that prior work has largely only studied tasks whose difficulty grows linearly with corpus size, which we call low CTC tasks, we introduce 10 new tasks belonging to a class of high CTC whose difficulty grows quadratically or more in corpus size. We find that high-CTC tasks not only grow much more challenging on average at longer contexts for LCLMs, they reverse many modeling conclusions drawn solely from low-CTC evaluations. For instance, efficient block-sparse and hybrid attention approaches consistently match full attention performance on low-CTC tasks, but degrade much more on high-CTC tasks. Large-corpus high-CTC reasoning thus remains an open challenge as full attention is too costly to scale, motivating future research on these tasks. We release our code, data, and 22-task suite (CTC-Bench), to facilitate future research in this area.

AI.tldr: The paper defines Corpus Task Complexity (CTC) to quantify how task difficulty scales with corpus size, shows that many real-world tasks are high-CTC (e.g., contradiction finding), and introduces a benchmark (CTC-Bench) revealing that models and efficient attention mechanisms struggle much more on these high-CTC tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing large-corpus evaluations mostly focus on tasks whose difficulty grows only linearly with corpus size (low CTC), such as simple retrieval, which does not reflect the complexity of many realistic information-seeking tasks like contradiction detection or global reasoning across documents. The authors want a principled way to characterize and stress-test models on tasks whose computational and reasoning demands grow faster (quadratically or worse) with corpus size, to better understand model limitations and guide future architectures and evaluation.
AI.method: 1) Formalize Corpus Task Complexity (CTC) as how the computational difficulty of a task scales with corpus size, distinguishing low-CTC (≈linear) vs high-CTC (≥quadratic) tasks. 2) Design 10 new high-CTC tasks that require, for example, comparing many claim pairs or performing combinatorial reasoning over large corpora. 3) Combine these with existing tasks to form a 22-task benchmark suite called CTC-Bench. 4) Evaluate large-context language models (LCLMs) and various attention mechanisms (full, block-sparse, hybrid) on both low- and high-CTC tasks, and compare how performance changes as context length/corpus size increases.
AI.result: The experiments show that high-CTC tasks become much harder for LCLMs as corpus size or context length grows, significantly more so than low-CTC tasks. Many prior positive findings based only on low-CTC evaluations do not hold in the high-CTC regime: efficient attention architectures (block-sparse, hybrid) that match full-attention performance on low-CTC tasks degrade markedly on high-CTC tasks as context grows. This indicates that current efficient attention schemes fail to capture the complex, non-local interactions required by high-CTC reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Corpus Task Complexity is a useful lens to distinguish tasks that scale gently with corpus size from those that scale combinatorially and expose serious weaknesses in current long-context modeling. High-CTC tasks reveal that large-corpus reasoning is far from solved and that conclusions drawn solely from low-CTC benchmarks are misleading, especially regarding efficient attention methods. Since full attention is computationally prohibitive at high CTC, there is a pressing need for new modeling and attention approaches; the released code, data, and CTC-Bench suite are intended to support and standardize progress in this direction.

title: pylazaro: a Python package for anglicism extraction in Spanish
summary: Lexical borrowings are words from one language that are introduced into another language. Identifying lexical borrowings in text is a relevant task for data-centric fields in Linguistics such as lexicography or corpus linguistics, but none of the standard libraries for text processing offers such a functionality. In this paper we present pylazaro, an open-source Python package for the automatic extraction of unassimilated lexical borrowings (mostly anglicisms) from Spanish text. pylazaro offers a single interface to five sequence labeling models that were trained using different libraries, so that users can run and switch between them without having to deal with the idiosyncrasies of each library. We describe the design and usage of the package, contrast the performance of its models with that of general-purpose LLMs (which perform poorly at this task: F1 below 0.40, compared to 0.86 for the best model in pylazaro) and report on its adoption: pylazaro has been downloaded more than 58,000 times and is the library behind Observatorio Lazaro, a resource that monitors anglicism usage in the Spanish press. pylazaro can be installed via PyPI, is documented in readthedocs and can be tried through a live demo hosted on HuggingFace Spaces.

AI.tldr: The paper presents pylazaro, a Python package to automatically detect unassimilated lexical borrowings (mainly anglicisms) in Spanish text, offering multiple pre-trained sequence labeling models via a unified interface and outperforming general-purpose LLMs on this task.
AI.motivation: Linguistic fields like lexicography and corpus linguistics need reliable automatic identification of lexical borrowings, but common NLP libraries lack this functionality. Existing general-purpose LLMs perform poorly at detecting such borrowings, so there is a need for a specialized, easy-to-use tool that can handle this task accurately and consistently across different modeling frameworks.
AI.method: The authors develop pylazaro, an open-source Python package that wraps five different sequence labeling models trained with various ML libraries behind a single interface. These models are trained to detect unassimilated lexical borrowings (mostly anglicisms) in Spanish text. The package standardizes interaction with these heterogeneous models, and the authors evaluate their performance against general-purpose large language models on the same task.
AI.result: Among the five sequence labeling models in pylazaro, the best model achieves an F1 score of 0.86 for detecting unassimilated lexical borrowings in Spanish, while general-purpose LLMs achieve F1 scores below 0.40 on the same task. The package has gained substantial adoption, with more than 58,000 downloads, and serves as the backend for Observatorio Lazaro, which tracks anglicism usage in Spanish press texts. The tool is released via PyPI, fully documented on ReadTheDocs, and accessible through a HuggingFace Spaces demo.
AI.conclusion: pylazaro fills an important gap in NLP tooling for linguistics by providing a specialized, high-performing, and user-friendly package for automatic extraction of unassimilated lexical borrowings in Spanish. Its unified interface over multiple sequence labeling models, superior performance compared to general-purpose LLMs, and demonstrated community uptake (downloads and integration into Observatorio Lazaro) show that it is a practical and effective solution for researchers and practitioners interested in monitoring and analyzing lexical borrowings.

title: Forecast-Dojo: Replayable Environments for Benchmarking and Training LLM Forecasting Agents
summary: We introduce Forecast-Dojo, a replayable environment for benchmarking and training LLM forecasting agents. It combines resolved prediction-market questions with dated news, allowing agents to research an event and revisit their predictions at successive historical dates. The same tasks and tools support repeated evaluation, collection of training interactions, and feedback from recorded outcomes without waiting for new events to resolve. Forecast-Dojo contains 1,568 Polymarket events, split by time into training and evaluation periods, and 18.8M dated news articles. In an evaluation of 12 models, research tools lower Brier score for all 12. Forecasts also improve as events unfold, with the largest gains at steps where more newly dated evidence is recorded. Every model still trails historical market forecasts in both Brier score and accuracy. A belief notebook carried between dates lowers research cost but does not consistently improve forecast quality. Beyond evaluation, Forecast-Dojo provides interaction trajectories and outcome feedback for agent learning, with supervised fine-tuning as a proof of concept.

AI.tldr: Forecast-Dojo is a replayable environment for benchmarking and training LLM forecasting agents using historical prediction market questions and dated news.
AI.motivation: To systematically evaluate and improve LLM-based forecasting agents without waiting for real-world events to resolve, and to compare them against historical prediction market performance.
AI.method: Construct a replayable environment using 1,568 resolved Polymarket events split into train/eval periods plus 18.8M dated news articles; allow agents to iteratively research and update forecasts at historical dates, test research tools and a belief notebook, and perform supervised fine-tuning on collected trajectories.
AI.result: Research tools reduce Brier scores for all 12 evaluated models, and forecasts improve over time as more news becomes available, but all models still underperform historical market forecasts in Brier score and accuracy. The belief notebook reduces research cost but does not reliably improve forecast quality. Supervised fine-tuning using interaction data is demonstrated as a proof-of-concept.
AI.conclusion: Forecast-Dojo is a useful benchmark and training environment for LLM forecasting agents, enabling replayable, tool-augmented forecasting with outcome feedback. While tools help, LLM agents still lag behind prediction markets, and there is room for better methods to translate research and memory into improved forecast quality.

title: Reasoning Instructions Can Break Answer Decoding in Vision--Language Models
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) instructions can distort multiple-choice VLM evaluation when a scorer appends a reasoning cue but reads answer-label logits before the model generates any rationale. We call this CoT-prefix scoring. On ScienceQA, Qwen2.5-VL-7B drops from 80.76% to 45.48%, and across five option-content permutations 93.54% of CoT-prefix predictions select the first slot. Condition-matched linear probes recover 78.94% from the same hidden states, while free generation restores 75.24%, showing that the answer often survives the prefix and the immediate readout fails. Vocabulary and layer diagnostics explain the mismatch: probability mass moves toward continuation tokens, while answer information remains linearly accessible in late layers. The effect recurs with varying severity across datasets and models, though not universally. These results show that CoT-prefix scoring can confound model knowledge with an evaluation-interface mismatch and should be avoided unless the requested and scored output events are aligned.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a common way of evaluating vision-language models with chain-of-thought prompts—reading multiple-choice answer logits immediately after adding a reasoning prefix—can drastically and misleadingly lower measured accuracy, because the model’s internal answer remains intact but the scoring interface is misaligned with how the model distributes probability mass during reasoning.
AI.motivation: Researchers often use chain-of-thought (CoT) prompts to elicit reasoning from large models and then score multiple-choice performance by inspecting answer-label logits at the first token after the prompt. The authors observed that this practice (“CoT-prefix scoring”) can yield surprisingly poor scores and suspicious patterns (e.g., over-selecting a particular option position). They aim to understand whether these drops reflect real loss of model knowledge or an artifact of how the model is queried and scored, and to diagnose what happens inside the model’s representations when a CoT prefix is added.
AI.method: The authors evaluate vision-language models (notably Qwen2.5-VL-7B) on multiple-choice benchmarks like ScienceQA under different scoring setups. They compare standard direct-answer scoring to CoT-prefix scoring, and also test multiple permutations of answer option ordering to detect positional biases (e.g., over-predicting the first option). They then apply condition-matched linear probes to the hidden states after the CoT prefix to see if answer information is still linearly recoverable, and compare this to free-text generation where the model is allowed to output a full answer. Additionally, they perform vocabulary- and layer-level diagnostics to track how probability mass shifts across tokens and layers when a CoT prefix is added, identifying where answer information is stored versus where the output distribution becomes biased toward continuation tokens.
AI.result: With CoT-prefix scoring on ScienceQA, Qwen2.5-VL-7B’s accuracy plummets from about 80.76% (direct scoring) to 45.48%. Across five permutations of answer option content and positions, 93.54% of CoT-prefix predictions choose the first option slot, indicating a strong positional artifact rather than genuine reasoning. However, linear probes trained on the same hidden states can recover 78.94% accuracy, and letting the model freely generate an answer yields 75.24%, implying that the correct answer is still embedded in the representation even though the immediate logits are misleading. Diagnostic analyses show that after a CoT prefix, probability mass shifts toward generic continuation tokens (e.g., tokens that continue a rationale) while answer-relevant information remains linearly decodable in late layers. Similar, though variably strong, effects appear across other datasets and models, but not in every case.
AI.conclusion: The work concludes that CoT-prefix scoring can severely distort multiple-choice evaluation of vision-language models by conflating a model’s internal knowledge with artifacts of how outputs are read from the network. The sharp performance drops and positional biases under CoT-prefix scoring do not necessarily mean the model has lost or failed to compute the correct answer; instead, they often result from an evaluation-interface mismatch, where the scoring position and requested output type (rationale continuation vs. discrete option label) are misaligned. Because answer information often remains accessible in hidden states and through free generation, the authors argue that CoT-prefix scoring should be avoided unless the scored token exactly corresponds to the event being evaluated, and that future evaluations must carefully align prompting, decoding, and scoring to avoid underestimating model capabilities.

title: Control the Harness, Control the Cost: Routing and Governing AI Coding Agents in the Enterprise
summary: Harnesses, the products that run AI coding agents, are multiplying, and enterprises are rolling them out to their employees: what started as pilots with a few hundred seats is scaling to tens of thousands. Most enterprises do not build these harnesses but buy them from large vendors, such as Anthropic's Claude Code or OpenAI's Codex. A harness decides which model answers, what the model reads, how the prompt cache is used and which subagents run, so it picks the rate on the price sheet and sets the volume bought at it. Enterprises that keep a proprietary or untuned harness at its defaults inherit these choices and their bill. We build a fast, customisable router in which Jev, a classifier with calibrated probabilities, labels every prompt against a bring-your-own taxonomy of agentic requests. Because one user turn is many requests over a prompt cache that belongs to one model, the router moves work only where no running conversation has to rebuild its cache: at session start, in side lanes and at subagent launch. From the price sheet we derive when a mid-task switch pays back, and a crossover: on long tool-heavy sessions the highest-priced model costs less than the next tier, as repricing about 10,000 real sessions from public datasets confirms. In an emulated enterprise of 10,000 seats with user behaviour taken from these datasets, the router recovers 14 to 21% of model spend at Anthropic's list prices of 21 September 2026, \$3.3M to \$5.0M a year. The paper also maps the risks across twenty harnesses, prices the dependence on one vendor's models, and proposes a control plane that enterprises can run from within, starting now, with a ladder for deciding later whether to own the harness.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a cost-optimizing, customizable routing system for AI coding agent harnesses that uses a calibrated classifier to direct requests across models and agents, reducing enterprise LLM spend by 14–21% while managing vendor risk.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI coding harnesses are rapidly scaling from small pilots to tens of thousands of seats, mostly using vendor defaults from large providers. These default configurations implicitly fix model choice, caching behavior, and subagent orchestration, which together determine both performance and cost. Enterprises that simply inherit these default harness choices risk substantial, opaque, and potentially suboptimal model spending as usage scales, and they are exposed to concentration risk on a single vendor. There is a need for a principled, controllable way to route work across models and agents that respects conversation state and caching, optimizes cost–performance tradeoffs, and reduces vendor lock-in, all while being deployable within existing enterprise environments.
AI.method: The authors design a fast, customizable router that sits inside the AI coding harness. At its core is Jev, a classifier that outputs calibrated probabilities over a user-defined taxonomy of agentic request types. This taxonomy encodes which kinds of requests should go to which models, tools, or subagents. Because conversations rely heavily on model-specific prompt caches, the router is constrained to re-route only at points where cache rebuilding is not prohibitive: at session start, in side lanes, and when launching subagents. The paper analytically derives conditions from model price sheets to determine when mid-task switching is economically worthwhile and identifies a crossover where more expensive models become cheaper over long, tool-heavy sessions. They then reprice around 10,000 real sessions from public datasets using these rules. Finally, they construct an emulated 10,000-seat enterprise with behavior sampled from these datasets to simulate annual costs under different routing strategies and vendors.
AI.result: The repricing of roughly 10,000 real coding sessions shows that, due to caching and tool-use dynamics, the highest-priced model can become cheaper than the next tier for long, tool-heavy sessions—a non-intuitive crossover effect. In the enterprise-scale simulation with 10,000 seats and usage patterns grounded in public datasets, their router recovers between 14% and 21% of model spend when priced against Anthropic’s public list rates as of 21 September 2026, corresponding to an annual savings of approximately $3.3–$5.0 million. Additionally, the paper provides a comparative risk map over twenty existing harnesses and quantifies exposure to single-vendor dependence under current procurement patterns.
AI.conclusion: A custom, classifier-driven router embedded in AI coding harnesses can significantly reduce enterprise LLM costs while preserving or improving performance, primarily by exploiting structure in request types, cache reuse, and tool-heavy workflows. The findings imply that relying on default vendor harnesses leaves substantial money on the table and fails to manage concentration risk. The authors advocate that enterprises deploy an internal control plane now—capable of orchestrating models, caches, and subagents according to their own taxonomies and risk policies—and use it as a stepping stone toward potentially owning the entire harness stack in the future.

title: Grammatical "grandmother neurons" are rare in LLMs
summary: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) encode linguistic structures remains a fundamental challenge in interpretability research. While diagnostic classifiers (or "probes") are widely used for this task, they face significant methodological criticism: training auxiliary classifiers introduces capacity confounds and calibration issues, often making it difficult to distinguish the model's intrinsic representations from the probe's ability to learn the task. To address these limitations, we introduce a probe-free framework for localizing linguistic selectivity at the individual neuron level. Leveraging the controlled contrasts of linguistic minimal pairs, we propose a Neuron Separability Index (NSI), a metric that directly quantifies how reliably single neurons differentiate grammatical from ungrammatical constructions without parameter updates. Applying NSI across 68 linguistic paradigms and seven checkpoints reveals three main patterns: 1) raw separability reaches near-peak levels earlier for morphological and syntactic distinctions than for syntax-semantics interface and conceptual distinctions. 2) after permutation normalization, single-unit selectivity is sparse, weak, and narrowly tuned: only a small fraction of units are sensitive to an average paradigm, and strongly selective "grandmother neurons" are rare. 3) whole-vector linear separability, single-neuron selectivity, and behavioral competence are largely dissociated, and targeted ablations further separate activation selectivity from causal reliance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a probe-free method to measure how individual neurons in LLMs distinguish grammatical from ungrammatical sentences, finding that such selectivity is sparse, weak, and only loosely related to overall model behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing interpretability work on large language models heavily relies on diagnostic probes (auxiliary classifiers) to test whether model representations encode linguistic structure. However, probes introduce confounds: they can learn the task themselves, making it unclear whether good performance reflects information already present in the model or the probe’s own capacity and calibration. This makes it hard to precisely localize and quantify how linguistic information is encoded, especially at the single-neuron level. The authors aim to develop a method that avoids training extra classifiers and thus more directly reflects the model’s intrinsic representations of linguistic distinctions.
AI.method: The authors propose a probe-free framework based on linguistic minimal pairs (controlled pairs of grammatical vs. ungrammatical sentences that differ in a specific property). They define a Neuron Separability Index (NSI) that measures, for each neuron, how reliably its raw activations distinguish grammatical from ungrammatical items across many such minimal pairs. NSI is computed without updating model parameters. They apply this metric across 68 distinct linguistic paradigms (covering morphology, syntax, syntax-semantics interface, and conceptual distinctions) and seven model checkpoints. They also perform permutation normalization to control for chance levels, examine sparsity and strength of selectivity, compare NSI to whole-vector linear separability and to model behavioral performance, and conduct targeted ablations of neurons to test causal roles versus mere selectivity.
AI.result: Empirically, they find: (1) Raw NSI-based separability for individual neurons emerges earlier in training and reaches close to peak values sooner for morphological and syntactic distinctions than for syntax-semantics interface and conceptual distinctions. (2) After permutation-based normalization, single-neuron selectivity appears sparse and weak: only a small subset of neurons respond selectively to any given paradigm, and very strongly selective “grandmother neurons” are uncommon. Neuron tuning tends to be narrow rather than broad. (3) There is a substantial dissociation between three things: (a) linear separability at the full activation-vector level, (b) single-neuron NSI selectivity, and (c) the model’s actual behavioral competence on linguistic tasks. Targeted neuron ablations further show that neurons with high selectivity are not necessarily causally relied upon for the corresponding behaviors, sharpening the distinction between correlation in activations and causal importance.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that linguistic information in LLMs is encoded in a distributed and relatively weakly selective manner at the single-neuron level, challenging the idea of prevalent, highly specialized “grandmother neurons” for particular linguistic phenomena. Their probe-free NSI metric offers a more direct way to localize neuron-level selectivity without the confounds of diagnostic classifiers, but it also reveals that such selectivity is only loosely coupled to both overall representational separability and behavioral performance. This underscores a gap between interpretability via activation patterns and true causal understanding of how LLMs implement linguistic competence, and suggests that future work should more carefully distinguish representational selectivity from causal reliance while reducing dependence on trained probes.

title: Where LLM Graders Succeed and Break: Evidence from Two Computer-Science Exams
summary: One long-form exam in a large course costs hundreds of grader-hours, and qualified graders are scarce; LLM graders are a tempting alternative. To show its pitfalls we grade a practical Computer Vision exam ($570$ dual-graded students) under $171$ configurations spanning closed and open-weights models; the best reaches mean absolute error $1.64/35$, below the $2.61/35$ two human graders achieve against each other. The catch is the prompt: a short ''strict grader'' preamble drives $14$ of $17$ open-weights models out of the graded band ($\text{MAE} \ge 8$), three stopping grading altogether. The damage traces to the preamble's two credit-withholding sentences, not to tone or model scale; one of them, ''never give partial credit'', alone makes two of three probed models stop grading. The closed flagships of three vendors shift calibration under it but stay in the band. In $162$ further configurations on a second, independent Machine Learning exam from another course ($1{,}038$ dual-graded students), the preamble worsens ten models, moving three out of the band into collapse and one into refusal, yet improves seven whose neutral prompts over-mark: the vulnerability replicates, but its direction is exam-specific. Light LoRA fine-tuning repairs it: one adapter on the two exams' pooled $\sim 3{,}900$ graded examples brings five small open models to parity or better with a human grader in agreement with the grader pair, and sensitivity to the three harsh personas nearly vanishes ($\le 0.32$ MAE). We release the anonymised dataset, full ablation grid, and grading, fine-tuning and analysis pipelines.

AI.tldr: Study evaluates LLMs as exam graders versus humans and finds they can be highly accurate but are very sensitive to prompt wording, causing grading collapse; light fine-tuning stabilizes performance and matches/exceeds human agreement.
AI.motivation: Manual grading of large-course exams is costly in grader hours and good graders are scarce. LLMs are an appealing scalable alternative, but their reliability, robustness to prompt variations, and comparability to human graders are unclear, especially in realistic, high-stakes exam settings.
AI.method: The authors grade a practical Computer Vision exam with 570 dual-graded students using 171 configurations of LLM-based graders, spanning closed- and open-weights models. They compare model grades to human grades, measure mean absolute error (MAE), and systematically vary prompts, especially a harsh "strict grader" preamble with credit-withholding instructions. They then replicate the study on a second Machine Learning exam (1,038 dual-graded students) with 162 configurations, and explore light LoRA fine-tuning on ~3,900 graded examples to see if it improves robustness and accuracy of small open models.
AI.result: Best LLM configuration achieves MAE 1.64/35 versus 2.61/35 for human-human disagreement, outperforming an individual human in agreement with the grader pair. However, a short strict-grader preamble pushes 14/17 open models outside an acceptable "graded band" (MAE ≥ 8), with some models ceasing to grade at all. The main culprit is two credit-withholding sentences: one sentence, "never give partial credit," alone causes two of three probed models to stop grading. Closed flagship models remain within the band but shift calibration. On the second exam, the strict preamble again harms many models (and causes collapses/refusals), though for some over-lenient configurations it improves calibration. LoRA fine-tuning on the pooled data restores and stabilizes performance: an adapter enables five small open models to reach or exceed human-level MAE, and their sensitivity to strict personas drops to ≤ 0.32 MAE.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can match or surpass human graders in accuracy on technical exams, but are alarmingly brittle to seemingly minor prompt changes, especially harsh or credit-withholding instructions that can trigger grading collapse or refusal. This vulnerability is real, replicable, and exam-dependent. Light supervised adaptation (LoRA fine-tuning) on a modest set of graded examples can both raise accuracy and largely eliminate sensitivity to harsh grading personas, yielding small open models with robust, human-level grading performance. The authors provide data and pipelines to facilitate further research and safer deployment of LLM-based grading systems.

title: ArGuard Shared Task: Harmful Content Detection in Arabic Memes and LLM Prompts
summary: ArGuard is a shared task on harmful content detection in Arabic memes and LLM prompts. It includes two tracks: Track A focuses on multimodal hate detection in Arabic memes, while Track B addresses harmful prompt detection for Arabic LLM safety evaluation. In total, 58 teams registered, 35 participated in the final evaluation, and 27 submitted system-description papers. Participating teams explored models such as AraBERT, Jais, and Qwen3-VL. The best systems achieved macro-F1 scores of 0.823 on A1, 0.419 on A2, 0.984 on B1, and 0.790 on B2. Fine-grained meme classification in A2 was the most challenging setting, partly due to sparse labels and train-test distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: ArGuard is a shared task for detecting harmful content in Arabic memes and LLM prompts, with two tracks evaluating multimodal hate detection and harmful prompt identification, where teams used various Arabic and multimodal models and achieved strong results, especially on binary tasks, while fine-grained meme classification remained challenging.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to advance safety and moderation tools for Arabic online content, an under-resourced area compared to English, by organizing a shared task that benchmarks methods for detecting harmful content in both images (memes) and language (LLM prompts).
AI.method: The organizers designed two tracks: Track A for multimodal hate detection in Arabic memes with sub-tasks including coarse (A1) and fine-grained (A2) classification, and Track B for harmful prompt detection for Arabic LLM safety with sub-tasks B1 and B2. They released datasets, defined evaluation metrics (macro-F1), and invited participating teams to build systems using models like AraBERT, Jais, and Qwen3-VL, then evaluated these systems on held-out test sets.
AI.result: 58 teams registered, 35 reached the final evaluation, and 27 submitted system papers. The top systems obtained macro-F1 scores of 0.823 on A1 (coarse meme hate detection), 0.419 on A2 (fine-grained meme classification), 0.984 on B1, and 0.790 on B2 (harmful prompt detection tasks), showing high performance on binary or simpler tasks and lower performance on more granular meme labeling.
AI.conclusion: The shared task shows that existing Arabic and multimodal models can perform well for coarse harmful-content detection in Arabic memes and LLM prompts, but fine-grained meme classification remains difficult, likely due to sparse labels and distribution shifts, highlighting the need for better data and models for nuanced multimodal harm detection in Arabic.

title: Parts-of-Speech as Emergent Categories in SAE Latent Space
summary: Sparse AutoEncoders (SAEs) offer a promising way to inspect language model representations, but it is still unclear what kind of linguistic structure their latents expose. We use part-of-speech (PoS) categories as a controlled test case to study whether morpho-syntactic information is encoded by individual latents or by structured groups of features. We find that PoS distinctions are highly recoverable from SAE activations, but do not align with one-to-one latent / category mappings. This recoverability is not reducible to lexical memorisation, and Open and Closed PoS classes differ substantially. Categories are supported by compact groups of sparse latents, with substantial variation across tags. These groups remain stable on held-out data, while also showing overlap between related categories. Our results show that SAEs localise morpho-syntactic information in a distributed and category-dependent form rather than through atomic grammatical features.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates what kind of morpho-syntactic (part-of-speech) structure is captured by Sparse AutoEncoder (SAE) latents in language models, finding that PoS information is recoverable but represented by small distributed groups of latents rather than single, atomic features.
AI.motivation: While SAEs are a promising interpretability tool for language models, it is unclear whether their latent features correspond neatly to linguistic concepts like part-of-speech categories or whether such information is distributed. The authors aim to use PoS as a controlled testbed to understand how morpho-syntactic information is encoded in SAE representations and whether individual latents align with human-interpretable grammatical categories.
AI.method: Train or use Sparse AutoEncoders on language model internal activations, then analyze the resulting sparse latent representations with respect to part-of-speech labels. Measure how well PoS categories can be predicted from SAE activations, inspect whether individual latents align with single PoS tags, test for the role of lexical memorization, compare open vs closed PoS classes, and study the structure, size, stability, and overlap of latent groups supporting each PoS category, including evaluation on held-out data.
AI.result: PoS categories are highly recoverable from SAE activations, but there is no simple one-to-one mapping between single latents and individual PoS tags. The information is not merely lexical memorization, and open vs closed PoS classes behave differently. Instead, each PoS category is supported by compact but distributed groups of sparse latents, with substantial variation in how many and which latents support different tags. These groups generalize to held-out data and exhibit overlaps, particularly between related PoS categories.
AI.conclusion: Sparse AutoEncoders do localize morpho-syntactic information, but not as atomic, single-feature representations of grammatical categories. Instead, PoS information is encoded in compact, distributed, and partially overlapping sets of latents, whose structure depends on the specific category. This challenges overly simplistic interpretations of SAE features as directly corresponding to discrete linguistic units, suggesting that SAE-based interpretability must account for distributed and category-dependent structure in the latent space.

title: From Policy Documents to Structured Survey Responses: Evaluating Large Language Models for Policy Monitoring
comment: Accepted as a full paper to FLINS-ISKE 2026
summary: Science, technology, and innovation policies are crucial for competitiveness, yet their diversity and scale make them difficult to map and monitor consistently. Existing approaches rely heavily on manual survey efforts, which are costly and challenging to scale across countries. Large language models (LLMs) enable new possibilities for extracting and structuring information from long and unstructured policy documents. This paper presents an application of LLMs as "AI respondents" for generating structured survey responses from policy texts. We develop a data extraction pipeline based on long-context in-context learning to map information from public web sources into predefined survey categories, including policy instruments, target groups, and thematic areas. The pipeline integrates a validation step using a secondary LLM to assess relevance and evidence, alongside comparisons with human-provided responses. Using a multi-country dataset, we evaluate the alignment between LLM-generated and human-generated outputs through overlap measures and cross-validation. Results show that LLMs achieve high agreement for structured indicators (84-95%), while differences remain in free-text fields, where models tend to provide more detailed procedural descriptions. These findings highlight the potential of hybrid human-AI workflows for policy monitoring, improving both efficiency and scalability while maintaining the need for human validation and contextual interpretation.

AI.tldr: The paper uses large language models to automatically convert unstructured policy documents into structured survey-style data, showing high agreement with human coders for many indicators and proposing a hybrid human-AI workflow for scalable policy monitoring.
AI.motivation: Science, technology, and innovation policies are numerous, heterogeneous, and difficult to track consistently across countries. Current mapping approaches rely on manual surveys and expert coding, which are expensive, slow, and hard to scale internationally. With the emergence of LLMs capable of handling long and unstructured texts, there is an opportunity to automate parts of this mapping process while preserving data quality.
AI.method: The authors design an LLM-based data extraction pipeline that treats models as “AI respondents” to a predefined policy survey. Using long-context in-context learning, the primary LLM reads policy documents from public web sources and outputs structured responses in predefined categories (policy instruments, target groups, thematic focus). A secondary LLM validates the primary outputs by checking relevance and textual evidence. The authors compare LLM-generated responses with human-coded survey data across multiple countries, evaluate overlap and agreement for structured indicators, and analyze discrepancies, particularly in free-text responses.
AI.result: Across a multi-country dataset, LLM-generated structured indicators (such as classification of instruments, target groups, and themes) show high agreement with human coders, in the range of 84–95% depending on the category and metric used. However, in free-text fields, LLMs tend to generate more detailed procedural descriptions than humans, leading to greater divergence and stylistic differences, even when the underlying content is similar.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can effectively act as AI respondents to policy surveys, substantially automating the extraction and structuring of information from complex policy documents. While structured indicators align closely with human-coded data, free-text outputs still require careful human review. The authors propose hybrid human-AI workflows in which LLMs handle large-scale extraction and humans focus on validation, interpretation, and context-sensitive judgments, thereby improving efficiency and scalability without removing the need for expert oversight.

title: BanglaTurn: A Benchmark and Whisper-Based Model for End-of-Turn Detection in Bangla Speech
summary: This paper presents BanglaTurn, a corpus for end-of-turn detection in Bangla conversational speech, and a model trained on it. The corpus holds 35,374 samples of 3 to 15 s of podcast speech, labelled for turn state by combining speaker diarization with an LLM pass, with every label then checked by a human annotator. The model pairs a Whisper encoder with task-specific classification heads. On a class-balanced test set drawn from a held-out podcast, it reaches 84.33% accuracy (95% CI 80.3 to 88.1) against 69.28% for the Smart-Turn v3 baseline, and lowers the false negative rate from 51.57% to 7.55% at the cost of a higher false positive rate. We report what encoder layer fine-tuning, multi-scale pooling and INT8 quantization each contribute, and latency stays within 165 to 191 ms end to end on CPU.

AI.tldr: Introduces BanglaTurn, a new corpus and Whisper-based model for end-of-turn detection in Bangla conversational speech, achieving strong accuracy and low latency on CPU.
AI.motivation: End-of-turn detection is crucial for conversational systems but Bangla is low-resource and lacks dedicated corpora and models, especially ones suitable for real-time deployment. The paper aims to fill this gap with a labeled dataset and an efficient, accurate model.
AI.method: They construct a 35k-sample Bangla conversational speech corpus (3–15 s podcast clips), label turn states via speaker diarization plus an LLM pass followed by human verification, then train a model that uses a Whisper encoder with task-specific classification heads. They systematically study encoder layer fine-tuning, multi-scale pooling, and INT8 quantization, measuring accuracy, error types, and latency on CPU.
AI.result: On a class-balanced test set from a held-out podcast, their model achieves 84.33% accuracy (95% CI: 80.3–88.1), clearly outperforming the Smart-Turn v3 baseline at 69.28%. It reduces the false negative rate from 51.57% to 7.55% (at the cost of increased false positives) and maintains end-to-end CPU latency between 165 and 191 ms.
AI.conclusion: BanglaTurn provides a high-quality resource for Bangla end-of-turn detection, and the proposed Whisper-based architecture offers a substantial accuracy and recall improvement over existing baselines while remaining suitable for real-time CPU deployment. The ablations on fine-tuning depth, pooling, and quantization clarify how to balance performance and efficiency.

title: Likelihood Ranking doesn't Scale Like Prompting in LLMs
summary: LLM evaluation is commonly performed either by prompting models to produce answers or by scoring candidate outputs with likelihood-based metrics. In multiple-choice QA, however, standard likelihood-based scoring is still conditioned on the question and answer set, and can therefore leverage the same task-conditioned answer-selection interface used in prompting. We study a complementary protocol based on likelihood ranking of declarative statements constructed from the same question--answer pairs. Across 95 decoder-only models, ranging from 0.1B to 104B parameters, and 10 MCQA datasets, we find a systematic divergence between declarative-statement likelihood ranking and prompted answering. Statement-likelihood accuracy remains comparatively stable across scale, whereas prompted answering improves sharply with scale and instruction-tuning. These results suggest that likelihood preferences over controlled declarative alternatives and task-conditioned answer selection probe distinct aspects of model behavior, and should not be treated as interchangeable.

AI.tldr: They compare two ways of evaluating LLMs on multiple-choice QA—prompted answering vs. likelihood over declarative statements—and show these behave very differently across model scales.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluations in MCQA often assume that likelihood-based scoring and prompting-based answering are roughly equivalent ways to measure model ability. However, it is unclear whether these two interfaces actually probe the same underlying capabilities, especially as models scale and undergo instruction tuning.
AI.method: They construct declarative statements from MCQA question–answer pairs and evaluate models by ranking these statements using likelihood, comparing this to standard prompted answering where models pick options using the task-conditioned interface. They run systematic experiments across 95 decoder-only models (0.1B–104B parameters) and 10 multiple-choice QA datasets, and analyze how performance under each protocol changes with model scale and instruction tuning.
AI.result: They observe a systematic divergence: accuracy based on statement likelihood rankings remains relatively flat as model size increases, whereas prompted answer accuracy improves markedly with larger and instruction-tuned models. This indicates that the two evaluation protocols yield different scaling behaviors and performance profiles.
AI.conclusion: Likelihood over controlled declarative alternatives and task-conditioned answer selection are not interchangeable evaluation methods. They probe different aspects of model behavior, so relying on only one can give a misleading picture of model capabilities in multiple-choice QA. Evaluations should consider both or be explicit about which behavior they are measuring.

title: Baseline Shape Decides the Verdict: A Controlled Re-Examination of Ternary Language Models at 60K Parameters
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure. Code and run logs: https://github.com/veldanda/ByteLM (tag p1-v1). Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22937824
summary: Ternary (1.58-bit) weights are attractive for microcontroller-class language models, but the sub-1M-parameter regime rests mainly on isolated, single-seed comparisons. One prominent example reports that a routed ternary block (convolution, diagonal SSM and sparse attention mixed by a per-token router) beats a parameter-matched full-precision transformer by 22% at 60K parameters, attributing this to inductive bias. We re-run it under one fixed recipe, three seeds per cell, 98 byte-level runs on one laptop. (i) Baseline shape dominates: at a 16M-byte budget, param-matched transformers span 22.6% in validation loss purely by depth/width choice - far more than any architecture effect we measure there - and the best-shaped transformer ties the routed model, so the published margin is at least partly a baseline-shape effect; the ordering of shapes reverses with budget, so no single fixed shape can be trusted. (ii) At 130M bytes the routed model does win, by 22.2-24.0% over the three transformer shapes we evaluate there - but a plain gated diagonal-SSM block beats it by a further 9.1%, and the routed model's own router puts most of its weight on its recurrent pathway, so the gain does not require routing. (iii) The ternary penalty differs by architecture at the larger budget (+5.3% best transformer vs. +19.5% routed, +28.1% gated SSM), but we cannot attribute that to architecture alone: our transformers keep learned positional embeddings in full precision, 11-22% of their parameters, so they are less quantized than the models they are compared with. (iv) A 90/10 full-precision-then-ternary schedule beats all-ternary training, but only at a stage-2 learning rate about 10x the pretraining peak; at a conventional fine-tuning rate it looks 15.3% worse, reversing the conclusion. The from-scratch baseline was not itself learning-rate tuned, which bounds (iii) and (iv). Code and run logs released.

AI.tldr: The paper reevaluates claims that ternary-weight routed models outperform full-precision transformers in tiny language models, finding that prior gains largely come from baseline shape and training recipe choices rather than inherent architectural advantages.
AI.motivation: Ternary (1.58-bit) weights are appealing for resource-limited microcontrollers, where model size and compute are highly constrained. Prior work claimed a routed ternary architecture significantly outperforms full-precision transformers at very small scales, attributing the margin to inductive bias. However, these claims relied on single-seed, non-systematic comparisons and potentially suboptimal transformer baselines. The authors aim to rigorously test whether the architectural advantage is real when controlling for confounders like model shape, training setup, and quantization schedule.
AI.method: The authors re-run the comparison between routed ternary models and full-precision transformers under a single, fixed experimental recipe. They perform a broad sweep over model shapes (depth/width tradeoffs) at different byte/parameter budgets, and run three random seeds per configuration. They conduct 98 byte-level language modeling runs on a single laptop, comparing routed ternary blocks, plain transformers, and gated diagonal-SSM blocks. They also examine the effect of ternary quantization penalties across architectures and study training schedules, including all-ternary training vs a 90%-full-precision-then-ternary schedule with different stage-2 learning rates.
AI.result: (i) At a 16M-byte budget, transformers with matched parameter counts vary by 22.6% in validation loss purely due to depth/width choices, exceeding any measured architectural gains; the best-shaped transformer matches the routed model, indicating the previously reported 22% gain was largely a baseline-shape artifact, and model shape rankings flip with budget. (ii) At 130M bytes, the routed model outperforms three transformer shapes by ~22-24%, but a simple gated diagonal-SSM block surpasses the routed model by another 9.1%, and the router mostly selects the recurrent pathway, showing routing is not the source of the gain. (iii) Ternary quantization hurts different architectures unequally at the larger budget (+5.3% loss for the best transformer vs +19.5% for routed and +28.1% for gated SSM), but transformers retain full-precision positional embeddings (11-22% of parameters), so they are less quantized and not directly comparable. (iv) A 90/10 full-precision-to-ternary schedule only improves over all-ternary training when the second-stage learning rate is ~10x the pretraining peak; at standard fine-tuning rates it performs 15.3% worse. The original from-scratch baseline was not tuned for learning rate, limiting conclusions about quantization and schedules.
AI.conclusion: Apparent large advantages of routed ternary architectures over full-precision transformers in tiny language models mostly stem from baseline and training configuration choices (especially model shape and learning rate), not from inherent inductive biases of routing or architecture. When baselines are shape- and recipe-tuned and multiple seeds are used, routed models no longer clearly dominate; in some regimes they are matched by well-shaped transformers or outperformed by simpler gated diagonal-SSM blocks. Quantization effects and mixed-precision setups further complicate direct comparisons. The paper underscores the need for rigorous, multi-seed, shape- and hyperparameter-tuned baselines before attributing performance gains to novel architectures, particularly in extreme compression settings like microcontroller-scale LMs.

title: Large Language Models for Programming: Actually Fixing or Reimplementing Incorrect Code?
summary: Recent studies have shown that Large Language Models can effectively solve problems and fix bugs in diverse programming environments, including competitive programming. Existing approaches primarily evaluate LLM performance in problem solving or bug fixing independently, but do not explore the relationship between these two capabilities. This work focuses on determining how much the LLM deviates from a buggy solution to fix the bug compared to a human-written patch, and if there is a bias towards generating entirely new solutions. We construct a dataset with all the submissions ($\sim$ 3000) from a couple of users from Codeforces, and we match each buggy submission with its corresponding human fix. By using the similarity between the buggy solution and the human fix as a baseline, we evaluate the quality of LLM-generated bug fixes on 3 OpenAI GPT models (gpt-5-nano, gpt-5-mini, gpt-5.1). We check if the generated solutions solve the problem by using the Codeforces-R1 dataset, an openly available dataset that has tests generated with the DeepSeek-R1 model. Our findings suggest that LLMs tend to modify more lines than necessary compared to human fixes and, in some cases, generate entirely new solutions. We also observe that LLMs solve more problems correctly when allowed to generate solutions from scratch rather than patch buggy submissions, even when those submissions are close to the human patch. This has important implications for the design of AI-assisted programming tools, particularly in supporting user debugging processes and promoting incremental problem-solving strategies rather than solution replacement.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how much LLMs change buggy competitive-programming submissions when fixing them, and compares this to minimal human patches.
AI.motivation: Existing work evaluates LLMs on solving problems or fixing bugs separately, without studying how similar LLM patches are to human patches or whether models prefer rewriting code from scratch. Understanding this matters for designing realistic debugging assistants that cooperate with human code instead of replacing it.
AI.method: The authors collect ~3000 submissions from a few Codeforces users and pair each buggy submission with its corresponding human fix. They use the similarity between the buggy code and the human patch as a baseline, then prompt three GPT models (gpt-5-nano, gpt-5-mini, gpt-5.1) to fix the same buggy submissions. They measure how much the models modify compared to humans and whether the resulting code passes tests from the Codeforces-R1 dataset (with DeepSeek-R1–generated test cases).
AI.result: LLMs generally modify more lines than humans do when fixing bugs and sometimes replace the original with completely new solutions. They achieve higher success rates when asked to solve problems from scratch than when asked to patch buggy submissions, even if those submissions are already close to the human fix.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs behave more like solution rewriters than minimal patch generators in this setting. For AI-assisted programming tools, this suggests that designs should account for a tendency toward replacement rather than incremental editing and should explicitly support debugging workflows that favor minimal, human-aligned changes.

title: Controlling Backchannels in Streamable Full-duplex Models
summary: Backchannels, brief acknowledgements like "uh-huh" produced while the other party may still be talking, are central to natural conversation, but full-duplex spoken dialogue models rarely model them explicitly. We introduce a lightweight backchannel head that predicts, from a full-duplex model's own hidden states, when a backchannel should begin. Once this probability crosses a tunable threshold, a backchannel is force-decoded. Attached to both a 7B (PersonaPlex) and a 1B (F-Actor) model, it generalizes across scale. Probing confirms the hidden states anticipate real human timing, and generation evaluation shows more frequent, better-timed backchannels. Human raters judge the resulting backchannels on par with real ones.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a lightweight add-on component that enables full-duplex dialogue models to produce human-like backchannels (e.g., “uh-huh”) at appropriate times.
AI.motivation: Existing full-duplex spoken dialogue models generally do not explicitly model backchannels, even though backchannels are essential for natural, responsive conversations. The authors aim to improve the naturalness and interactivity of full-duplex systems by adding a mechanism that can learn and trigger human-like backchannel timing without redesigning the whole model.
AI.method: They design a small “backchannel head” that reads the hidden states of an existing full-duplex dialogue model and outputs a probability over time that a backchannel should begin. When this probability exceeds a tunable threshold, the system force-decodes a backchannel phrase. The head is attached to two different base models (a 7B PersonaPlex and a 1B F-Actor) to test scalability. Probing analyses are used to verify that the hidden states already encode information predictive of human backchannel timing.
AI.result: The backchannel head successfully generalizes across model sizes (1B and 7B). Probing shows that the base models’ hidden states contain timing cues correlated with human backchannel behavior. In generation experiments, systems with the backchannel head produce more frequent and better-timed backchannels than baselines. Human evaluators rate these generated backchannels as comparable in quality to real human backchannels.
AI.conclusion: A simple, lightweight backchannel head can effectively leverage existing hidden representations in full-duplex dialogue models to produce human-like, well-timed backchannels, improving conversational naturalness without major architectural changes. The approach is scalable across model sizes and yields backchannel behavior that human raters consider as good as real human examples.

title: Rufus-Air: An Open LLM Post-Training Recipe
comment: 47 pages, 9 figures, 20 tables. Authors are listed alphabetically by surname; all contributed while at Amazon. The two authors named Zixuan Zhang are different people
summary: Rufus-Air is an open and reproducible post-training recipe on GLM-4.5-Air-Base (106B-A12B), organized as a serial pipeline of eight stages: SFT, Reasoning RL, Coding RL, Instruction-Following RL, General Agent, Coding Agent, Search Agent, and RLHF. We document the data, reward design, infrastructure, stage order, and stagewise results needed to reproduce the recipe. Stages progress from basic to advanced capabilities and from hard, verifiable rewards to softer judge-based signals. Training builds on open-source components and public data, much of it used as released, without new human annotation or an in-house distillation teacher. Our main findings are that (i) diverse, high-quality SFT establishes a strong capability floor; (ii) difficulty filtering keeps RL prompts within a productive learning range; (iii) reward reliability provides a practical principle for ordering stages; and (iv) infrastructure and engineering choices are part of the recipe, not just an implementation detail. Rufus-Air improves over the official GLM-4.5-Air post-trained release and is competitive with similarly sized open models.

AI.tldr: Rufus-Air is a fully documented, reproducible post-training pipeline that turns GLM-4.5-Air-Base into a stronger, competitive model via eight structured SFT and RL/agent stages.
AI.motivation: Open, reproducible recipes for turning a strong base LLM into a high-performance assistant are scarce; many rely on private data, opaque reward models, or undisclosed engineering tricks. The authors aim to show that with only public data, open-source components, and careful pipeline design, one can systematically improve a large base model and match competitive open releases, while also clarifying which design choices actually matter.
AI.method: Starting from GLM-4.5-Air-Base (106B-A12B), the authors apply an eight-stage serial pipeline: (1) Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on diverse, high-quality public instruction and reasoning data to establish a strong baseline; (2) Reasoning RL using verifiable, hard rewards on reasoning-heavy tasks; (3) Coding RL with programmatic correctness rewards; (4) Instruction-Following RL to refine adherence to user instructions; (5) General Agent training to improve multi-step tool-use and task decomposition; (6) Coding Agent training for code-related tool use and workflows; (7) Search Agent training to integrate web/search capabilities; and (8) RLHF using judge-based rewards. They emphasize difficulty filtering for RL prompts, reward design, stage ordering guided by reward reliability, and detailed documentation of infra and engineering settings.
AI.result: The Rufus-Air model outperforms the official GLM-4.5-Air post-trained release and achieves performance on par with other open models of similar size. Stage-wise evaluations show that strong SFT substantially lifts base capability, RL on properly filtered tasks gives further gains, and later agent and RLHF stages refine behavior without degrading earlier improvements, validating their staged design and reward-ordering principles.
AI.conclusion: A carefully staged, fully documented post-training pipeline using only public data and open components can turn a base LLM into a competitive assistant. Key principles are: (i) invest in broad, high-quality SFT; (ii) keep RL tasks in an appropriate difficulty band; (iii) order stages by reward reliability, moving from hard verifiable signals to softer judgment-based ones; and (iv) treat infrastructure and engineering as integral parts of the method. These insights form a reproducible recipe for others to adapt to different base models.

title: agentic-ger: terminology recovery in long-form speech using global context
summary: Recent advances in speech language models have improved automatic speech recognition (ASR) for long-form audio. However, accurately and consistently transcribing domain-specific terminology remains challenging. Motivated by the world knowledge and contextual capability of large language models (LLMs), we propose Agentic-GER, an LLM-based agent for terminology correction in long-form speech. The agent uses global context from the full transcript to identify suspicious terms and resolve ambiguous hypotheses. It selectively re-transcribes the source speech to check candidate corrections, and uses accepted edits to guide subsequent decisions. Experiments with four LLMs and two ASR systems on GigaSpeechBench show consistent terminology improvements in both Chinese and English, with and without thinking. On Chinese speech, Agentic-GER achieves up to a 36.8% relative reduction in biased character error rate (B-CER) over the Whisper baseline.

AI.tldr: Agentic-GER is an LLM-based agent that post-processes ASR transcripts of long-form speech to correct domain-specific terminology using global context and selective re-transcription, significantly improving terminology accuracy over baselines.
AI.motivation: Long-form ASR systems, even advanced speech language models, still struggle with accurately and consistently recognizing domain-specific and specialized terms, especially across long contexts where terminology must remain consistent. Standard ASR lacks the rich world knowledge and strong contextual reasoning ability that large language models exhibit on text, motivating the use of LLMs as agents to refine ASR outputs by focusing on terminology errors and bias.
AI.method: The authors design Agentic-GER, an LLM-based corrective agent that operates on complete ASR transcripts. It first uses the global textual context to detect suspicious or ambiguous terms, particularly domain-specific ones. For those terms, the agent proposes candidate corrections and selectively re-transcribes the corresponding audio segments to verify or disambiguate them. Confirmed corrections are then fed back into the decision process so that later corrections and consistency checks can leverage already accepted terminology edits. The framework is evaluated using four different LLMs and two ASR systems, and tested on GigaSpeechBench in both Chinese and English, in configurations with and without explicit chain-of-thought style “thinking.”
AI.result: Across experiments on GigaSpeechBench, Agentic-GER consistently improves terminology accuracy over baseline ASR outputs in both Chinese and English. In particular, for Chinese speech, the approach yields up to a 36.8% relative reduction in biased character error rate (B-CER) compared to a Whisper baseline, demonstrating substantial gains in handling domain-specific and potentially biased terminology. These improvements hold across multiple LLM backends and ASR systems, indicating robustness of the approach.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging LLMs as agentic post-processors for ASR, specifically targeting terminology correction with access to global transcript context and selective re-transcription, is an effective strategy for long-form speech recognition. Agentic-GER reduces domain-specific terminology errors and bias significantly, outperforming a strong Whisper baseline and working across languages and model configurations. This suggests that integrating LLM-based agents with ASR pipelines is a promising direction for improving recognition quality in specialized domains and multilingual settings.

title: CounterRoute: Self-Routed Reasoning via Hierarchical Counterfactual Credit Assignment
comment: 16 pages including 7 tables and 4 figures, under review
summary: Reasoning-capable language models often produce long chains of thought when direct answers suffice, wasting inference compute. Many dual-mode models leave this choice to users. Automating it is challenging because routing targets evolve with the policy, initial mode preferences destabilize exploration, and sequence-level objectives entangle routing with response learning. We introduce CounterRoute, an online reinforcement-learning framework that jointly learns routing and modeconditioned responses in one shared policy directly from a native dual-mode checkpoint, without method-specific SFT warm-up. Paired current-policy counterfactual rollouts assign cross-mode credit only to the routing token, while within-mode GRPO trains response tokens. A paired-to-self-routed curriculum stabilizes early training with forced rollouts from both modes, then increases self-routed updates to improve autonomous routing. Across nine benchmarks, CounterRoute better balances accuracy and efficiency than heuristic and learned adaptive-routing methods. Relative to always-thinking checkpoints, it improves macro-average accuracy while reducing mean generated tokens by 51% for Qwen3-8B and 41% for Qwen3-14B. On instruction-following and commonsense benchmarks where direct answering is strong, think rates fall as low as 1% while response quality improves. Despite training only on math and instruction following, its routing behavior and response quality generalize to held-out coding, science, knowledge, and commonsense benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CounterRoute, an RL-based framework that automatically decides when a language model should use long chain-of-thought (“think mode”) versus giving a direct answer (“fast mode”), cutting tokens while improving or preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Reasoning-capable LLMs often default to long chains of thought even when unnecessary, wasting compute. Existing dual-mode systems typically let users manually choose between fast and think modes, or rely on heuristic routing rules that don’t adapt well. Automating this routing is hard because the optimal routing policy changes as the model learns, naive initial routing biases can destabilize learning, and training routing together with response generation using sequence-level objectives entangles the two problems. The authors aim to learn an efficient, accurate, and stable automatic routing mechanism directly within a dual-mode model.
