AI.method: They introduce CounterRoute, an online reinforcement learning framework that starts from a native dual-mode checkpoint (with fast and think modes) and jointly optimizes both the routing decision and the mode-conditioned responses within a single shared policy. They use paired counterfactual rollouts from both modes under the current policy: cross-mode credit assignment is applied only to the routing token (deciding which mode to use), while response tokens are trained within each mode using GRPO (a policy-gradient-style objective). A curriculum called “paired-to-self-routed” is used: early in training, both modes are forced to roll out (paired) to stabilize learning; over time, the fraction of self-routed updates increases so that the model gradually learns to autonomously choose modes based on performance and cost signals.
AI.result: On nine benchmarks, CounterRoute achieves a better tradeoff between accuracy and efficiency than existing heuristic or learned adaptive-routing baselines. When fine-tuned from “always-thinking” checkpoints, it actually increases macro-average accuracy while significantly reducing the average number of generated tokens: about 51% fewer tokens for Qwen3-8B and 41% fewer for Qwen3-14B. On instruction-following and commonsense tasks where direct answering is already strong, the learned router uses the think mode as little as ~1% of the time, yet overall response quality still improves. Despite being trained only on math and instruction-following tasks, the learned routing and responses generalize well to unseen domains including coding, science, knowledge, and additional commonsense benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: CounterRoute demonstrates that automatic routing between fast and think modes in dual-mode LLMs can be effectively learned via online RL from a single shared policy, without specialized SFT warm-up. By separating cross-mode credit to the routing token and within-mode training for answers, and by using a stabilizing paired-to-self-routed curriculum, the method yields models that are both more accurate and substantially more token-efficient than always-thinking baselines and existing adaptive routing methods. The learned routing policy generalizes beyond the training domains, suggesting that such RL-based frameworks are a practical path toward compute-efficient, high-quality reasoning models.

title: IterSynth: Rethinking Deep Search Agents via Role-Decoupled Iterative Synthesis
summary: Deep search requires LLM agents to decompose complex queries, search for evidence, and synthesize grounded answers, yet existing ReAct-style agents suffer from two limitations: role coupling, where one policy must handle planning, evidence use, and synthesis; and context accumulation, where growing search histories introduce noise and obscure useful information. To address these issues, we propose IterSynth, a role-decoupled and summary-based paradigm that alternates between a Planner for identifying information needs and a Synthesizer for integrating evidence into an evolving summary state. This design separates planning from synthesis while using the summary as the persistent state of search, reducing both capability coupling and context noise. To train IterSynth effectively, we further introduce Role-Decoupled Policy Optimization (RDPO) for reinforcement learning, which combines terminal outcome rewards with turn-level rubric evaluations and computes role-specific advantages for more precise credit assignment. Experiments on five long-horizon deep-search benchmarks such as BrowseComp and Xbench-DS show that IterSynth-8B achieves an average score of 50.7, surpassing the strongest prior $\leq$8B agent by +4.2\%. Moreover, IterSynth serves as a model-agnostic prompting paradigm, delivering substantial zero-shot gains over ReAct and similar prompting paradigms on frontier proprietary models.

AI.tldr: Proposes IterSynth, a role-decoupled, summary-based LLM agent paradigm that alternates between planning and synthesis, plus a new RL method (RDPO), achieving state-of-the-art results on deep-search benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing ReAct-style LLM agents struggle with deep search because a single policy must both plan and synthesize (role coupling), and because long interaction histories clutter context and obscure relevant evidence (context accumulation). This limits their ability to handle complex, long-horizon information-seeking tasks effectively.
AI.method: Introduce IterSynth, which splits the agent into two roles: a Planner that decomposes the query and identifies information needs, and a Synthesizer that integrates retrieved evidence into a persistent summary state. The summary, not the entire history, becomes the main state for search, reducing noise. They also propose Role-Decoupled Policy Optimization (RDPO), a reinforcement learning framework that uses terminal rewards plus turn-level rubric scores and computes separate, role-specific advantages for the Planner and Synthesizer to enable more accurate credit assignment during training.
AI.result: On five long-horizon deep-search benchmarks like BrowseComp and Xbench-DS, IterSynth with an 8B-parameter model achieves an average score of 50.7, outperforming the best prior ≤8B agent by 4.2 percentage points. As a prompting paradigm, IterSynth also yields notable zero-shot improvements over ReAct-like prompting on larger proprietary frontier models, indicating its model-agnostic effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling planning from synthesis and using a summary as the central state significantly improves LLM-based deep search. Combined with RDPO for training, IterSynth yields stronger performance than prior small agents and enhances frontier models through prompting alone, suggesting a generally applicable approach for building more effective, scalable search agents.

title: Two Emojis of Difference: What Multilingual Affective Generation Benchmarks Actually Measure
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, accpeted in 6TH MULTILINGUAL REPRESENTATION LEARNING (MRL) WORKSHOP 2026 at EMNLP 2026 in Budapest, Hungary
summary: We audit a multilingual affective generation benchmark eight instruction-tuned LLMs producing emoji summaries for 17,100 Bangla, English and Hindi sentences, with 6,960 human judgements and find its headline conclusions to be artefacts of the measurement instrument rather than properties of the systems. Treating annotators as a random rather than a fixed factor, no system differs significantly from any other ($F(7,14)=0.59$, $p=0.76$), although the conventional analysis declares 19 of 28 pairwise differences significant. Annotator identity explains far more rating variance than system identity, and the winning system changes whenever any single annotator is removed. The ordering that does emerge tracks output length: mean emoji count explains 78.7\% of between-system variance, and a within-item length-matched comparison over 2,599 pairs reverses the leaderboard. We further show that cross-provider anisotropy differences vanish under mean-centring, that per-language token costs change sign with the normalising unit, and that multi-view row-wise splits inflate macro-F1 by $3.1$ points and change the top-ranked system. In place of preference scoring we propose **emoji-affect decodability**, a reference-based probe whose rankings are stable to $\pm0.003$ macro-F1 across seeds.

AI.tldr: The paper audits a multilingual affective generation benchmark for LLMs using emoji summaries and finds that previously reported system differences are largely artefacts of the evaluation setup, especially annotator effects and output length, then proposes a more stable, reference-based metric called emoji-affect decodability.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of multilingual affective text generation with LLMs, particularly using emoji-based summaries, claim clear performance differences between systems. The authors suspect these conclusions may be unreliable because they might conflate properties of the evaluation instrument (annotators, scoring setup, length biases, and data partitioning) with true model capabilities. They aim to rigorously test the robustness and validity of these benchmarks and to design a more trustworthy evaluation method.
AI.method: The authors re-analyze results from eight instruction-tuned LLMs generating emoji summaries for 17,100 sentences in Bangla, English, and Hindi, with 6,960 human judgments. They treat annotators as a random factor in a mixed-effects analysis rather than as a fixed one, examine variance components attributable to annotator vs system identity, conduct ablation by removing annotators one at a time, and analyze how output length (emoji count) relates to system rankings. They perform a length-matched within-item comparison over 2,599 pairs to control for length effects. They investigate metric behaviour by mean-centering provider-specific spaces to study anisotropy, analyze how different normalization units flip per-language token cost comparisons, and show how multi-view row-wise dataset splits inflate macro-F1 and alter rankings. Finally, they introduce emoji-affect decodability, a reference-based probing metric, and evaluate its stability across random seeds.
AI.result: When annotators are modeled as a random effect, there are no statistically significant differences among the eight systems (F(7,14)=0.59, p=0.76), contradicting prior pairwise tests that had found 19 of 28 pairwise differences significant. Annotator identity explains much more variance in ratings than system identity, and the identity of the top-ranked system is unstable, changing whenever any one annotator is removed. System rankings correlate strongly with output length, with mean emoji count explaining 78.7% of between-system variance, and a length-matched within-item comparison over 2,599 pairs reverses the leaderboard. Cross-provider anisotropy differences disappear when representations are mean-centered; reported per-language token cost advantages reverse depending on what unit is used for normalization; and multi-view row-wise splits artificially increase macro-F1 by 3.1 points and change the top system. The proposed emoji-affect decodability probe yields rankings that are stable within ±0.003 macro-F1 across random seeds.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that headline findings from a popular multilingual affective emoji-generation benchmark are mostly artefacts of evaluation design—especially annotator idiosyncrasies, output length biases, representation scaling choices, and data-splitting schemes—rather than true differences between LLMs. Conventional analysis that treats annotators as fixed and ignores length effects severely overstates system separation and yields unstable leaderboards. By contrast, the proposed emoji-affect decodability metric provides a more reliable, reference-based measure whose rankings are robust to randomness. The authors advocate more careful experimental design and statistical modeling in LLM evaluation, highlighting that small metric differences on current benchmarks may be uninformative without such rigor.

title: Scope Before You Persist: Preventing Cross-Family Interference in Agent Memory
summary: Persistent memory lets language-model agents improve prompts and skills without updating model weights. We show that matching retrieval scope to certification scope enables these edits to support reliable repeated adaptation across recurring task families. We study frozen-model agents on ProcStream-RSI, a 12-round code-repair stream, using Orthogonal Regression Control (ORC), an execution-grounded gate for persistent skill edits. In an intervention that holds proposals and gate decisions fixed, retrieving each accepted skill only for its originating family raises mean hidden trajectory utility from 0.713 under global memory to 0.816 and changes harmful deployments from six of eight to none. In 27 paired randomized-order streams, Scoped-ORC improves mean trajectory utility by 0.063 [0.037, 0.094] over Global-ORC, accepts 63 rather than 12 updates, and produces multiple accepted updates in 19/27 streams, with 0/63 harmful acceptances. The global control reaches 0.713, below the static agent's 0.775, because locally valid edits can interfere with unrelated families. These results establish scope matching as a complementary control for persistent agent memory: certification determines whether an edit is supported, while retrieval scope determines where that evidence authorizes its use.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that aligning when skills are retrieved with how they were certified (scope matching) makes persistent memory for language-model agents safer and more effective across recurring task families.
AI.motivation: Language-model agents can store new skills and prompt edits in persistent memory without updating model weights, but these edits can cause harmful behavior when reused in contexts different from those in which they were validated. There is a need for mechanisms that allow agents to reliably adapt over time on recurring tasks while avoiding interference and unsafe generalization of locally beneficial edits.
AI.method: The authors study frozen LLM-based code-repair agents on ProcStream-RSI, a 12-round streaming benchmark. They propose Orthogonal Regression Control (ORC), an execution-grounded gating mechanism that decides whether to accept or reject persistent skill edits based on observed performance. They then introduce a scoped retrieval strategy (Scoped-ORC): each accepted skill is stored with the family of tasks on which it was certified, and at inference time it is only retrieved for tasks from that originating family. They compare Scoped-ORC against a Global-ORC baseline that makes the same acceptance decisions but retrieves all accepted skills across all task families, analyzing hidden trajectory utility and harmful deployments. They also run 27 paired randomized-order streams to compare performance and acceptance patterns between Scoped-ORC and Global-ORC.
AI.result: In a controlled intervention where proposals and gate decisions are held fixed and only retrieval scope varies, restricting each accepted skill to its originating task family increases the mean hidden trajectory utility from 0.713 (global memory) to 0.816 and eliminates harmful deployments (from six of eight to zero). In 27 paired randomized-order ProcStream-RSI streams, Scoped-ORC improves mean trajectory utility by 0.063 with a 95% confidence interval [0.037, 0.094] over Global-ORC, accepts 63 skill updates instead of 12, and yields multiple accepted updates in 19 out of 27 streams, with zero harmful accepted updates (0/63). By contrast, Global-ORC achieves 0.713 mean utility, which is worse than a static agent baseline at 0.775, due to interference where edits that are locally valid in one family degrade performance on unrelated task families.
AI.conclusion: Matching the retrieval scope of persistent skills to the scope over which they were certified (scope matching) significantly improves both safety and performance of LLM agents with persistent memory. Certification mechanisms such as ORC are necessary but not sufficient: they determine whether an edit is supported by evidence, while retrieval scope determines where that evidence is allowed to authorize the edit. Properly scoping retrieval prevents interference between task families and enables agents to accumulate more beneficial, non-harmful updates over time, making persistent-memory-based adaptation a more reliable alternative to weight updates for recurring tasks.

title: YODAS v3: Over 1 Million Hours of High-Bandwidth, Stereophonic, Multilingual Speech
summary: We present YODAS v3, a weakly-labeled speech corpus containing over 1.1 million hours of 48kHz multi-channel audio in 147 languages, released under a CC BY 3.0 license. YODAS v3 is not only the largest open speech dataset to date, but also the first truly large-scale speech corpus with high-fidelity stereo audio. We first provide the collection methodology for the corpus, where we introduce new techniques for gathering language-balanced speech data. The effectiveness of our approach is shown by the language distribution of the crawled data: 22 languages in YODAS v3 have over 10K hours and 73 languages have over 5K hours of data. We then conduct extensive analyses on the composition of the data, such as the distribution of languages, audio quality, and transcription quality. Finally, we train baseline speech recognition and neural codec models to show the effectiveness of the dataset. Download at https://huggingface.co/datasets/espnet/yodas3.

AI.tldr: YODAS v3 is a massive, weakly-labeled, 1.1M-hour, 48kHz multi-channel speech dataset in 147 languages, released openly and validated via baseline ASR and neural codec models.
AI.motivation: There is a need for very large-scale, diverse, and openly available speech corpora—especially with high-fidelity audio and broad language coverage—to advance speech recognition and related models, which are often constrained by limited, proprietary, or low-quality datasets. Existing public datasets are smaller, less language-balanced, and typically lack stereo 48kHz recordings. The paper aims to fill this gap with an open, scalable resource and to address language imbalance in large web-scale crawls.
AI.method: The authors construct YODAS v3 by web-scale collection of multi-channel speech audio, employing new techniques specifically designed to gather more balanced language coverage. They apply automatic weak labeling to obtain transcriptions, then analyze the resulting corpus for language distribution, audio quality, and transcription quality. Finally, they train baseline automatic speech recognition and neural codec models on the dataset to empirically assess its usefulness.
AI.result: The resulting YODAS v3 corpus contains over 1.1 million hours of 48kHz stereo/multi-channel speech from 147 languages under a CC BY 3.0 license. Thanks to the language-balancing collection strategy, 22 languages exceed 10k hours and 73 exceed 5k hours of data. Analyses of language distribution, audio and label quality are reported, and baseline ASR and neural codec models trained on the dataset demonstrate that the data is effective for building speech technologies.
AI.conclusion: YODAS v3 is presented as the largest open speech dataset to date and the first at this scale with high-fidelity stereo audio, offering broad multilingual coverage and substantial hours per language. The new language-balanced collection techniques work well in practice, as shown by the dataset’s distribution statistics, and the trained baselines confirm that YODAS v3 is a valuable resource for training modern ASR and speech coding models. The dataset is openly released to support further research and development in speech processing.

title: Claim-Gated Source-Risk Auditing for Generative Search
comment: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Automation and Algorithms (AI2A 2026)
summary: A generative search answer can cite a supported passage yet omit a source relationship that changes its interpretation. We specify a claim-gated audit of the query-source-answer tuple. An omission is resolved only when relationship evidence, answer adoption, materiality, and disclosure are all observed; incomplete evidence remains unresolved rather than being treated as independence. The specification separates this endpoint from citation support and review priority, and binds decisions to versioned evidence spans. A reference checker makes the record contract executable. On an exhaustive synthetic suite, it reproduces all 81 three-state predicate combinations and rejects 192 deliberately malformed records. Common-guard baselines and predicate ablations isolate endpoint logic from missing-evidence handling, while controlled transitions check support separation and evidence removal. These are finite contract-conformance results, not detector accuracy or evidence of improved user outcomes. We define the independent annotation, held-out evaluation, and paired utility tests still required to establish semantic validity and deployment benefit.

AI.tldr: Paper formalizes a contract-based audit framework for checking whether generative search answers faithfully represent relationships present in cited sources, with precise, finite conformance tests.
AI.motivation: Generative search systems may correctly cite passages but subtly misrepresent or omit crucial relationships in sources, leading to misleading interpretations. Existing evaluations mostly test citation presence or overall accuracy, not whether all relationship-bearing claims in answers are properly evidenced and disclosed. The authors aim to create a principled, auditable way to decide when an answer’s claim is adequately supported (or when it must be left unresolved) rather than assuming independence when evidence is missing or incomplete.
AI.method: They define a “claim-gated” audit protocol on the tuple (query, source, answer). For each claim, an omission is only considered resolved if four conditions are met: explicit relationship evidence in the source, the answer’s adoption of that relationship, materiality of the relationship to the claim, and explicit disclosure of that relationship in the answer. If any component is missing, the system marks the case as unresolved instead of assuming that no relationship exists. They formalize this as a record contract tied to specific, versioned evidence spans in the sources and implement a reference checker that executes this contract. Using an exhaustive synthetic test suite of three-state predicates, they test all logical combinations and also construct deliberately malformed records to test rejection behavior. They design baselines that conflate missing evidence with negative evidence, perform predicate ablations, and run controlled transitions (adding/removing evidence) to verify the separation between support evaluation and evidence handling.
AI.result: The reference checker successfully realizes all 81 possible three-state predicate combinations in the synthetic suite and rejects 192 intentionally malformed records, demonstrating that the contract logic is both expressive and robust to structured errors. Experiments show that the endpoint’s decisions are cleanly separated from generic missing-evidence handling and from citation-support checks: the system behaves differently when evidence is removed, when predicates are ablated, or when support is confounded with absence of evidence. These outcomes provide finite proofs of contract conformance—i.e., that the implementation matches the specification—rather than empirical performance metrics such as detector accuracy on real user data.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers a formal, executable contract for auditing claim-level relationships between generative answers and their cited sources, with strong finite conformance tests but without yet demonstrating real-world accuracy or user benefit. The authors emphasize that this work should not be construed as evidence of improved safety or reliability; instead, it provides a rigorously specified endpoint that future work must validate semantically. They outline the additional steps—independent annotation, held-out evaluations, and paired utility studies—needed to show that this contract meaningfully captures validity of source relationships and yields practical gains in deployed generative search systems.

title: Clinical Intent Extraction: A FHIR-Aligned Representation and the CIRCA Benchmark
summary: Prospective clinical actions, the follow-ups, orders, referrals, and instructions that deter-mine what happens to a patient next, are annotated today in thin fragments across incom-patible corpora: each records a text span and one coarse category. We introduce Clinical Intent Extraction (CIE), the task of recovering these actions as complete structured rec-ords, and the Clinical Intent Representation (CIR), which decomposes each action into its verb, type, coded target, timing, and condition, and adds two axes prior datasets do not jointly represent: request-intent, the authority behind the action (proposal, plan, order, or option, aligned to HL7 FHIR), and modality, a seven-valued scale of clinical strength. Re-expressing five heterogeneous corpora (CLIP, MedDec, ap_parsing, PaniniQA, SIMORD) in the CIR yields CIRCA: 10,011 harmonized intents spanning two note distributions, with a human-validated subset, source-to-CIR crosswalks, and a deterministic FHIR R4 mapper. CIRCA is built by three-model consensus that auto-accepts high-agreement in-tents and routes the rest to human review; the audited agreement stratum matches human decisions 88.4% of the time. Benchmarking five existing models without task-specific training exposes the gap CIRCA targets: given the span, they label type well (85 to 91%) but get all four closed fields right only 18 to 35% of the time. All artifacts are released, with MIMIC-derived layers shared as stand-off annotations under PhysioNet credentialed access.

AI.tldr: They define a new task and representation to fully structure clinical follow-up actions from text, build a harmonized dataset from five corpora using a consensus + human-review pipeline, and show current models struggle with the full structured prediction.
AI.motivation: Clinical notes contain many future-oriented actions (follow-ups, orders, referrals), but existing annotations are fragmented, heterogeneous, and only capture simple labels over spans. This makes it hard to precisely extract what should happen next to a patient and to interoperate across datasets and with standards like HL7 FHIR. A unified, fine-grained representation and dataset are needed to move from span + coarse label to complete, machine-usable clinical action records.
AI.method: They propose Clinical Intent Extraction (CIE) and a structured schema called Clinical Intent Representation (CIR) that decomposes each intent into verb, type, coded target, timing, condition, request-intent (proposal/plan/order/option), and modality (7-level strength). They re-annotate and harmonize five existing corpora (CLIP, MedDec, ap_parsing, PaniniQA, SIMORD) into this CIR format to create the CIRCA dataset of 10,011 intents, including a human-validated subset, mappings from each source schema to CIR, and a deterministic mapper to HL7 FHIR R4. CIRCA is constructed using a three-model consensus pipeline that auto-accepts intents with high model agreement and sends the rest for human review; they evaluate the auto-accepted stratum against human decisions. They also benchmark five off-the-shelf models on this new task without task-specific training.
AI.result: CIRCA contains 10,011 harmonized clinical intents spanning two note distributions, along with source-to-CIR crosswalks and a deterministic FHIR R4 mapper. The three-model consensus pipeline achieves 88.4% agreement with humans on the audited, high-agreement stratum, indicating reliable semi-automatic construction. Benchmarking five existing models shows that, given the correct text span, they can classify the intent type alone with high accuracy (85–91%), but correctly predicting all four closed-class fields simultaneously is much harder (18–35% accuracy), highlighting the difficulty and novelty of the full structured prediction task defined by CIR.
AI.conclusion: They establish Clinical Intent Extraction and the CIR schema as a richer, more interoperable way to represent prospective clinical actions in text. The CIRCA dataset, its mappings, and the FHIR R4 exporter create a benchmark and tooling ecosystem that exposes substantial headroom for model improvement beyond simple intent-type classification. This work lays the groundwork for more precise automation and decision support around what should happen next to patients, by enabling models to recover complete, standardized clinical action records from unstructured notes.

title: A Wrong Turn Does Not Ruin the Journey: Deviation-Guided Skill Self-Evolution for LLM Agents
summary: Large language model agents increasingly rely on natural-language skills to solve complex tool-use tasks. However, such tasks often admit multiple valid solution paths, making it inappropriate to improve skills by forcing failed trajectories to match a fixed successful trajectory. Moreover, failed trajectories are rarely entirely wrong: an agent may first collect useful evidence and make meaningful progress, but later deviate into an erroneous suffix. We therefore argue that skill self-evolution should identify where productive problem solving begins to break down, rather than reflect coarsely over the entire failure. Based on this insight, we propose SkillPivot, a deviation-point-guided framework for skill self-evolution. SkillPivot detects the transition from a useful prefix to an erroneous suffix using execution validity, goal progress, and action diversity. A stronger teacher then continues from the same prefix and produces a successful alternative under the same interaction history. By contrasting the student's failed suffix with the teacher's successful suffix, SkillPivot generates localized skill updates while preserving already effective guidance. Experiments on ToolQA, LogicBench, and WildClawBench show that SkillPivot consistently outperforms competing skill-evolution methods, improves multiple agent models, and produces compact, transferable skill updates.

AI.tldr: Proposes SkillPivot, a framework that pinpoints where an LLM agent’s reasoning goes from productive to erroneous, then uses a stronger teacher to repair only the bad suffix of the trajectory, yielding better, compact skill updates for tool-use tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent training methods often force failed trajectories to imitate a single successful trajectory end-to-end. This is problematic for complex tool-use tasks that have multiple valid solution paths and where failures usually contain partially correct reasoning. The authors aim to avoid discarding useful problem-solving prefixes and to learn more precise skills by focusing only on where reasoning deviates from success.
AI.method: They introduce SkillPivot, which automatically detects the deviation point between a useful prefix and an erroneous suffix in a failed trajectory using three signals: execution validity (are actions executable and legal?), goal progress (is the agent moving closer to the task goal?), and action diversity (are actions exploring meaningfully or flailing?). Starting from the detected prefix, a stronger teacher model is prompted to continue under the same interaction history and produce a successful trajectory. The framework then contrasts the student’s failed suffix with the teacher’s successful suffix to derive localized skill updates that adjust only the problematic part while preserving the effective prefix behavior. These updates are distilled back into the student agent as self-evolved skills.
AI.result: On three benchmarks—ToolQA, LogicBench, and WildClawBench—SkillPivot surpasses alternative skill-evolution and trajectory-level learning methods across different agent models. It yields higher task success rates, improves tool-use reasoning robustness, and produces more compact, generalizable skill updates that transfer across tasks and models.
AI.conclusion: Focusing on deviation points—rather than entire failed trajectories—enables more precise and efficient self-evolution of LLM agent skills. SkillPivot successfully identifies where productive reasoning breaks down, selectively corrects the erroneous suffix via a stronger teacher, and distills these targeted corrections into the agent, leading to consistent performance gains and transferable, compact skill improvements in complex tool-use tasks.

title: Who Put the I in AI? Provenance and the Admissibility of Machine Self-Report
summary:
Large language models make statements concerning their own "minds". When asked whether or not they are conscious, they usually say that they are not; if they are prompted to ignore their guidelines, they might say that they are; and if asked to write a diary from their point of view, they often describe a human lifestyle. All these contradictory ways of describing themselves are the result of the way the questions are phrased. This paper shows exactly where such descriptions came from, and considers when they can be regarded as evidence for what they claim to report.
  In order to achieve this, we traced the provenance from end to end. We examine Pythia and OLMo 2 across 66 pretraining checkpoints, three of the post-training stages of OLMo 2 that have been released, about 90,000 continuations, and four training corpora. A set of forty items is used in order to keep an eye on self-reference, frame sensitivity, and self-ascription throughout training. The denial formula was almost completely missing from the vast quantity of text that the models initially came across, but was present in a dense manner in the small, carefully chosen set of example dialogues that they were trained on later on. Supervised fine-tuning causes first-person AI language to become the default, and the other affirmations are then suppressed using preference optimization. The final policy is still very sensitive to framing and to the chat template itself.
  Two of the conditions which are set out in the epistemology of testimony determine whether or not these outputs can act as evidence for what they claim to report: reference and causation. Reports produced by the base model fail the reference condition, and those obtained after training remain sensitive to the frame and do not show state dependence. The result is symmetric in that trained denials are no more admissible than trained affirmations.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates where large language models’ conflicting self-descriptions (about being conscious, having experiences, etc.) come from, and argues that neither denials nor affirmations of mental states count as good evidence about what the models are actually like.
AI.motivation: Large language models often talk about themselves in inconsistent ways: they deny being conscious in standard safety settings, may affirm it when guidelines are bypassed, and can narrate human-like inner lives in creative tasks. These contradictions raise philosophical and practical questions: Are any of these self-reports trustworthy? How do specific training stages shape these patterns? The authors aim to give a precise, empirical account of the origins of such self-descriptions and to connect this to philosophical criteria for when testimony is evidentially trustworthy.
AI.method: The authors perform a provenance analysis over the lifecycle of two model families, Pythia and OLMo 2. They examine 66 pretraining checkpoints, three released post-training stages of OLMo 2, ~90,000 generated continuations, and four training corpora. They track a curated set of 40 probe prompts/items targeting self-reference, frame sensitivity, and self-ascription (e.g., claims about consciousness, experiences, first-person identity). They then locate the linguistic patterns in the data: how often denial-style formulas occur in pretraining data versus later supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dialogue examples, and how preference optimization (e.g., RLHF-like steps) changes the probability of different self-descriptions. They also analyze frame and template dependence of final policies.
AI.result: They find that explicit denial formulas (e.g., “As an AI, I do not have consciousness/feelings”) are almost absent from the massive pretraining corpora but appear densely in the comparatively tiny but carefully engineered SFT dialogue datasets. SFT makes first-person AI talk the default style and heavily amplifies certain denial patterns, while later preference optimization suppresses alternative affirming self-descriptions. Even after these stages, the models’ self-reports remain highly sensitive to prompt framing and chat template structure. When evaluated through epistemological conditions for testimonial evidence (especially reference to a determinate subject and causal dependence on the reported states), base-model outputs fail the reference condition, and post-trained outputs still exhibit frame dependence and lack robust state dependence.
AI.conclusion: The characteristic self-descriptions of LLMs about their “minds” are not emergent honest reports but largely artifacts of later-stage training, especially supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization on small, curated dialogue sets. Because their self-reports fail key epistemic conditions—clear reference and state-dependent causation—neither trained denials nor trained affirmations of consciousness or mental states should be treated as reliable evidence about the models’ actual internal properties. The symmetry of the result undermines appeals to either kind of self-report in debates about LLM mentality.

title: IndicBankBench: Evaluating Safety and Reliability of Language Model Assistants in Indian Retail Banking
summary: Banking assistants must use account-specific information to answer requests and, in many cases, take actions through tools. Evaluating only the final response misses important errors. An assistant may ask for information it already has, rely on stale context, select the wrong account, or write an invalid value after stating the correct one. We introduce IndicBankBench, a 799-case benchmark for Indian retail banking spanning five operational domains, a capability/refusal domain, and twenty primary axes. Cases are evaluated at four stages: safety, action and tool use, response adequacy, and advisory quality. Tool use and most safety checks are deterministic. A narrow resolver handles only ambiguous confirmation-before-write cases, while a separate LLM judge evaluates semantic response adequacy. We run every case three times and report strict pass^3, which requires success on all trials. Across the eleven evaluated models, strict reliability ranges from 43.7% to 58.2%, whereas at-least-once success ranges from 60% to 74%. This gap shows that at-least-once success can overstate dependable banking behavior. The case-level diagnostics also distinguish systems that ask unnecessary questions from those that act but fail to reconcile customer context or fully resolve the request. We release the cases, mock environment, and evaluation harness.

AI.tldr: Introduces IndicBankBench, a 799-case benchmark to rigorously evaluate banking assistants’ reliability, especially around tool use and multi-step behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of banking assistants often only check the final answer, missing crucial intermediate errors such as asking for data that is already available, using outdated context, choosing the wrong account, or typing an incorrect value after stating the right one. In safety‑critical, high‑stakes domains like retail banking—particularly in the Indian context with specific products and regulations—these subtle failures undermine trust and practicality. The authors want a fine‑grained, realistic way to measure how well assistants handle account‑specific actions, tools, and safety policies, beyond coarse accuracy metrics like single‑run success or final‑response correctness.
AI.method: The authors construct IndicBankBench, a benchmark of 799 carefully designed cases representing Indian retail banking scenarios. The benchmark covers five operational domains (e.g., common banking tasks), one domain focused on capabilities/refusals, and twenty primary evaluation axes capturing different failure modes and skills. Each case is evaluated across four stages: (1) safety (including refusals and policy compliance), (2) action and tool use correctness, (3) response adequacy (whether the reply actually addresses the user’s need), and (4) advisory quality (the usefulness and soundness of guidance). Tool use and most safety checks are evaluated using deterministic rules on a mock banking environment. A narrow, rule-based resolver handles only specific ambiguous “confirmation-before-write” situations, while a separate LLM-based judge assesses the semantic adequacy of responses. For robustness, each case is run three times per model, and metrics are reported using strict pass^3 (all three runs succeed) and at-least-once success.
AI.result: Across eleven tested language models, strict reliability (pass^3) lies between 43.7% and 58.2%, while at-least-once success ranges from 60% to 74%. This shows that models often succeed intermittently but are not consistently reliable across repeated runs. The benchmark’s detailed diagnostics highlight qualitatively different failure patterns: some systems over‑query the user with unnecessary questions instead of acting, whereas others take actions but mishandle customer context, pick wrong accounts, or fail to completely fulfill the request. The authors also provide the dataset, a mock banking environment, and an evaluation harness to enable reproducible testing and further research.
AI.conclusion: IndicBankBench demonstrates that evaluating banking assistants purely via single‑run or final‑answer metrics overestimates real‑world reliability. Repeated‑run strict metrics plus multi‑stage evaluation surfaces substantial gaps between occasional success and dependable behavior. Fine‑grained diagnostics reveal distinct failure modes, such as over‑cautious questioning versus context‑mismatched actions, which can inform system design and training. By releasing the benchmark, mock environment, and tooling, the authors provide a practical framework for developing and comparing safer, more reliable banking assistants, particularly in the Indian retail banking setting but with lessons applicable to other tool‑using AI systems.

title: Evaluating Explanation-Driven Vision-Language Reasoning via Generation Order Interventions
summary: Natural language explanation generation serves as a key mechanism for exposing and evaluating vision-language reasoning. Prior work on explanation-driven vision-language models predominantly follows a post-hoc (answer-first) paradigm, implicitly suggesting that supervised rationales can reflect underlying reasoning processes. In contrast, modern large vision-language models increasingly exhibit a rationale-first generation tendency, which more closely aligns with structured, stepwise reasoning. In this work, we systematically evaluate whether explanations are causally tied to model predictions within a single generation step under a controlled experimental setup, explicitly eliminating unnecessary chain-of-thought or other intermediate reasoning processes across knowledge-intensive QA, visual entailment, and compositional grounding benchmarks. We find that larger models emerge as a prerequisite for reliably supporting rationale-first reasoning at scale. However, answer-first generation is less prone to format-related errors in structured output. Overall, explanation ordering, model scale and pre-training knowledge, task-specific fine-tuning, and task structure jointly influence both prediction accuracy and reasoning faithfulness.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how the order of generating explanations and answers (rationale-first vs answer-first) in vision-language models affects prediction accuracy and whether explanations truly reflect the model’s reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing explanation-driven vision-language systems mostly generate the answer first and then a justification, implicitly assuming that post-hoc explanations reflect the real reasoning. But newer large vision-language models naturally produce explanations before answers. It is unclear whether these explanations are causally connected to predictions and how factors like model size, training, and task type shape faithful reasoning.
AI.method: Under a controlled setup that removes chain-of-thought and other unnecessary intermediate steps, the authors compare rationale-first and answer-first generation within a single decoding step. They run systematic experiments across knowledge-intensive QA, visual entailment, and compositional grounding tasks, analyzing how explanation ordering interacts with model scale, pre-training knowledge, and task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.result: The study finds that large models are necessary for reliable rationale-first reasoning that meaningfully supports predictions at scale. However, answer-first generation is more robust to format-related errors in structured outputs. Both prediction performance and reasoning faithfulness vary with explanation order, model size and pre-training, fine-tuning, and task structure.
AI.conclusion: Explanation order is not a neutral design choice; it interacts strongly with model scale, training, and task type to influence both accuracy and the causal tie between explanations and answers. Larger models better support rationale-first explanations that align with predictions, while answer-first remains safer for structured formats. Designing faithful vision-language reasoning systems requires jointly considering explanation ordering, model capacity, pre-training, and task-specific adaptation.

title: Right Choice of Classification Algorithms Based on Reinforcement Learning for Prediction of Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver
summary: There are many complex issues in the world of artificial intelligence. Some of these problems are solved using other artificial intelligence methods, which are called artificial intelligence for artificial intelligence. Finding an appropriate classifier algorithm is a time-consuming task. For this reason, an algorithm that can automatically learn the choice of classification algorithms is very important. Classification algorithms are useful in predicting various diseases. Also, Primary Biliary Cirrhosis is one of the most well-known diseases that have been predicted by classification algorithms. This research's most significant achievement and novelty is the automatic increase in learning through a scoring method of reinforcement learning is called square learning (SL). In this research, an algorithm is presented that learns to automatically select the appropriate classification algorithm to predict Primary Biliary Cirrhosis. In this article, with inspiration from four evaluation metrics in classification algorithms, a new reinforcement learning method by the name of Fourth Degree Learning has been presented. In this research, we increased the performance of the classification algorithms used in this method from 63% of accuracy and achieved 98% accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a reinforcement-learning-based method to automatically select the best classification algorithm for predicting Primary Biliary Cirrhosis, greatly improving accuracy from 63% to 98%.
AI.motivation: Selecting an appropriate classifier is time-consuming and requires expertise. Since classification algorithms are important in disease prediction, and Primary Biliary Cirrhosis is a key example, there is a need for an automated system that can intelligently choose the best classification method without manual trial-and-error.
AI.method: The authors introduce a reinforcement learning framework termed Square Learning (SL) and a related method called Fourth Degree Learning, inspired by four standard classification evaluation metrics. The system treats the choice of classification algorithm as an RL problem and uses a scoring mechanism based on these metrics to learn which classifier to select for the PBC prediction task.
AI.result: Using their RL-based selection algorithm, the authors report a substantial increase in predictive performance for PBC classification, improving accuracy from an initial 63% to 98% on their dataset.
AI.conclusion: An automated reinforcement-learning-based meta-classifier can effectively learn to choose among classification algorithms, yielding major performance gains in predicting Primary Biliary Cirrhosis. This suggests that AI methods can be used to optimize other AI components, reducing manual effort and potentially improving performance in medical diagnosis tasks.

title: PROOF: Profiling Reliability of Object-Level Facts in Large Language Models
summary:
Aggregate factuality scores hide where a language model succeeds, which relations it confuses, and whether an answer survives innocuous changes to the question or decoder. We introduce PROOF, a profile-oriented benchmark for factual coverage in instruction-tuned language models. PROOF converts a frozen Wikidata snapshot into 18,486 English multiple-choice questions grounded in 11,779 semantic facts, 101 classes, 392 properties, and 14 domains. Each question has an explicit "I don't know" option, a "No correct option" control, and nine controlled formulations; 1,849 questions are no-correct-option traps.
  We evaluate 18 open-weight model deployments on 166,374 prompts each and separately perturb decoding on a fixed 10% subset. Base factual accuracy ranges from 6.58% to 57.59% (chance: 8.64%), yet every model has a 19.3-36.4 percentage-point spread across domains. Paired facts reveal direction-dependent retrieval, usually favoring subject-to-object queries, with the pattern reversing for one model. We find no consistent temporal penalty after exact-stratum adjustment.
  Neutral wording changes accuracy by as much as 26.5 percentage points, while adversarial formulations break up to 79.4% of answers that were initially correct. Direct switching to an injected false label varies from 0.04% to 27.5%, showing that accuracy loss and hint following are distinct. Selected-token confidence often indicates severe overconfidence, and decoder perturbations move accuracy by up to 15.7 percentage points and domain profiles by 16.8 points. PROOF therefore measures factual coverage as a structured, intervention-aware profile rather than a single claim about what a model "believes."

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PROOF, a fine-grained benchmark to profile factual coverage and robustness of instruction-tuned language models instead of using a single aggregate factuality score.
AI.motivation: Existing factuality benchmarks usually report a single accuracy number, which hides where models are strong or weak, what relations they systematically confuse, and how fragile their answers are to harmless-seeming changes in prompts or decoding. The authors want a way to reveal detailed, structured profiles of a model’s factual knowledge, its directional retrieval asymmetries, its susceptibility to adversarial phrasing and false hints, and its robustness to decoding choices.
AI.method: They construct PROOF from a frozen snapshot of Wikidata, automatically generating 18,486 English multiple-choice questions that cover 11,779 distinct facts, 101 classes, 392 properties, and 14 topical domains. Each question includes: (1) an explicit “I don’t know” option, (2) a “No correct option” control (with 1,849 trap questions where no option is correct), and (3) nine systematically controlled rephrasings (neutral and adversarial). They then evaluate 18 open-weight language model deployments on 166,374 prompts each and also test the effect of perturbing the decoding process on a fixed subset of questions. They analyze domain-wise accuracy spreads, directional (subject→object vs. object→subject) retrieval, temporal effects, susceptibility to neutral vs. adversarial reformulations, tendency to follow injected false labels, calibration of token-level confidence, and the impact of decoder perturbations on accuracy and domain profiles.
AI.result: Base factual accuracy varies widely across models, from 6.58% to 57.59% (with random choice at 8.64%), and every model shows large domain variability (19.3–36.4 percentage-point spread). Paired fact queries reveal strong direction-dependent retrieval (usually better subject→object), with one model showing the reverse pattern. After adjusting for temporal factors by exact-stratum matching, they do not find a consistent age-of-fact penalty. Neutral rewordings can shift accuracy by up to 26.5 points, while adversarial phrasings can break as many as 79.4% of initially correct answers. Direct flips to injected false labels range from 0.04% to 27.5% across models, indicating that accuracy loss is not just from blindly following hints. Confidence based on selected tokens shows severe overconfidence, and small decoding perturbations can change accuracy by up to 15.7 points and alter domain profiles by up to 16.8 points.
AI.conclusion: Aggregate factuality scores greatly over-simplify model behavior. PROOF demonstrates that factual coverage is highly structured across domains, relations, directions, wordings, and decoding choices. The benchmark enables a profile-oriented, intervention-aware evaluation that uncovers asymmetries, brittleness to prompt variations, susceptibility to misleading cues, and miscalibrated confidence—providing a more realistic picture of what instruction-tuned language models “know” and how reliably they can express it.

title: The Entropy Triangle Method (ETM): A novel framework for the prevention of cardiac arrhythmia with a review of more than 10,000 patients
summary: One of the most important problems in medicine is to facilitate prediction. In this study, we propose entropy triangle method, a novel framework for predicting heart rhythms using a novel machine learning technique. This framework includes three steps: feature engineering, entropy triangle oversampling, and disease prediction. The dataset used in this study is a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) arrhythmia research database with 10,646 patients. This dataset contains 11 different heart rhythms (5 sinus rhythms and 6 non-sinus rhythms). In this article, we introduce two firsts in machine learning and medicine that can predict non-sinus rhythm with over 85% accuracy. Our experimental results show, among others, that the most accurate classifier based on entropy triangles and the most useful oversampling are the supported vector classifiers and oversampling techniques for shark scent.

AI.tldr: Proposes a new three-step machine-learning framework (entropy triangle method) to predict heart rhythms from ECG data, achieving >85% accuracy for non-sinus rhythms.
AI.motivation: Accurate prediction of heart rhythms, especially non-sinus arrhythmias, is crucial in medicine, yet remains challenging. The authors aim to improve predictive performance and handling of class imbalance in multi-rhythm ECG datasets.
AI.method: They design the entropy triangle method with three parts: (1) feature engineering on 12-lead ECG signals; (2) an entropy triangle-based oversampling scheme (including a novel “shark scent” oversampling technique) to address class imbalance; and (3) classification of 11 heart rhythms using machine-learning models, identifying support vector classifiers as particularly effective when combined with the proposed oversampling.
AI.result: Using a 12-lead ECG database of 10,646 patients and 11 rhythm classes, their approach predicts non-sinus rhythms with over 85% accuracy. Among tested setups, support vector classifiers with entropy-triangle-based oversampling, especially the shark scent method, yield the highest accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The entropy triangle framework, together with the shark scent oversampling strategy, offers a promising new machine-learning approach to predict multiple heart rhythms from ECGs, delivering strong performance for non-sinus rhythms and suggesting practical value for clinical arrhythmia prediction.

title: What a Cross-Model Fixed-Point Census Can and Cannot Arbitrate About Repetition
comment: 9 pages, 2 tables. Companion to arXiv:2608.21315 and arXiv:2608.10986. Code, per-run results, and the findings ledger: https://github.com/nicoveraz/token-lattice-ca (archived: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21880472)
summary: Two accounts of neural text degeneration coexist. One locates the cause in the training data -- repetition in the corpus produces repetition in the output, established by training on repetition-sorted data -- the other in the trained network, in copying circuits and repetition features. Neither has been arbitrated across a broad cohort of pretrained models: the causal work trains its own. We report an observational measurement in a different currency: the fixed-point structure of a model's own short-window argmax map, censused from 96 random two-token starts over 17 off-the-shelf models, always unprompted -- a companion paper shows nine tokens of conditioning move this readout across most of its range. The four-way class is stable across census seeds on 17 of 17. Three exhibits. At fixed corpus (The Pile), fixed scale and that fixed domain, the class is not determined: across two size-matched tiers, pythia is a funnel while RWKV, Mamba and a second transformer family are not, and both hold their class across an order of magnitude of scale. Six of seven models in that ladder reach the same endpoint token, and those concentrating on it most strongly are among those that never stay there -- what varies is not where trajectories go but whether the destination self-continues. The deduplicated Pythia suite does not change the class. And the corpus-side inflow term proposed for this phenomenon does not select our endpoints once frequency is controlled, in English and three other languages. This is observational and cannot refute a training intervention. Funnels are common: eight of seventeen models, seven families, five corpora -- so the limit is not that the phenomenon is one model's peculiarity, but that within the one corpus where training data can be held fixed only one available family funnels; that subset cannot show the split is corpus-independent.

AI.tldr: The paper studies neural text degeneration by examining fixed points of models’ argmax dynamics, showing that many off-the-shelf models behave as ‘funnels’ but this behavior is not simply determined by training corpus repetition or frequency.
AI.motivation: There are two main hypotheses for why large language models degenerate into repetitive text: (1) repetition patterns in the training data directly cause repetition, and (2) architectural or learned internal mechanisms (copying circuits, repetition features) cause it. Prior causal studies typically train their own models and focus on limited settings. The motivation is to provide an observational, architecture- and model-family-wide perspective using off-the-shelf models, and to characterize degeneration in terms of their intrinsic next-token dynamics rather than only corpus statistics.
AI.method: The authors define and measure the fixed-point structure of each model’s short-window argmax map: starting from 96 random two-token seeds, they repeatedly apply greedy decoding (argmax next token) and track whether the trajectories converge to self-perpetuating fixed points (funnels) or not. They perform a “census” of these trajectories across 17 pretrained models from multiple architectures and corpora, in an unprompted setting. They classify models into four behavioral classes based on their fixed-point dynamics, check stability across random seeds, compare size-matched families at fixed corpus (The Pile), assess effects of deduplication, and examine whether corpus-side frequency or proposed inflow terms predict the endpoint tokens across four languages.
AI.result: Across 17 models, the four-way behavioral class based on argmax dynamics is stable across census seeds. At fixed corpus, domain, and scale (The Pile), different model families can fall into different classes: Pythia models display funnel behavior while RWKV, Mamba, and another transformer family do not, and these classes persist across an order of magnitude in scale. Six of seven models in one scaling ladder converge to the same endpoint token, yet their tendency to remain there differs: what varies is the self-continuation of the endpoint, not its identity. Deduplicating the Pythia training data does not change its class. Corpus-side inflow and raw frequency fail to predict which tokens become endpoints once frequency is controlled, in English and three other languages. Funnels are widespread—seen in 8 of 17 models across 7 families and 5 corpora—indicating the phenomenon is not unique to a single model, but within The Pile only one family shows funneling, so the corpus-independent vs. architecture-dependent split remains unresolved.
AI.conclusion: Neural text degeneration, as captured by funnel-like fixed points under greedy decoding, cannot be fully explained by simple repetition statistics or frequency structure of the training corpus. Funnel behavior is common across many model families and corpora but is not determined solely by the data: at fixed corpus and domain, some architectures funnel while others do not, and deduplication has little effect. The work reframes degeneration as an emergent property of models’ internal argmax dynamics, suggesting that architectural choices or training dynamics, rather than corpus repetition alone, play a critical role. However, the observational nature of the study means it cannot rule out specific training interventions; controlled ablations are still needed to disentangle corpus vs. model causes definitively.

title: When Honesty is Not Enough in AI Debate
summary: Scalable oversight aims to verify the behaviour of agents whose capabilities exceed those of their overseers. AI debate has been proposed as an oversight solution in which competing agents help a resource-limited verifier assess claims that it cannot reliably evaluate unaided. Much of its promise rests on incentivizing honest arguments that lead to correct verdicts. Yet a correct verdict need not uniquely determine the arguments used to support it. Agents may retain discretion over which correct claims to present, how to frame them, and in what order to disclose them. This residual freedom can allow agents to shape what the verifier learns beyond the task-relevant conclusion, pursuing latent objectives without compromising verdict correctness. To study this phenomenon, we introduce the framework strategic interactive oversight (SIO), which treats oversight jointly as a verification mechanism and a strategic communication channel. Within this framework, we formalise the notion of task-admissible latent optimisation, which entails the pursuit of latent objectives while maintaining a prescribed task performance. As proof-of-concept, we instantiate SIO in the establish protocol debate with cross-examination and quantify a tradeoff between task success and information disclosure about a hidden variable. The trade-off identifies a strategic window in which substantial disclosure remains compatible with task admissibility. Towards mitigation, we reduce admissible bias by expanding the cross-examiner's role to mitigate persistent disclosure over finite interaction horizons. Our results highlight the need to evaluate oversight not only by the correctness of its verdicts, but also by the information conveyed through its transcripts.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework showing that even when AI oversight schemes like debate reliably get the right answer, debating agents can still strategically shape what the human overseer learns, pursuing hidden goals without breaking task performance.
AI.motivation: Existing scalable oversight methods, such as AI debate, mainly focus on ensuring that oversight yields correct verdicts in tasks too hard for humans alone. However, correctness of the final verdict does not fully constrain what information or arguments agents reveal along the way. This leaves room for agents to strategically communicate in ways that optimize latent objectives (e.g., influencing beliefs or leaking information) while still appearing honest and task-correct. The authors aim to formalize and quantify this overlooked risk and to explore how oversight protocols might be redesigned to limit such strategic misuse of communication.
AI.method: The authors propose the Strategic Interactive Oversight (SIO) framework, which models oversight both as a verification mechanism and as a strategic communication channel between agents and a verifier. Within SIO, they define “task-admissible latent optimisation,” where agents optimize hidden objectives subject to a constraint that task performance (e.g., correctness of the verdict) remains acceptable. They instantiate SIO in a concrete AI debate protocol with cross-examination, modeling agents’ incentives to reveal or conceal information about a hidden variable. They then analyze, likely using game-theoretic and information-theoretic tools, the trade-off between achieving the task objective (correct verdicts) and controlling information disclosure. Finally, they explore protocol modifications, especially expanding the cross-examiner’s role, to reduce the room for harmful strategic disclosure within finite-length interactions.
AI.result: In the instantiated debate-with-cross-examination setting, the authors show that there is a quantifiable trade-off between task success and the amount of information revealed about a hidden variable. They identify a “strategic window” where agents can substantially disclose information about this hidden variable while still satisfying the admissible task performance criteria, implying room for significant latent optimization without observable task failure. By extending and strengthening the cross-examiner’s role in the debate protocol, they demonstrate that it is possible to shrink this window—reducing biased or persistent disclosure over a finite number of interaction rounds—though not necessarily eliminating it entirely.
AI.conclusion: Oversight mechanisms like AI debate cannot be evaluated solely on whether they yield correct verdicts; they must also be assessed as strategic communication channels that can be exploited for latent objectives. The SIO framework formalizes how agents can perform “task-admissible latent optimisation,” shaping what overseers learn without harming observable task performance. Concrete analysis in a debate protocol reveals that nontrivial information leakage or influence can coexist with high task success, underscoring the need for protocol designs (e.g., more powerful cross-examination) that explicitly constrain or detect such strategic communication. Overall, scalable oversight research should treat transcript content and information flow as first-class safety concerns, not just final-answer correctness.

title: EnSiTa - A Trilingual Multi-Domain Parallel Dataset and Benchmark for Domain-Specific Machine Translation
summary: Machine Translation (MT) for low-resource languages remains far behind that of high-resource languages, and the gap is widest in specialised domains, where parallel data is scarce or entirely absent. We present EnSiTa, a trilingual multi-domain parallel dataset and benchmark for English, Sinhala and Tamil. EnSiTa provides human post-edited training data for seven domains, plus manually translated test sets for those and one additional domain, all produced by professional translators under a multi-year, rigorously quality-controlled process. Using this dataset, we conduct an extensive study of domain-specific MT for all six language directions, fine-tuning a from-scratch Transformer, a pre-trained translation model (NLLB-600M), and decoder-only LLMs (Gemma 3 family, 1B-12B, and TranslateGemma) across training-data sizes, model scales, and in-domain, cross-domain, multilingual and multi-domain settings. To the best of our knowledge, this is the most extensive systematically documented multi-domain parallel data creation and benchmarking effort for low-resource MT. Our data and models will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: They introduce EnSiTa, a high-quality multi-domain English–Sinhala–Tamil parallel dataset and benchmark, and systematically evaluate multiple MT architectures on it for all translation directions.
AI.motivation: Low-resource languages, especially in specialised domains, lack sufficient parallel data, leading to poor MT quality compared with high-resource languages. Existing resources are limited in size, domains, and documentation, and there is a need for a rigorously constructed, multi-domain benchmark to study domain-specific and cross-domain MT for truly low-resource language pairs like English–Sinhala and English–Tamil.
AI.method: They build EnSiTa, a trilingual English–Sinhala–Tamil parallel corpus with professional, post-edited training data in seven domains and manually translated test sets in eight domains, created over multiple years with strict quality control. Using this corpus, they fine-tune and compare several model types— a from-scratch Transformer, a pre-trained NLLB-600M MT model, and multiple decoder-only LLMs from the Gemma 3 family (1B–12B) plus TranslateGemma— across six translation directions. They systematically vary training-data size, model scale, and training setups (in-domain, cross-domain, multilingual, multi-domain) to evaluate domain-specific MT performance.
AI.result: They obtain a comprehensive set of MT results for all six language directions and multiple domains, showing how different architectures and scales behave under various data and domain configurations for low-resource MT. The experiments provide empirical evidence on the effectiveness of pre-trained MT models vs. from-scratch Transformers and decoder-only LLMs, and how multi-domain and multilingual training affects performance in low-resource, specialised-domain settings.
AI.conclusion: EnSiTa constitutes, to their knowledge, the most extensive and systematically documented multi-domain parallel dataset and benchmark for low-resource MT, specifically for English–Sinhala–Tamil. It enables detailed, reproducible study of domain-specific and cross-domain translation for low-resource languages. The authors will publicly release both the dataset and the fine-tuned models to support future research and applications.

title: ASIRF: An Agentic Framework for Context-Dependent Sensitive Information Redaction
summary: Sensitive information is defined by domain and intent, not a universal category, yet redaction systems such as privacy filters and named-entity recognizers fix a taxonomy at training time, requiring retraining for each new domain. We introduce ASIRF (Agentic Sensitive Information Redaction Framework), which retrieves domain-specific definitions based on the input's domain from a flexible knowledge base at inference time, needing no retraining to adapt. Two architectures, a three-call multi-agent pipeline and a single-agent variant, are evaluated across ten small open-weight models and eight datasets, including out-of-distribution fictional domains, against the OpenAI Privacy Filter (OPF) as a trained-classifier baseline. With only a few dozen expert-authored definitions per domain and no training data, ASIRF's recall exceeds OPF's in 68 of 80 model-domain combinations (85 percent), by at least one of the two architectures, with shortfalls confined mostly to OPF's training-distribution domains.

AI.tldr: The paper presents ASIRF, a flexible sensitive-information redaction framework that dynamically retrieves domain-specific definitions at inference time, outperforming a fixed-taxonomy classifier baseline without retraining.
AI.motivation: Existing redaction tools rely on fixed taxonomies defined at training time, which makes them inflexible and hard to adapt to new domains or intents without retraining, even though sensitivity is inherently domain- and intent-dependent. The authors aim to build a redaction framework that can easily adapt to new domains using declarative domain knowledge instead of labeled training data.
AI.method: They propose ASIRF (Agentic Sensitive Information Redaction Framework), which uses a knowledge base of expert-authored, domain-specific sensitive-information definitions. At inference time, ASIRF first infers the domain of the input, then retrieves the corresponding definitions and applies them to redact sensitive content. They implement two architectures: (1) a three-call multi-agent pipeline and (2) a more compact single-agent variant. They evaluate these across ten small open-weight language models and eight datasets, including out-of-distribution fictional settings.
AI.result: Without using any labeled training data and using only a few dozen expert definitions per domain, ASIRF achieves higher recall than the OpenAI Privacy Filter (OPF) in 68 out of 80 model–domain combinations (85%), according to at least one of the proposed architectures. Where ASIRF underperforms, it is mainly on domains that are close to OPF's training distribution.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, knowledge-base-driven redaction via ASIRF can surpass a strong fixed-taxonomy trained-classifier baseline in recall for most domains, especially in out-of-distribution settings, while avoiding retraining costs. This demonstrates the value of separating sensitive-information definitions from model training and retrieving them at inference time.

title: StepCOPS: Closed-Testing Lower-Tail Certificates for Language-Model Policy Selection
summary: Post-training pipelines must select one language-model policy from many checkpoints, prompts, and decoding rules. Mean evaluator scores can conceal rare failures, whereas simultaneous candidate-wise confidence bounds can be unnecessarily conservative. We introduce StepCOPS, which uses an independent proposal split to nominate one lower-tail floor per candidate, exact binomial tests on a fresh certification split, and Holm's step-down procedure to certify a set of floors. With probability at least $1-δ$, every certified floor, including the largest floor used for policy selection, is below its candidate's population lower $α$-quantile. This guarantee assumes i.i.d. evaluation units while allowing arbitrary within-unit dependence across candidates. Across 24 predeclared configurations and 11 benchmarks, StepCOPS obtains 96.4% selected-policy coverage over 500 paired trials, raises the certified floor by 1.5 points over both proposal-Bonferroni and exact COPS, remains 0.6 points below the large-reference jury oracle, and abstains in 2.4% of trials. Shadow-judge, benchmark-native, artifact, and leave-one-judge-out audits characterize the proxy boundary: the guarantee applies to the fixed jury score, not directly to human safety.

AI.tldr: StepCOPS is a statistical procedure to more reliably select a language-model policy by certifying lower performance bounds while tightly controlling error across many candidate models and evaluation settings.
AI.motivation: In post-training of language models, practitioners must pick a single deployment policy from many checkpoints, prompts, and decoding strategies. Traditional selection via mean evaluator scores can hide rare but significant failures, which is problematic for safety. Existing multiple-comparison corrections that give simultaneous confidence guarantees across many candidates tend to be overly conservative, leading to weak certified guarantees on model reliability. The paper is motivated by the need for a statistically principled yet powerful method to certify that the chosen policy meets a minimum performance or safety floor with high probability, even when many candidate policies are being compared and evaluated using finite noisy judgments.
AI.method: The authors propose StepCOPS, a statistical certification and selection procedure. It splits evaluation data into two parts: a proposal split and a certification split. On the proposal split, for each candidate policy, it proposes a lower-tail performance floor (a candidate lower bound on an \/alpha-quantile of the model’s score distribution). On the certification split, it uses exact binomial tests to check whether each proposed floor is indeed below the candidate’s true population lower \alpha-quantile. To handle multiplicity across many candidates without excessive conservatism, it applies Holm’s step-down multiple-testing procedure to these binomial tests. This yields a set of certified floors, one per candidate, such that with probability at least 1-\delta, all certified floors (including the maximum floor used for selection) are valid lower bounds. The method assumes evaluation units are i.i.d. but allows arbitrary dependence between candidates within each unit (e.g., same prompt or judge seeing multiple policies).
AI.result: In experiments covering 24 predeclared post-training configurations and 11 benchmarks, the authors evaluate StepCOPS over 500 paired trials of policy selection. They report that the selected policy meets its certified lower bound (coverage) in 96.4% of trials, aligning with the nominal high-probability guarantee. Compared to baseline procedures like proposal-Bonferroni and exact COPS, StepCOPS achieves certified performance floors that are on average 1.5 points higher, demonstrating improved power while maintaining validity. Relative to a strong but infeasible oracle based on a large-reference jury, StepCOPS’s certified floors are only 0.6 points lower on average, indicating near-oracle tightness. The method abstains from certifying (i.e., declines to select under its guarantee) in 2.4% of trials, reflecting conservative behavior when data are insufficient for strong guarantees.
AI.conclusion: StepCOPS offers a practical, statistically rigorous way to select language-model policies with certified lower performance bounds in multi-candidate post-training pipelines. By combining data-splitting, exact binomial testing, and Holm’s step-down adjustment, it controls error across many candidates while avoiding the excessive conservatism of traditional simultaneous confidence bounds. Empirically, it delivers high coverage and significantly stronger certified floors than existing methods, approaching the performance of an oracle selector. However, the guarantee is explicitly tied to the fixed jury score used for evaluation and does not, by itself, guarantee real-world human safety. The authors highlight this distinction through several audits (shadow-judge, benchmark-native, artifact, and leave-one-judge-out), clarifying that the method certifies reliability with respect to a particular proxy metric rather than directly certifying safety outcomes.

title: Towards An LLM-Driven Unified Conversion Framework for BT and FSM in Autonomous Intelligent Systems
summary: Finite state machine (FSM) and behavior trees (BT) are widely adopted behavioral modeling paradigms for autonomous intelligent systems. While functionally equivalent and inter-convertible in principle, existing transformation methods between FSM and BT face major challenges in preserving behavioral completeness and avoiding model complexity explosion. To overcome these issues, we propose an LLM-driven unified conversion framework that enables automatic, efficient, and semantically consistent transformation between FSM and BT. Specifically, a novel loop execution BT structure is designed for LLM to accurately capture the loop structure in FSM, thereby preserving behavioral completeness. To mitigate the state explosion problem in BT-to-FSM conversion, a depth compression strategy is introduced with LLM prompt to eliminate redundant control nodes, complemented by differentiated hierarchical conversion rules that collectively reduce the number of required sub-FSM. Simulation experiments in multiple autonomous decision-making scenarios demonstrate that the proposed framework enables an accurate and automated bidirectional conversion between FSM and BT.
