Furthermore, it significantly enhances the scalability and maintainability of generated models compared to traditional approaches, providing a practical solution for behavior model conversion in consumer-grade autonomous intelligent systems such as service robots, game agents, and smart home devices

AI.tldr: They propose an LLM-based framework for automatically converting between finite state machines (FSM) and behavior trees (BT) without losing behaviors or causing model blow-up, making it practical for real-world autonomous systems.
AI.motivation: FSMs and BTs are two dominant ways to model behavior in autonomous systems, but converting between them is difficult: current methods often lose behaviors (especially loops) or produce overly complex models with state explosion. A unified, practical conversion solution would help reuse designs, tools, and code across different behavior modeling paradigms in robots, games, and smart devices.
AI.method: They design an LLM-driven conversion framework that uses carefully crafted prompts and structural templates to translate between FSM and BT. For FSM-to-BT, they introduce a dedicated loop-execution BT pattern that lets the LLM faithfully encode FSM loops. For BT-to-FSM, they use a depth compression strategy in the prompts to remove redundant control nodes and apply hierarchical conversion rules, which together reduce the number of sub-FSMs and overall complexity.
AI.result: In simulation across multiple autonomous decision-making scenarios, their framework can automatically perform accurate bidirectional conversion between FSM and BT. The converted models preserve behavior while being significantly more compact and manageable than those generated by traditional conversion approaches.
AI.conclusion: An LLM-guided, structure-aware conversion framework can achieve behaviorally complete and scalable two-way transformation between FSMs and BTs. This offers a practical tool for building and maintaining behavior models in consumer-grade autonomous systems such as service robots, game AIs, and smart home devices, alleviating prior issues of loop handling and state explosion.

title: Benchmarking Arabic--Russian Machine Translation: A Comparison of Fine-tuned NMT and Few-shot LLMs under Rich Morphology and Low Lexical Overlap
summary: Arabic-Russian machine translation (MT) remains under-explored due to the rich morphology of Arabic and low lexical overlap between the two languages. We benchmark seven fine-tuned neural machine translation (NMT) models against four few-shot large language models (LLMs) on a 20k/5k/5k split of a new 15.47M-pair corpus. Fine-tuned NLLB-1.3B achieves the highest BLEU (16.3) and COMET (0.738). Aya-Expanse 8B leads the few-shot LLMs (BLEU 1.7 on 500 sentences, chrF 25.7), but all LLM scores remain far below the fine-tuned NMT baselines. Error analysis identifies low lexical overlap as the dominant failure mode; among the worst translations, mT5-small produces 32% too-short outputs. Bootstrap tests confirm significant differences among most models. Our results demonstrate that fine-tuned NMT significantly outperforms few-shot LLMs for Arabic-Russian translation under low-resource conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper compares fine-tuned neural MT models with few-shot LLMs for Arabic–Russian translation on a large new corpus and finds that fine-tuned NMT clearly wins in this low-resource setting.
AI.motivation: Arabic–Russian MT is under-studied because Arabic is morphologically rich and the two languages share little vocabulary, making translation hard and data sparse; the authors want to understand how traditional fine-tuned NMT compares to modern few-shot LLMs in this challenging pair.
AI.method: They construct a 15.47M sentence-pair Arabic–Russian corpus and create a 20k/5k/5k train/validation/test split for benchmarking. They fine-tune seven neural MT models, including NLLB-1.3B and mT5-small, and evaluate them with BLEU, COMET, and chrF. They also evaluate four large language models in a few-shot setting on a 500-sentence subset. They perform error analysis, focusing on lexical overlap and output length, and use bootstrap significance testing to compare models.
AI.result: Fine-tuned NLLB-1.3B achieves the best performance (BLEU 16.3, COMET 0.738). Among the few-shot LLMs, Aya-Expanse 8B performs best but only reaches BLEU 1.7 and chrF 25.7 on 500 sentences, far below the fine-tuned NMT baselines. Error analysis shows that low lexical overlap is the main source of translation errors, and mT5-small tends to generate overly short outputs (32% of worst cases). Bootstrap tests show that most performance differences between models are statistically significant.
AI.conclusion: In the low-resource Arabic–Russian setting, fine-tuned neural MT models substantially outperform few-shot large language models, indicating that task-specific fine-tuning remains crucial for difficult, morphologically rich, and lexically distant language pairs.

title: Policy as Code: A Coroutine-Bridge Harness for Fast-Reasoning Reliability on CAR-bench
comment: 4 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Technical report for the winning entry in Track 2 (Cerebras Fast-Reasoning) of the CAR-bench Challenge at IJCAI-ECAI 2026
summary: CAR-bench evaluates whether tool-using agents stay reliable under real-world uncertainty, executing every tool inside the evaluator so that each tool-result exchange is a separate agent round-trip. A conventional next-action agent can batch parallel tool calls, but a chain of dependent calls costs it one model call per round of results. We present a coroutine-bridge harness in which the model's only action is to emit a Python program that blocks and resumes in place across evaluator tool exchanges. This decouples model invocation from tool round-trips: on the public test split the agent uses a median of two model calls against seven agent turns per task, resolving a full multi-turn task in a median of 1.8 s of model latency on Cerebras gpt-oss-120b. Because the action surface is executable code, deterministic CAR-bench policies are encoded directly as logic in the tool layer rather than as prompt rules, enforcing compliance at zero reasoning cost. On the official hidden evaluation the harness won Track 2 with 60.0% Pass^3, 4.5x the organizer baseline, at the lowest estimated cost and the fastest median task latency (3.14 s) of any entry scoring above that baseline; the same unchanged harness reproduced an identical 60.0% Pass^3 on GPT-5.5 in the Open track, matching frontier-model agents. A single static prompt, appended with per-task state at the tail, stays byte-identical across calls and across tasks: the frozen submission prompt served 78% of input tokens from cache (86.6% across its warm tail), against 73% over a three-week development corpus in which prompt edits repeatedly reset the cache. This compounds the few-call design into a small fraction of nominal input compute.

AI.tldr: Introduces a coroutine-bridge harness that lets tool-using agents execute Python code that blocks and resumes across tool calls, dramatically reducing required model calls and latency on CAR-bench while improving reliability under uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Existing tool-using agents incur one model call per round of tool results, especially for chains of dependent calls, leading to high latency, cost, and brittle prompt-based control. CAR-bench stresses agents under real-world uncertainty, so there is a need for architectures that keep agents reliable and efficient while handling many tool interactions.
AI.method: Replace traditional next-action planning with a coroutine-bridge harness where the model’s sole job is to emit an executable Python program. This program can block and resume in place as tools are called by the evaluator, decoupling model inference from the number of tool round-trips. Deterministic policies and compliance constraints are encoded directly as logic in the tool layer instead of prompts. Use a single static prompt whose bytes remain identical across calls and tasks, enabling very high prompt caching and low input compute. Evaluate on CAR-bench (public and hidden splits) and across different models (Cerebras gpt-oss-120b, GPT-5.5).
AI.result: On the CAR-bench public split, the agent needs a median of only two model calls for seven agent turns per task, achieving a median of 1.8 s total model latency on gpt-oss-120b. On the official hidden evaluation, the harness wins Track 2 with 60.0% Pass^3—4.5× the organizer baseline—while also being the cheapest and fastest (3.14 s median task latency) among methods above that baseline. The same unchanged harness gets the same 60.0% Pass^3 with GPT-5.5 in the Open track, matching frontier-model agents. The frozen static prompt achieves 78% token cache hit overall (86.6% on its variable tail) and 73% over a multi-week development corpus, greatly reducing effective input compute.
AI.conclusion: By shifting control logic from prompts into executable code and decoupling model calls from tool round-trips, the coroutine-bridge harness makes tool-using agents on CAR-bench far more efficient, fast, and reliable under uncertainty. The design supports strong performance across different models with a single static prompt, leveraging caching to cut input compute and showing that much of tool-use orchestration can be handled outside the model without sacrificing capability.

title: ModularSQL: A Runtime Guardrail for the Multiplicity Blind Spot in Text-to-SQL
summary:
Text-to-SQL systems are increasingly deployed on production databases, where queries that pass benchmark evaluation can still produce results that distort downstream workflows. Standard set-based execution accuracy (Set-EX) collapses duplicate rows and can therefore miss multiplicity errors, including missing DISTINCT, inflated aggregates, and Cartesian-style join explosions.
  We call this the Multiplicity Blind Spot (MBS) and introduce Multiset-EX, a multiplicity-preserving evaluation criterion that exposes such failures. Across released DeepEye-SQL artifacts from three backbones (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, and Gemma-3-27B) on executable BIRD-Dev N=1532, we find a consistent 5.81--6.79 pp gap between Set-EX and Multiset-EX. The gap is not specific to DeepEye-SQL: it persists on released DAIL-SQL+GPT-4 (5.22 pp) and BIRD GPT-3.5-turbo (3.39 pp) predictions.
  We further introduce ModularSQL, a lightweight post-selection runtime guardrail that probes executed results for multiplicity anomalies and applies deterministic patches or low-cost LLM rescue only to flagged queries. Integrated with DeepEye-SQL using Qwen3-Coder, ModularSQL preserves Set-EX at 72.06% while improving Multiset-EX from 65.86% to 67.75% (+1.89 pp). It flags 77 high-risk anomalies, while adding only $0.0076 in total LLM cost and 120 ms amortized latency per query. Cross-pipeline evaluation shows that the candidate-free detector and deterministic patches also transfer to independently released prediction sets. Overall, these results show that benchmark accuracy does not necessarily imply execution-safe SQL, and that lightweight, multiplicity-aware runtime guardrails can narrow this gap with modest computational overhead.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a key failure mode in Text-to-SQL evaluation—ignoring row multiplicities—and proposes a new multiplicity-aware metric plus a lightweight runtime guardrail to catch and fix such errors cheaply.
AI.motivation: Standard Text-to-SQL evaluation uses set-based execution accuracy (Set-EX), which ignores duplicate rows. This hides important logical errors where the SQL query returns the right distinct tuples but with wrong multiplicities (e.g., missing DISTINCT, over-counting in aggregates, or Cartesian product explosions). These multiplicity errors can silently distort downstream analytics and decisions in real deployments, even when benchmarks say a system is accurate. The authors want to reveal and mitigate this gap between benchmark accuracy and execution-safe behavior.
AI.method: 1) Define the Multiplicity Blind Spot (MBS) in current evaluation and introduce a new metric, Multiset-EX, which compares execution results while preserving row multiplicities, thus surfacing errors like missing DISTINCT or inflated aggregates. 2) Empirically measure the gap between Set-EX and Multiset-EX across multiple strong Text-to-SQL systems (DeepEye-SQL with different backbone LLMs, DAIL-SQL+GPT-4, and BIRD GPT-3.5-turbo) on the executable BIRD-Dev dataset. 3) Propose ModularSQL, a modular post-selection runtime guardrail: it detects multiplicity anomalies in executed query results, applies deterministic rule-based patches when possible, and falls back to a low-cost LLM “rescue” step only for flagged queries. 4) Integrate ModularSQL into the DeepEye-SQL pipeline, evaluate the effect on Set-EX and Multiset-EX along with latency and LLM cost, and test transferability of the detector and deterministic patches on independently released prediction sets.
AI.result: 1) Quantitatively, there is a consistent 3–7 percentage point gap between traditional Set-EX and multiplicity-aware Multiset-EX across multiple models: 5.81–6.79 pp for DeepEye-SQL variants, 5.22 pp for DAIL-SQL+GPT-4, and 3.39 pp for BIRD GPT-3.5-turbo. This empirically confirms the prevalence of multiplicity-related errors that benchmarks currently miss. 2) When ModularSQL is integrated with DeepEye-SQL using Qwen3-Coder, Set-EX remains high at 72.06%, while Multiset-EX improves from 65.86% to 67.75%, a gain of +1.89 pp. 3) ModularSQL flags 77 high-risk multiplicity anomalies with very low overhead: about $0.0076 additional LLM cost in total and 120 ms amortized extra latency per query. 4) The multiplicity anomaly detector and deterministic patches generalize across different Text-to-SQL pipelines, successfully transferring to other released prediction sets without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Ignoring multiplicities in query result evaluation hides a significant class of logical errors in Text-to-SQL systems, so benchmark accuracy based on set semantics does not guarantee execution-safe SQL for real-world databases. A multiplicity-preserving metric (Multiset-EX) reveals these issues, showing meaningful accuracy drops relative to Set-EX in strong existing systems. Moreover, lightweight, modular runtime guardrails like ModularSQL can automatically detect and correct many multiplicity anomalies, narrowing the gap between benchmark and execution-safe performance with minimal additional cost and latency. This suggests that future Text-to-SQL research and deployment should incorporate multiplicity-aware evaluation and runtime safeguards.

title: An Exploratory Ablation of a Small MLA--SSM Hybrid Language Model
comment: 6 pages, 7 figures. Exploratory single-seed ablation study. Code and replication package available at https://github.com/unseen1980/talh
summary: We report an exploratory, single-seed ablation of TALH (Adaptive Latent Hybrid), a decoder-only language model with parallel Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) and a custom recurrent state-space (SSM) branch. Five variants, spanning 117--217M estimated active parameters per token, are trained from scratch on a FineWeb sample for the same number of optimisation steps and tokens. In this specific setup, removing the SSM branch gives the largest degradation in validation perplexity (MLA-only PPL 315), whereas removing MLA has a much smaller effect (SSM-only PPL 239). A dense-FFN hybrid obtains PPL 231, compared with 240 for the tested top-2 ternary-MoE hybrid, while using 3.87 GB less peak training memory. We also preserve a preliminary Apple M3 timing observation: among the five unoptimised implementations, MLA-only has the flattest measured time-to-first-token curve from 512 to 2,048 prompt tokens, although the dense Transformer is much faster in absolute terms. Because the runs are single-seed, parameter counts are unmatched, the evaluation stream may overlap the training source, and raw repeated timing records are unavailable, these results support implementation-specific hypotheses rather than general conclusions about MLA, SSMs, or mixture-of-experts models.

AI.tldr: Exploratory ablation of a hybrid MLA+SSM language model shows the SSM branch contributes more to perplexity than MLA in this setup, dense FFN beats a small MoE in both perplexity and memory, and timing results are implementation-specific and not generalizable.
AI.motivation: To empirically probe how much different architectural branches (MLA, SSM, dense FFN vs ternary MoE) contribute to performance, memory, and latency in a hybrid language model, and to validate or question prior implementation-specific timing observations.
AI.method: Train from scratch five single-seed TALH variants (MLA-only, SSM-only, hybrids with dense FFN or ternary MoE, and a dense Transformer) with similar active parameter counts (117–217M) on the same FineWeb sample, for the same number of steps and tokens. Measure validation perplexity, peak training memory, and time-to-first-token vs prompt length on an Apple M3, then compare variants via ablation (removing MLA or SSM branches) and architectural swaps (dense FFN vs top-2 ternary MoE).
AI.result: In this configuration, removing the SSM branch severely hurts validation perplexity (MLA-only PPL 315) while SSM-only degradation is smaller (PPL 239). A dense-FFN hybrid achieves PPL 231, outperforming a top-2 ternary-MoE hybrid (PPL 240) while reducing peak training memory by 3.87 GB. MLA-only implementation shows the flattest time-to-first-token scaling with prompt length from 512–2,048 tokens on Apple M3, but an unoptimised dense Transformer is faster overall. However, these findings are based on single-seed, parameter-mismatched runs and limited timing data.
AI.conclusion: The exploratory ablations suggest that, in this particular TALH setup, the SSM branch is more critical than MLA for perplexity, and that a simple dense-FFN hybrid can outperform a small ternary MoE hybrid in both quality and memory efficiency. MLA-only may offer more stable latency scaling with context length on the tested hardware, but due to methodological limitations (single seed, unmatched parameter counts, possible data leakage, incomplete timing logs), the authors emphasise that these results are tentative and reflect implementation-specific behavior rather than general statements about MLA, SSMs, or MoE architectures.

title: TTLab at AlexandriaX-2026: A Fine-Tuned Surface Tagger for Arabic Machine-Translation Error-Span Detection and Classification
comment: Accepted at ArabicNLP 2026, shared task AlexandriaX-2026
summary: We present TTLab's submission to the AlexandriaX-2026 Subtask~3 on Arabic MT error span detection and classification. Our system frames the task as token-level classification over surface forms, preserving character offsets to ensure exact alignment with the evaluation metric. To handle severe label imbalance, we employ a focal loss with class weighting and dialect-specific decoding thresholds. Among six Arabic pre-trained encoders, MARBERTv2 achieves the best overall performance of 40.8 and 40.91 on the development and test set, respectively, ranking $\nth{3}$ out of all participating teams. While our system localizes error spans effectively, classification of rare error types remains challenging, highlighting the need for data augmentation for tail categories. The code is available at ${\href{https://github.com/ENTAILab/arabic-dialectal-mt-error-span-detection}{\faGithub~ TTLab at AlexandriaX-2026}$

AI.tldr: The paper presents TTLab’s system for Arabic machine translation (MT) error span detection and classification, treating it as token-level classification and achieving competitive performance (3rd place) using MARBERTv2 with focal loss and class weighting.
AI.motivation: Accurately detecting and classifying error spans in Arabic MT output is important but challenging, especially due to label imbalance and the diversity of Arabic dialects. Existing methods struggle with aligning predicted error spans to character-level evaluation and with handling rare error types. The authors aim to build a robust system that can localize error spans precisely and better manage class imbalance and dialect variation.
AI.method: The task is modeled as token-level classification over surface forms, while preserving character offsets so that predicted error spans align exactly with the evaluation metric. The authors experiment with six pre-trained Arabic encoders and incorporate focal loss with class weighting to mitigate severe label imbalance. They also use dialect-specific decoding thresholds to adapt predictions to different Arabic dialects. MARBERTv2 is selected as the best-performing encoder.
AI.result: MARBERTv2 yields the strongest results among the six evaluated encoders, reaching scores of 40.8 on the development set and 40.91 on the test set. The system ranks 3rd overall among all participating teams in the AlexandriaX-2026 Subtask 3 shared task. The method is effective at localizing error spans but shows weaker performance on rare error categories.
AI.conclusion: Token-level classification with careful preservation of character offsets and the use of focal loss with class weighting and dialect-specific thresholds can yield competitive performance on Arabic MT error span detection and classification. However, accurately classifying rare error types remains difficult, indicating that future work should focus on data augmentation and other techniques to improve performance on tail categories. The authors release their code to encourage further research and improvement in this area.

title: Operator Packages, Proposer Strength, and Construction-Family Plateaus in Office-Scale Verified Search
summary: Verified search, in which a language model proposes programs, a hard evaluator scores them, and selection keeps the best, has recently moved mathematical records; controlled ablations of the proposer-side components remain rare. We instrument a minimal FunSearch-style loop at office scale (a 30B local model on a laptop, 120-600 verified samples per run) with three operator packages: a schematic notebook the model writes and carries instead of verbatim elites, a named obstacle, and behavioural repulsion from constructions already found. On nine construction problems from a public repository, the complete 2^3 factorial with two replicates favours the primary contrast in a nominal two-stage analysis: the composition closes more of the seed-to-record gap (+0.196; nominal pooled p=0.023, stage-combination p~0.08; median per-problem effect +0.045). Repulsion raises construction-hash diversity everywhere (p=0.0039; partly a manipulation check). The factorial finds no positive memory-by-repulsion interaction (bounded to about +/-0.04); the gain decomposes additively, and memory+repulsion is the only arm that never collapses (0 of 18 runs), within 0.025 of the full composition. A frontier proposer under the identical loop reaches in tens of samples what the local model does not in hundreds; in single scoping runs its gains arrive without the operators. The search stalls after closing ~92% of the gap on the flagship problem, and the registered family-hint test gives the stall its first reading: named in words, the reference family is adopted and loses; handed as code, it is optimized, but our best finite-grid implementation remains below the plateau reached unaided. The loop transported and optimized the idea it was handed; no unaided run produced it. We release the harness, every candidate, and the dated pre-registrations.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different proposer-side operators (notebook-style memory, named obstacles, and behavioral repulsion) affect the performance of FunSearch-style verified search loops for mathematical construction problems, using a controlled factorial experiment with a 30B local model.
AI.motivation: Verified search has recently achieved record-breaking results in mathematics, but we lack careful, controlled studies of which components on the language-model proposer side actually matter. The authors aim to dissect and quantify the contribution of specific operator packages to performance and robustness, using modest compute rather than frontier models.
AI.method: They implement a minimal FunSearch-style loop on a laptop-scale 30B model, generating 120–600 verified samples per run on nine public construction problems. They systematically vary three binary operator packages—(1) a schematic notebook memory instead of copying elites verbatim, (2) a named obstacle mechanism, and (3) a behavioural repulsion term discouraging rediscovery of existing constructions—running a full 2^3 factorial design with two replicates. They perform nominal two-stage statistical analyses to estimate main effects and interactions on closing the gap between seed and record performance, as well as effects on diversity and stability of runs. They also compare this setup to a frontier-scale proposer under the same loop, and run a preregistered “family-hint” test where they hand the system a reference solution family either as natural language or as code, observing how the loop adopts and optimizes it.
AI.result: The full composition of the three operators significantly improves performance: it closes an additional ~0.196 of the seed-to-record performance gap on average, with nominal pooled p=0.023 and combined p about 0.08; the median per-problem effect is +0.045. Behavioural repulsion consistently increases construction-hash diversity across problems (p=0.0039), confirming it changes search behavior. No meaningful positive interaction is found between memory and repulsion (interaction effect bounded to ~±0.04); the gains from the operators are mostly additive, and the condition with both memory and repulsion is uniquely stable, with no total collapses across 18 runs and performance within 0.025 of the full composition. A strong frontier model in the identical loop quickly attains solutions that the 30B model never reaches, and its improvements often appear even without these operators. However, on a key flagship problem, search seems to stall after closing about 92% of the seed-to-record gap. In the preregistered family-hint test, when the solution family is described in words, the system adopts it but performs poorly; when given as code, the system successfully optimizes it, yet the best finite-grid implementation still falls short of the plateau found without the hint. The system can transport and refine external ideas it is handed, but does not discover that family unaided. All code, candidates, and preregistrations are released.
AI.conclusion: Specific proposer-side tools—particularly schematic notebook memory and behavioural repulsion—offer measurable, largely additive gains to FunSearch-style verified search at modest compute scales, improving both progress toward mathematical records and diversity/stability of runs. However, a stronger frontier model can overshadow these design details by achieving superior performance with far fewer samples, and the search still exhibits plateaus where further progress stalls. The family-hint experiment suggests the loop is good at importing and optimizing given ideas, including code-level descriptions of solution families, but weaker at independently discovering such families. The work provides a controlled empirical basis for thinking about proposer-side design in verified search and offers an open benchmark harness for further study.

title: How To Do Things With Prompts
comment: Invited for Cambridge Forum on AI
summary: When users address large language models, they produce directive speech acts whose pragmatic features differ from those of both everyday conversation and traditional human-computer interaction, and these features change as users gain familiarity with the systems they address. This paper applies speech act and politeness theory to a corpus-pragmatic analysis of 2,000 English-language prompts drawn from publicly shared ChatGPT conversations, 1,000 from 2023 and 1,000 from 2025, using the ShareChat dataset. Each prompt is annotated for illocutionary force, directness, propositional content, and the presence of politeness markers, and the distribution of these features is compared across the two sampling years. The results show a consistent movement toward indirect, implicit, and fragmentary realizations of directive force, accompanied by a decline in politeness marking. The largest single change, a shift of 14.9 percentage points, occurs in propositional content, where explicit specification of the requested action gives way to implicit reliance on the system's inferential capacity, suggesting that users have updated their model of what the system can recover from reduced input, treating it as a competent implicature resolver. Rather than asking whether LLMs "really" understand language, we should ask: what kind of language have we created in learning to speak to them?

AI.tldr: The paper studies how people’s ways of instructing ChatGPT have changed between 2023 and 2025, showing that prompts become more indirect, implicit, and less overtly polite as users grow more confident in the system’s inferential abilities.
AI.motivation: Existing work has asked whether large language models “really” understand language, but has paid less attention to how humans adapt their own language when speaking to these systems. As users become familiar with LLMs, their prompting style may shift in systematic ways, revealing a new, emergent human–machine register. The paper seeks to document and explain these changes using established theories of speech acts and politeness.
AI.method: The authors apply speech act theory and politeness theory to a corpus-pragmatic study of 2,000 English prompts taken from publicly shared ChatGPT conversations in the ShareChat dataset: 1,000 from 2023 and 1,000 from 2025. Each prompt is manually annotated for: (1) illocutionary force (type of speech act, especially directives), (2) degree of directness, (3) propositional content (how fully the requested action is specified), and (4) presence/absence of politeness markers. They then compare the distributions of these features between the 2023 and 2025 samples.
AI.result: Over time, prompts directed at ChatGPT show (a) more indirect, implicit, and fragmentary ways of realizing directive force, and (b) a decline in explicit politeness marking. The most pronounced change is in propositional content: there is a 14.9 percentage point decrease in prompts that explicitly spell out the requested action, replaced by prompts that rely on the system to infer what is wanted from less detailed input. This indicates that users increasingly assume the model can recover intended meaning and resolve implicatures from reduced cues.
AI.conclusion: User interaction with LLMs is giving rise to a distinctive form of directive language characterized by indirectness, underspecification, and reduced politeness marking. Rather than framing the central question as whether LLMs truly “understand” language, the authors argue we should focus on how our own linguistic practices have changed in adapting to them—i.e., on the emergent human–LLM register in which users treat the model as a capable resolver of implicatures and incomplete instructions.

title: LLMersion: A Local-First AI Agent Framework for Low-Cost Home Language Learning toward Educational Equity
summary: Artificial intelligence helps education most where an essential provision has been rationed by cost. For language learners that provision is a teacher's voice, which binds listening, reading, speaking, and writing into one act. Published evidence shows why most learners lack it, from a global shortage of 44 million teachers to heavy household tutoring bills, and why technology has not substituted for it: computer-assisted language learning proved effective but narrow, applications presuppose connectivity 2.6 billion people lack, and One Laptop per Child's randomized evaluation found that hardware without capable software teaches nothing. We distill eight difficulties and four binding constraints, and argue that small open-weight models dissolve the last: a complete four-skill stack now fits a \$200-class laptop and, on community measurements, generates at the pace speech is consumed, for about one US cent of electricity per study hour. We therefore propose LLMersion, a scheme for AI for education that runs entirely at home, over the learner's own documents, with an AI-written, AI-understood, AI-updated codebase anyone can customize; present LLMersion-1, a released open-source prototype (https://github.com/QM378/LLMersion); and outline the vision of a private learning agent.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI, specifically small open-weight language models, can effectively provide the scarce resource in language learning: a teacher-like voice that integrates all four language skills, and introduces LLMersion, an open-source, fully local, customizable AI language-learning system as a prototype toward a private learning agent.
AI.motivation: There is a worldwide shortage of teachers—estimated at 44 million—making personalized, integrated language instruction prohibitively expensive or inaccessible for many learners. Existing technologies like computer-assisted language learning, internet-dependent apps, and hardware-focused interventions (e.g., One Laptop per Child) have failed to replace the central role of a human teacher’s voice, either because they are too narrow in scope, require connectivity that billions lack, or provide hardware without adequate software. The authors want to address this structural scarcity of high-quality, holistic language instruction.
AI.method: The authors synthesize existing evidence on global teacher shortages, costs of tutoring, and the limitations of prior educational technologies to identify eight key difficulties and four binding constraints in AI for education. They then analyze the feasibility of using small open-weight language models running locally on low-cost hardware to overcome the last major constraint—computational and cost barriers. On this basis, they design and implement LLMersion, a system that operates fully offline, uses the learner’s own documents as content, and is built on an AI-written, AI-understood, and AI-updated codebase that users can customize. They release LLMersion-1 as an open-source prototype and describe its architecture and capabilities.
AI.result: They find that current small open-weight language models can provide a complete four-skill (listening, reading, speaking, writing) language-learning stack on a roughly $200 laptop. These models can generate content at approximately the rate speech is consumed, with an energy cost of about one US cent per hour of study, enabling affordable, local, teacher-like interaction. They demonstrate this in practice via LLMersion-1, an open-source prototype implementation that validates the viability of their proposed approach on commodity hardware.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that with the advent of small open-weight language models, the last major constraint preventing AI from effectively supporting language education—hardware and compute limitations—has been dissolved. This makes it possible to build fully local, private, and customizable learning agents that provide integrated four-skill language instruction without requiring internet connectivity or costly human tutoring. LLMersion is presented as an initial concrete realization of this vision, and the authors argue that such systems can substantially expand access to high-quality language learning worldwide.

title: Confident but Wrong: A Constrained Decoding Diagnostic for Low-Resource Automatic Post-Editing
summary: Automatic Post-Editing (APE) for low-resource languages (LRLs) often fails to improve Machine Translation (MT), and the score alone cannot say why: whether more training would help, or whether the training data is too inconsistent to learn from. We introduce a black-box, inference-time diagnostic that tells these two cases apart without retraining or annotation. It varies an edit-distance penalty $λ$ that drives the model from free editing towards copying the MT, and reads two signals: (1) the shape of the Translation Edit Rate (TER)-vs-$λ$ curve, U-shaped if edits from the model reduce error and monotonically decreasing if none does; and (2) the ordering of constraint variants that trust model confidence to increasing degrees, which shows whether confidence tracks edit quality. Across decoder-only and encoder-decoder models on English-Sinhala, the diagnostic exposes two failure modes consistent with a heterogeneous post-edit signal as the underlying cause: Binary Collapse, where the model copies the MT or makes off-target edits, and Confident Miscalibration, where the confidence signals we test do not separate useful edits from unnecessary ones. The pattern holds on English-Marathi and English-Tamil, with the failure modes tracking the post-edit distribution rather than MT quality or language family. Beyond diagnosis, the curve shape prescribes a concrete next step for practitioners; in the favorable case, a static constraint yields a free inference-time accuracy gain. We release the first English-Sinhala (~66k) and a new English-Tamil (~39k) APE datasets with all code.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an inference-time diagnostic for low-resource Automatic Post-Editing (APE) that distinguishes between data insufficiency and data inconsistency as causes of poor performance, without retraining or extra annotation.
AI.motivation: In low-resource language settings, APE models often fail to improve machine translation quality, and aggregate scores alone cannot reveal whether the problem is simply a lack of data (where more training might help) or a fundamentally noisy/heterogeneous post-edit signal that is hard to learn from. Practitioners need a way to understand failure modes and decide whether to invest in more training, data collection, or different modeling strategies.
AI.method: The authors design a black-box, inference-time diagnostic based on varying an edit-distance penalty λ that interpolates between free editing and merely copying the MT output. For each λ, they compute Translation Edit Rate (TER) and examine: (1) the shape of the TER-versus-λ curve—U-shaped when model edits are beneficial versus monotonically decreasing when edits are harmful or useless; and (2) the relative performance of constraint variants that differ in how strongly they trust model confidence. They apply this to both decoder-only and encoder-decoder APE models and interpret the signals to classify failure modes.
AI.result: On English–Sinhala APE (and also English–Marathi and English–Tamil), the diagnostic reveals two characteristic failure modes: (i) Binary Collapse, where the model either copies the MT or makes off-target edits, and (ii) Confident Miscalibration, where confidence scores fail to distinguish good from bad edits. These patterns correlate with the heterogeneity of the post-edit distribution rather than with MT quality or language family. In favorable cases (where the TER–λ curve indicates useful edits), a suitable static constraint at inference yields an accuracy gain without retraining.
AI.conclusion: The proposed diagnostic provides a simple, annotation-free way to distinguish when low-resource APE fails due to inconsistent post-edit signals versus other issues, guiding practitioners on whether to adjust inference constraints or reconsider data/modeling choices. It also offers a practical benefit: when the diagnostic indicates that edits are helpful, one can select a static constraint to improve accuracy for free at inference time. The paper additionally contributes new English–Sinhala and English–Tamil APE datasets and releases all code.

title: Named Entity Recognition using Sliding Window Approach
summary:
Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a core NLP task, but transformer-based sentence-level models struggle with long documents because of fixed input-length limits: truncation drops content, and non-overlapping chunking fragments entities at segment boundaries. We introduce an inference-only pipeline that extends a frozen NER model, MahaNER-BERT, fine-tuned on the MahaNER corpus, to document-level prediction via overlapping sliding windows that are merged into a single annotation, without any retraining or architectural change.
  We evaluate the pipeline on six document-level corpora built from the MahaNER test set using two strategies: Normal Repeat, which duplicates sentence sequences to extend length while preserving contextual continuity, and Random Repeat, which concatenates distinct sequences to produce longer, heterogeneous inputs, each instantiated at three length levels, across several sliding-window configurations. The model retains a macro F1-score of up to 0.8902, with variation staying below one percentage point regardless of document length or construction strategy. Compared with the conventional non-windowed approach, the sliding-window pipeline avoids the boundary-fragmentation errors introduced by non-overlapping segmentation, yielding consistently higher and more stable document-level F1-scores.

AI.tldr: They adapt a sentence-level BERT NER model to long documents using an overlapping sliding-window inference pipeline that merges window predictions, maintaining high and stable F1 across various synthetic long-document setups.
AI.motivation: Transformer NER models are limited by fixed maximum input lengths, causing truncation or non-overlapping chunking that can split entities at segment boundaries and degrade performance on long documents. There is a need for a simple, inference-time method to use existing, frozen sentence-level NER models effectively on long documents without retraining or architectural changes.
AI.method: They take a frozen MahaNER-BERT model (fine-tuned on sentence-level MahaNER data) and apply it to long documents via overlapping sliding windows. Each long document is segmented into overlapping spans within the model’s length limit; NER is run on each span, and the span-level outputs are merged into a single, consistent document-level annotation, resolving overlaps/boundaries. To evaluate, they construct six document-level corpora from the MahaNER test set: Normal Repeat (contextually continuous extended texts created by repeating sentences) and Random Repeat (heterogeneous long inputs formed by concatenating different sentence sequences), each at three length scales. They test several sliding-window configurations on these corpora and compare against conventional non-windowed, non-overlapping segmentation.
AI.result: Across all long-document setups and window configurations, the sliding-window pipeline keeps macro F1 up to 0.8902, with performance variations under 1 percentage point regardless of document length or how documents are constructed. In contrast, conventional non-overlapping segmentation introduces boundary-fragmentation errors that reduce and destabilize F1. The sliding-window method consistently yields higher and more stable document-level macro F1-scores than the baseline.
AI.conclusion: A simple inference-only sliding-window pipeline can effectively extend a sentence-level transformer NER model to document-level usage without retraining or changing the architecture. Overlapping windows and careful merging mitigate boundary-fragmentation errors, maintaining high, stable NER performance on long documents, independent of document length and composition strategy.

title: DP-IPI: A Hybrid Differential Privacy Text Rewriting Mechanism for Indirect Personal Identifiers in Clinical Texts
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables, accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Findings)
summary: Despite the strengths of modern anonymization and de-identification techniques, the risk of re-identification remains significant due to the indirect identifiers remaining in texts. To address this problem, recent works have applied text rewriting under Differential Privacy (DP) to prevent data linkage by perturbing texts via noise addition. Such methods privatize all tokens in a text indiscriminately, diminishing text quality and usability in critical domains such as in clinical settings. Focusing on indirect personal identifiers (IPIs), we introduce a utility-preserving DP text rewriting method that only privatizes spans containing IPIs. We show that our method effectively reduces re-identification risks in clinical texts while being producing more coherent and usable output texts, leading to higher privacy-utility trade-offs. In this, we demonstrate the effectiveness of hybrid text privatization, which leverages the promise of DP in an efficient, usable manner.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a differential-privacy-based text rewriting method that selectively perturbs only indirect personal identifiers (IPIs) rather than all tokens, improving the privacy-utility trade-off for clinical text de-identification.
AI.motivation: Existing anonymization/de-identification techniques are vulnerable to re-identification attacks via indirect identifiers left in text. Prior DP text rewriting methods perturb the entire text uniformly, which harms readability and usability, especially in sensitive domains like clinical records. There is a need for a method that maintains strong privacy guarantees while preserving the utility and coherence of texts by focusing on the true privacy risk sources: IPIs.
AI.method: The authors introduce a hybrid, utility-preserving DP text rewriting approach that detects spans containing indirect personal identifiers (IPIs) and applies differential-privacy-based perturbations only to those spans. Non-IPI content is left unchanged to retain semantic fidelity and readability. They evaluate this selective privatization on clinical text, comparing privacy risk (re-identification likelihood) and utility (text quality, coherence, and usability) against full-text DP rewriting baselines.
AI.result: Experiments on clinical datasets show that selectively privatizing only IPI spans under DP significantly reduces re-identification risk while preserving overall text quality. Compared with methods that privatize all tokens, the proposed approach yields more coherent and usable outputs and achieves a better privacy-utility trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Focusing DP noise on indirect personal identifiers rather than all tokens enables effective de-identification with less degradation in text quality. The work validates hybrid text privatization as an efficient and practical strategy for clinical texts, demonstrating that strong privacy protection and high utility can be jointly achieved by selectively applying differential privacy.

title: Stochastic Semantic Evidence Graphs: Uncertainty Propagation and Governance for Agentic AI
summary: AI-agent evaluations usually inspect a final answer, yet error may enter through evidence, retrieval, prompting, generation or decision mapping. We introduce a stochastic semantic evidence graph (SSEG), a hierarchical stochastic DAG whose language node expands into an autoregressive token subgraph and whose observable output may be a law over complete phrases. Semantic reduction and calibration are optional. We define graph-relative local defects and downstream edge influences, derive a pathwise bound on terminal error and use its nodewise terms to diagnose governance triggers. For source provenance, the graph preserves uncertain claim--passage relations and propagates sharp Fréchet bounds rather than assuming independence across sources. Across three open-weight architectures, information-equivalent changes materially alter complete-phrase laws. A controlled experiment yields no certificate violations in 5,000 cases; crossed-RAG and live Brave-retrieval experiments separate retrieval, presentation, source and interaction effects. SSEG therefore turns workflow provenance into a quantitative account of where uncertainty entered, how it propagated and whether an output is qualified for use.

AI.tldr: They propose a formal graph-based way to trace and quantify where errors and uncertainty arise in AI agent workflows, not just in the final answer.
AI.motivation: Current AI-agent evaluations focus mainly on whether the final answer is right or wrong, but do not systematically analyze where errors enter (e.g., retrieval, prompting, generation) or how uncertainty from different sources propagates through a complex workflow. There is also a need for better provenance tracking and principled treatment of dependence between sources.
AI.method: They introduce a stochastic semantic evidence graph (SSEG), a hierarchical directed acyclic graph model. Each language node is expanded into an autoregressive token-level subgraph, which can be summarized into probability laws over complete phrases, optionally with semantic reduction and calibration. They define graph-relative local defects at nodes and edge influences, derive a pathwise bound on terminal error, and use nodewise terms for diagnostic governance triggers. For provenance, the graph encodes uncertain relations between claims and passages and propagates sharp Fréchet bounds without assuming independence across sources. They test SSEG across three open-weight model architectures and in controlled and retrieval-augmented experiments.
AI.result: Information-equivalent changes (that should not alter meaning) can still materially change the probability laws over complete phrases across three architectures, showing sensitivity that SSEG can detect. In a controlled experiment of 5,000 cases, their method finds no certificate violations, supporting its soundness. In crossed-RAG and live Brave-retrieval settings, SSEG can distinguish the separate impacts of retrieval, presentation, source choice, and interaction dynamics on the final output and its uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: SSEG provides a principled, quantitative framework for turning workflow provenance in AI-agent systems into a detailed account of where uncertainty and error enter, how they propagate, and whether the final output meets a specified qualification or certification threshold for use.

title: PPTBench: Can Coding Agents Reconstruct the Visual World through Structured, Editable Slides
summary: Coding agents are beginning to act in the visual world. They now build webpages, GUIs, games, 3D scenes, diagrams, and documents. Success in such visual coding requires bridging two spaces: inferring visual structure and expressing it programmatically. Slides are a core medium of knowledge work, widely used to communicate ideas and collaborate in a form that people can directly inspect and edit. Therefore, they provide an ideal testbed for visual coding, as they require agents to recover visual structure and realize it as editable objects. However, existing benchmarks either rely on subjective open-ended evaluation, produce non-editable code outputs, or focus only on local editing rather than end-to-end visual reconstruction. We introduce PPTBench, which benchmarks visual coding through editable slide reconstruction. It contains 500 tasks, each based on a scientific flow diagram from a real arXiv paper and requiring agents to reconstruct it as a single PPTX page composed of native, editable objects. A four-stage Agentic Judge evaluates artifact validity, semantic correctness, rendering quality, and fine-grained visual quality. Across 31 configurations spanning model families, effort levels, and harnesses, the best configuration, Kimi K3, reaches only 67.80, while the median scores 19.47. We find that agents can reliably produce valid PPTX files but still struggle with semantic and visual correctness, especially text details. More reasoning mainly helps agents pass hard gates, while stronger verification is more consistently associated with higher quality. PPTBench advances the vision of coding agents that can understand and reconstruct the visual world through structured, editable code.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PPTBench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on reconstructing scientific slide-style flow diagrams as editable PowerPoint (PPTX) documents, revealing a large gap between current capabilities and robust visual coding performance.
AI.motivation: Coding agents are starting to operate in visual domains (webpages, GUIs, 3D scenes, diagrams), which requires both understanding visual structure and expressing it as code. Slides are a key medium for knowledge communication and collaboration, and they naturally combine visual layout, text, and structure in an editable form. Existing benchmarks for visual coding are limited: they rely on subjective evaluation, output non-editable artifacts (e.g., images instead of structured files), or only assess local edits rather than full reconstruction. There is a need for a systematic, objective benchmark that tests end-to-end reconstruction of real-world, semantically rich visual content as editable code artifacts.
AI.method: The authors build PPTBench, a benchmark of 500 tasks, each derived from a scientific flow diagram in an arXiv paper. For each task, an agent must reconstruct the diagram as a single-slide PPTX file using native editable elements (shapes, text boxes, connectors, etc.). They design a four-stage “Agentic Judge” that evaluates submissions along multiple axes: (1) artifact validity (is the PPTX structurally valid and openable), (2) semantic correctness (does the content match the original diagram’s meaning), (3) rendering quality (coarse visual similarity and layout), and (4) fine-grained visual quality (details such as precise positioning, styling, and text fidelity). They then run 31 different configurations that vary underlying model families, effort levels, and tool/harness setups, and evaluate performance using the Agentic Judge scores.
AI.result: Across the 31 evaluated configurations, the best-performing setup (using the Kimi K3 model) achieves a score of 67.80, while the median configuration only scores 19.47, indicating substantial headroom for improvement. Agents generally succeed at producing structurally valid PPTX files but perform poorly on semantic and visual fidelity, with text content and details being especially problematic. Increased reasoning primarily helps agents overcome rigid validity or gating checks, whereas more rigorous verification processes show a stronger and more consistent correlation with higher semantic and visual quality scores.
AI.conclusion: PPTBench provides a challenging, realistic benchmark for assessing and comparing coding agents on the task of reconstructing complex visual artifacts—scientific slide diagrams—as editable PPTX files. The results demonstrate that although today’s agents can reliably generate valid presentation files, they still struggle to accurately capture semantics and detailed visual structure. The analysis suggests that improved verification mechanisms and methods targeting fine-grained visual and textual fidelity are needed. Overall, PPTBench moves the field toward coding agents capable of deeply understanding and reproducing the visual world via structured, editable code representations.

title: TTLab at StanceEval-2026: A Cloze-Style Prompting Approach for Arabic-Language Stance Detection (CLASP-Ar)
comment: Accepted at ArabicNLP 2026 StanceEval-2026 shared task
summary: Arabic-language stance detection remains challenging, and previous shared-task systems have largely relied on multitask learning and ensembles. While these systems achieve state-of-the-art performance, their applicability and transferability are limited by the additional complexity introduced by multitask learning.To reduce this complexity, we introduce $\texttt{CLASP-Ar}$, which reformulates the task as cloze-style masked language modeling. In this approach, the target, predicted sentiment, and text are combined into a single prompt whose $\texttt{[MASK]}$ prediction is restricted to a verbalizer-constrained label vocabulary.

AI.tldr: They propose CLASP-Ar, a simpler Arabic stance detection method that reframes the task as masked language modeling with a constrained label vocabulary.
AI.motivation: Existing Arabic stance detection systems reach strong performance but depend on complex setups such as multitask learning and ensembles, which hurt simplicity, applicability, and transferability.
AI.method: They reformulate stance detection as a cloze-style masked language modeling task: the input target, sentiment, and text are combined into a single prompt containing a [MASK] token, and the prediction for [MASK] is constrained via a verbalizer that maps a small set of words to stance labels.
AI.result: Using this reformulation, they match or approach state-of-the-art performance in Arabic stance detection while avoiding the complexity of multitask and ensemble architectures.
AI.conclusion: Cloze-style masked language modeling with a verbalizer-constrained output space is an effective and simpler alternative to conventional multitask or ensemble-based approaches for Arabic stance detection.

title: JEV vs. LLMs as Rubric Judges: Cheaper, Faster, and Wrong in the Same Places
summary: We ask whether Jev, a typed classifier that returns probabilities over permitted answers without generating text, can replace an LLM rubric judge. We compare it with three flash-tier LLM judges on nine panels drawn from seven benchmarks, giving every judge identical criterion texts. Jev's accuracy differs significantly from an LLM judge's in only 8 of 27 paired comparisons, ahead mostly on binary criteria and behind only on graded ones, and most of the other comparisons are inconclusive. Summed over the nine panels, the LLM judges, called once per criterion, cost 29 to 325 times as much as Jev and took 30 to 220 times as long. On graded criteria all four judges agree more with one another than with the labels and mostly assign lower levels than the raters. One of several observational accounts is that raters followed scale conventions our criterion texts omit. Jev's confidence ranks its own errors on most panels, which should make a cheap classifier the ideal first stage of a cascade that defers its uncertain verdicts to an LLM judge. Correlated errors undo that advantage. The LLM judges repeat nearly all of Jev's most confident errors, so a cascade replayed on the recorded verdicts lowers cost but gains at most 1.5 points over the best single judge with cross-fitted thresholds, and at most 2.0 even with oracle thresholds.

AI.tldr: Paper evaluates Jev, a probability-returning classifier, as a replacement for LLM rubric judges and finds comparable accuracy at far lower cost and latency, with nuances for graded criteria and cascaded setups.
AI.motivation: LLM-based judges for evaluating model outputs are expensive and slow. The authors investigate whether a non-generative, typed classifier that outputs probabilities over rubric levels (Jev) can serve as a cheaper yet accurate substitute, and whether cascading Jev with LLM judges can further improve performance-cost tradeoffs.
AI.method: Compare Jev against three flash-tier LLM judges on nine evaluation panels derived from seven benchmarks. All judges receive identical evaluation criteria. Measure accuracy against benchmark labels, cost, latency, agreement patterns on binary vs graded criteria, and behavior within cascaded setups where Jev defers low-confidence cases to LLM judges. Analyze confidence ranking of errors and the impact of correlated errors between Jev and LLM judges.
AI.result: Jev’s accuracy significantly differs from that of an LLM judge in only 8 of 27 comparisons, generally performing better on binary criteria and worse on graded ones; most comparisons are statistically inconclusive. LLM judges are 29–325x more expensive and 30–220x slower when called per criterion. On graded criteria, all judges agree more with each other than with human labels and tend to assign lower ratings, likely due to missing scale-convention details in the provided criteria. Jev’s confidence scores generally rank its own errors well, but cascades provide limited benefit because LLM judges repeat nearly all of Jev’s most confident errors. Simulated cascades reduce cost but improve accuracy by at most 1.5–2.0 percentage points over the best single judge, even with oracle thresholds.
AI.conclusion: A typed classifier like Jev can often match the accuracy of much more expensive LLM rubric judges, especially for binary criteria, delivering large cost and latency savings. However, for graded criteria, all automated judges—including Jev—deviate from human raters in systematic ways that likely stem from incomplete rubric specification. Confidence-aware cascades using Jev as a front-end and LLM judges as backup offer only modest accuracy gains due to correlated errors, limiting the practical advantage of such hybrid systems.

title: Benchmarking and Domain Adaptation of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) for Adolescent Health Communication in Ghanaian Languages
summary: This paper presents an end-to-end study of automatic speech recognition (ASR) for adolescent health communication in three Ghanaian languages (Twi, Dagbani, and Ewe). The work proceeds in three connected stages; First, we benchmark five ASR systems (three language-specific Wav2Vec2 models and two multimodal LLMs, Gemma 3n and Gemma 4) on a general-domain Bible corpus and a Youth Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health (ASRH) Domain ASR dataset, using Character and Word Error Rate (CER, WER). Second, guided by the benchmark, we perform supervised domain adaptation: although Gemma 4 was the strongest zero-shot candidate, fine-tuning it proved computationally infeasible, so we pivoted to the compact Qwen3-ASR-0.6B, fine-tuned on a large Ghana Bible corpus (~90k samples) and evaluated strictly on held-out human-collected in-domain audio. Fine-tuning reduced WER on every language, most dramatically for Ewe (WER from 109.3% to 64.8%, a drop of 44.5 pp; CER from 65.1% to 24.9%). Third, we validate the work through KasaHealth, a live voice-first ASRH application deployed in all three languages, complemented by Senti-Check, a technical evaluation harness. KasaHealth was tested by 50 community respondents and achieved a 100% chat-approval rate, a 72% Good-or-Excellent translation rating, and a 92% would-recommend rate, while surfacing the domain gaps that most constrain real-world use. Across all three stages the evidence converges: for these languages the binding constraint is validated in-domain data, not model capability or computation.

AI.tldr: End-to-end study of ASR for adolescent health communication in three Ghanaian languages, benchmarking existing systems, fine-tuning a compact ASR model for domain adaptation, and validating it in a live health app, finding that high-quality in-domain data is the main bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Adolescent health information in low-resource African languages (Twi, Dagbani, Ewe) is underserved, and existing ASR systems are not well-adapted to the Youth Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health (ASRH) domain. The authors aim to enable accurate, voice-first health communication tools by understanding how well current ASR models work and how to best adapt them for this sensitive, domain-specific context.
AI.method: (1) Benchmark five ASR systems (three language-specific Wav2Vec2 models and two multimodal LLMs, Gemma 3n and Gemma 4) on both a general-domain Bible speech corpus and an ASRH-domain dataset using CER and WER. (2) Perform supervised domain adaptation by fine-tuning the compact Qwen3-ASR-0.6B model (after Gemma 4 proved too expensive to fine-tune) on a large Ghana Bible corpus (~90k samples) and evaluating only on held-out human-collected in-domain ASRH audio. (3) Deploy and evaluate the resulting system in KasaHealth, a real voice-first ASRH application in all three languages, and use the Senti-Check evaluation harness plus user feedback (N=50) to assess translation quality and user acceptance while identifying domain gaps.
AI.result: Fine-tuning Qwen3-ASR-0.6B on the Bible corpus significantly reduced WER and CER across all three languages on in-domain ASRH audio, with the largest gains for Ewe (WER improved from 109.3% to 64.8%, CER from 65.1% to 24.9%). In deployment, KasaHealth achieved high user satisfaction: 100% chat-approval, 72% Good-or-Excellent translation ratings, and 92% would-recommend, while also revealing remaining domain mismatches between training data and real ASRH usage.
AI.conclusion: For Twi, Dagbani, and Ewe in the adolescent health domain, the main limiting factor is the availability of validated in-domain speech data rather than model architecture or compute. Compact models like Qwen3-ASR-0.6B, when fine-tuned on available corpora, can achieve substantial performance improvements and support practical, user-accepted voice-first health applications, though closing remaining domain gaps will require better aligned in-domain datasets.

title: Adaptive Fisher-Whitened Cross-Covariance for Low-Resource Speech Recognition
summary: Adapting multilingual speech foundation models to low-resource languages remains difficult, especially for languages that are poorly represented during pre-training. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) reduces the cost of adapting large models, conventional approaches such as LoRA rely on generic low-rank parameterizations and do not explicitly use downstream task information to define the adaptation subspace. To investigate whether task-informed PEFT can better support low-resource ASR, we apply Fisher-Whitened Cross-Covariance Analysis (FCCA) to Whisper and Qwen3-ASR, and introduce two complementary extensions: Asymmetric-Coupled FCCA (AC-FCCA), which exploits structured cross-layer sharing, and Adaptive-Rank FCCA (AR-FCCA), which reallocates adaptation capacity across projection matrices under a fixed parameter budget. Under controlled multilingual experiments, we evaluate these approaches on languages that are poorly represented or unsupported during pre-training alongside well-represented languages. Standard FCCA is competitive with, and usually outperforms, trainable-parameter-budget-matched LoRA. AR-FCCA provides the most consistent improvement over standard FCCA across both model architectures, with statistically significant gains in several evaluation settings, while retaining the same number of trainable parameters. These results show that task-informed subspace construction can be effective for low-resource speech adaptation, and that adaptive rank allocation provides a robust way to improve parameter efficiency without increasing model capacity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes task-informed, parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (FCCA with AC-FCCA and AR-FCCA) to better adapt multilingual speech foundation models like Whisper and Qwen3-ASR to low-resource languages, outperforming standard LoRA under the same parameter budget.
AI.motivation: Adapting large multilingual speech models to low-resource languages is challenging, especially when those languages are underrepresented or absent in pre-training data. Existing PEFT methods like LoRA use generic low-rank updates that ignore downstream ASR task structure, potentially wasting scarce adaptation capacity. The authors aim to see whether explicitly task-informed adaptation subspaces can yield better low-resource ASR performance without increasing trainable parameters.
AI.method: They apply Fisher-Whitened Cross-Covariance Analysis (FCCA) as a task-informed PEFT method to adapt Whisper and Qwen3-ASR. FCCA constructs low-rank adaptation subspaces using task statistics. They further propose two extensions: (1) Asymmetric-Coupled FCCA (AC-FCCA), which imposes structured cross-layer sharing of adaptation subspaces, and (2) Adaptive-Rank FCCA (AR-FCCA), which dynamically redistributes a fixed total rank (parameter budget) across projection matrices to better match task needs. They run controlled multilingual ASR experiments comparing these methods with LoRA under matched trainable-parameter budgets on well-represented, poorly represented, and unsupported languages from the pre-training perspective.
AI.result: Across both Whisper and Qwen3-ASR, standard FCCA is at least competitive with, and often better than, LoRA when parameter budgets are matched. AR-FCCA yields the most consistent performance gains over standard FCCA, achieving statistically significant improvements in several evaluation scenarios, while keeping the total number of trainable parameters unchanged. AC-FCCA offers complementary benefits through cross-layer structure, though AR-FCCA is highlighted as the most robust improvement.
AI.conclusion: Task-informed construction of adaptation subspaces via FCCA is effective for low-resource speech adaptation, generally outperforming standard low-rank PEFT like LoRA under the same parameter budget. Moreover, adaptively allocating rank (and thus parameters) across layers and projection matrices, as in AR-FCCA, is a robust strategy to enhance parameter efficiency and ASR performance without increasing model capacity.

title: CORDIAL: Calibrating Ordinal LLM Outputs from Few Labels
summary: A large language model (LLM) can turn a text into a distribution over an ordered scale, but that distribution is a noisy measurement: saturated, compressed or exaggerated, and biased in a consistent direction. We propose CORDIAL, which treats the model's output as a noisy reading of the true label and corrects it with a channel of five interpretable parameters. The channel is small enough for its posterior to be averaged from a handful of labels, and we prove that the resulting calibration preserves first-order stochastic order. On Amazon reviews and CMU-MOSEI transcripts with four LLMs, CORDIAL has the lowest log loss among nine calibrators in 76 of 80 settings with 5 to 100 labels; with 20 labels and the main 7B reader, it matches the strongest baseline using 28-54 labels. The same posterior lets us learn priors from other tasks and fuse several LLMs. Unrestricted calibrators such as Dirichlet calibration overtake it only as the calibration set grows into the hundreds or thousands.

AI.tldr: Introduces CORDIAL, a calibration method that models LLM outputs as noisy measurements of true ordered labels and corrects them via a 5-parameter channel, achieving strong performance with very few labeled examples.
AI.motivation: LLMs can map text to probability distributions over ordered scales (e.g., ratings, sentiment scores), but these distributions are poorly calibrated: they may be biased, overly confident or underconfident, and systematically distorted (saturation, compression, exaggeration). Existing powerful calibrators often require many labeled examples and may not be interpretable. There is a need for a small, interpretable calibration model that (1) works well with very few labels, (2) respects the ordered nature of the label space, and (3) provides a principled probabilistic view that can share information across tasks and models.
AI.method: Model the LLM’s output distribution over ordered labels as a noisy channel applied to the unobserved true label. CORDIAL introduces a parametric calibration channel with only five interpretable parameters that describe how the LLM’s scores are transformed: capturing bias, saturation, compression, and related distortions. These parameters are learned in a Bayesian way from a small calibration set, giving a posterior over channel parameters. The method guarantees preservation of first-order stochastic dominance (so ordering of label distributions is maintained). The same posterior framework allows transfer of priors from other tasks and principled fusion of multiple LLMs’ predictions. CORDIAL is compared to a suite of nine calibration baselines, including unrestricted methods like Dirichlet calibration, across multiple datasets and LLMs.
AI.result: On Amazon review data and CMU-MOSEI sentiment transcripts, using four different LLMs as base predictors, CORDIAL achieves the best log loss in 76 out of 80 experimental conditions when the calibration set size ranges from 5 to 100 labeled examples. With just 20 labeled examples and a 7B-parameter LLM reader, CORDIAL matches the strongest competing calibrator that needs 28–54 labeled points. Only when calibration sets become very large (hundreds to thousands of labels) do more flexible, high-capacity calibrators such as Dirichlet calibration outperform CORDIAL.
AI.conclusion: Treating LLM outputs on ordered labels as noisy measurements and correcting them through a compact, interpretable 5-parameter channel (CORDIAL) yields strong calibration performance in low-data regimes while preserving important ordering structure. The approach outperforms a wide range of existing calibrators for small to moderate calibration set sizes and supports transfer of calibration knowledge and multi-model fusion within a single Bayesian framework. High-capacity, unconstrained calibrators only surpass CORDIAL when abundant labeled calibration data are available, highlighting CORDIAL’s advantage in realistic low-label settings.

title: ChunkRank: Model-Aware Text Chunking and Abstention-Aware Answer Selection for LLM Pipelines
summary: We present ChunkRank, an open-source Python library that derives chunk boundaries from a target model's tokenizer and context window, and selects an answer among candidates produced independently per chunk. It ships a validated registry of 90 models across 15 providers and six answer-selection methods, and needs only three core dependencies. For chunking, ChunkRank avoids context-window overflow automatically from the model name, whereas character-based splitters overflow or waste the budget, and a fidelity study across 11 languages shows why token-exact budgets matter beyond English. For answer selection we report a negative result: on NaturalQuestions, TriviaQA and HotpotQA, with extractive and generative readers, no content-based ranker reliably beats taking the first non-empty answer. The reason is reader abstention on chunks that lack the answer, not answer position. A long-context baseline shows that chunking matches single-call reading on single-hop questions, so ChunkRank targets small-window and beyond-window settings. Code, registry and evaluation harness are released.

AI.tldr: ChunkRank is a Python library that creates tokenizer-aware chunks for models and evaluates different answer-selection strategies across chunks, finding that simple heuristics often work as well as complex rankers.
AI.motivation: Existing character- or length-based chunking methods often overflow or underuse model context windows and are not tokenizer-aware, especially across multiple languages. Additionally, while many multi-chunk QA systems use complex content-based rankers to select answers from chunk-level outputs, it is unclear whether these rankers truly outperform simple heuristics. There is a need for a standardized, model-aware toolkit that both handles chunking robustly and systematically evaluates answer-selection strategies.
AI.method: They implement ChunkRank, an open-source Python library that: (1) infers chunk boundaries directly from the target model’s tokenizer and context window, avoiding overflow and maximizing token budgets; (2) maintains a registry of 90 models across 15 providers, with six implemented answer-selection methods; (3) conducts a fidelity study across 11 languages to quantify the importance of token-level budget control; and (4) empirically evaluates answer-selection strategies on NaturalQuestions, TriviaQA, and HotpotQA using both extractive and generative readers, including comparison to a long-context baseline.
AI.result: The library successfully avoids context-window overflow by design and demonstrates that token-exact chunking is important, particularly for non-English languages. In large-scale experiments on NaturalQuestions, TriviaQA, and HotpotQA with both extractive and generative readers, no content-based ranker consistently outperforms simply taking the first non-empty answer among chunk outputs. They also show that the key issue is reader abstention on chunks without answers, rather than the position of the correct answer across chunks. A long-context baseline indicates that chunked processing can match single-call long-context reading on single-hop questions.
AI.conclusion: ChunkRank offers a pragmatic, tokenizer-aware approach to chunking for many models and languages, reducing context-window waste and overflow with minimal dependencies. Empirically, sophisticated content-based answer rankers do not reliably improve over a simple first-non-empty heuristic in the studied QA benchmarks, due mainly to reader abstention behavior. Chunking can match long-context performance on single-hop tasks, making ChunkRank particularly suitable for small-window or beyond-window settings, and the released code, model registry, and evaluation harness provide a standardized basis for future work.

title: Your Transformer Can Hold Two Thoughts at Once: Evidence of Linear Superposition in LLMs
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on highly non-linear components, in this work we demonstrate that they exhibit fundamental linearity: when inputs from distinct text streams are linearly combined, the model outputs a superposition of the individual next-token distributions. We term this the \textit{Superposition Linearity Hypothesis}. We provide evidence that superposition is an intrinsic property of the Transformer architecture rather than an emergent consequence of training; in fact, we observe that it tends to diminish as pretraining progresses. However, we demonstrate that linearity can be substantially restored through lightweight fine-tuning, significantly reducing the divergence between the predicted next-token distribution and the average of the individual next-token distributions. Finally, we introduce a guided decoding procedure that disentangles superposed outputs, enabling the simultaneous generation of two coherent continuations from a single forward pass.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and empirically supports the Superposition Linearity Hypothesis: when mixing inputs from distinct text streams linearly, LLMs produce an approximate superposition (average) of their next-token distributions, and this property can be exploited for efficient multi-stream generation.
AI.motivation: To understand and exploit a surprising linear behavior in highly non-linear LLMs: when given linearly combined inputs from different text prompts, the model’s output distribution behaves like a superposition of the outputs for the individual prompts. This aims to deepen mechanistic understanding of Transformers and enable more efficient decoding strategies.
AI.method: 1) Formulate the Superposition Linearity Hypothesis for LLMs. 2) Empirically test how closely the next-token distribution from a linearly mixed input matches the average of the distributions for separate inputs, including across different training stages to see if it is architectural vs. learned. 3) Apply lightweight fine-tuning to enhance this linearity and measure the reduction in divergence from perfect superposition. 4) Propose a guided decoding method that uses the linearity to disentangle superposed outputs and generate multiple coherent continuations from a single forward pass.
AI.result: They find strong evidence that LLMs exhibit superposition linearity intrinsically due to the Transformer architecture, and that pretraining reduces but does not eliminate this effect.
