Simple fine-tuning largely restores the linearity, significantly decreasing divergence between the mixed-input next-token distribution and the mean of the individual distributions. The guided decoding scheme successfully produces two coherent, separable continuations from a single forward pass when given a superposed input.
AI.conclusion: LLMs based on Transformers have an inherent linear superposition property at the level of next-token distributions under linearly mixed inputs. Although standard pretraining weakens this behavior, targeted fine-tuning can restore and strengthen it. This linearity can be operationalized via guided decoding to efficiently generate multiple disentangled continuations from one forward pass, with implications for both understanding Transformer internals and building more efficient multi-output generation systems.

title: Encoded but Not Decoded: Layer-Localized Evidence for a Three-Level Gap in LLM Syntax
summary: A language model can fail a syntactic test in two distinct ways: by not encoding the relevant structure, or by encoding it but failing to use it at the output. Behavioral evaluation alone cannot tell these apart. We propose a three-level evaluation framework (behavioral deployment, LM-head readout, and probe recoverability) measured on the same items under the same binary decision. Using a compact trilingual (English, Chinese, German) control-dependency benchmark, we find that probe recoverability exceeds or equals LM-head readout, which in turn exceeds or equals behavioral deployment, across seven models and all three languages in the aggregate. The recoverability surplus is never negative across all 14 (model, task) conditions. The disconnect concentrates in subject-control, where a nearest-noun heuristic gives the wrong answer. The single largest gap (0.653) appears on Qwen3-0.6B Instruct in question answering. The gap persists at Qwen3-14B Instruct. Instruction tuning degrades deployment more than encoding in percentage terms. We rule out option-position bias, late-layer erasure, output-formatting artifacts, and probe-training variance. The pattern is consistent with decoding that favors surface shortcuts, and the behavior-probe gap measures the strength of that preference. Activation patching shows the gap is layer-localized. Under instruction tuning, the LM-head-decoded layer shifts approximately ten layers later than the probe-decoded layer. These findings argue that behavioral evaluation understates what models encode, while probing alone overstates what they deploy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a three-level evaluation framework to distinguish what language models encode about syntax from what they actually use when generating outputs, showing a consistent gap where models know more structure than their behavior suggests.
AI.motivation: Behavioral tests of language models only show whether a model answers correctly, not whether it internally represents the necessary syntactic structure. This makes it hard to tell whether failures are due to missing representations or due to decoding that ignores them in favor of heuristics. The paper aims to disentangle these two failure modes and to quantify how much syntactic knowledge is encoded but not behaviorally deployed.
AI.method: The authors propose a three-level framework applied to the same binary syntactic decision on the same items: (1) behavioral deployment (standard model outputs), (2) LM-head readout (using the model’s own output head directly on hidden states), and (3) probe recoverability (training diagnostic probes to recover the correct decision from hidden activations). They test seven models on a compact trilingual (English, Chinese, German) control-dependency benchmark, focusing on subject vs. object control. They analyze gaps between levels, investigate confounds like option-position bias and probe variance, and use activation patching to localize where in the network the behavior–probe gap arises, including before and after instruction tuning.
AI.result: Across all models and three languages, probe recoverability is always at least as high as LM-head readout, which is always at least as high as behavioral deployment. The probe–behavior gap is never negative across 14 model–task conditions and is especially large in subject-control cases where a nearest-noun heuristic fails. The largest gap (0.653) is observed for Qwen3-0.6B Instruct in QA, and a substantial gap remains even at 14B parameters. Instruction tuning disproportionately harms behavioral deployment relative to encoding strength. The authors rule out several alternative explanations (option-position bias, late-layer erasure, formatting artifacts, probe-training variance). Activation patching shows that the behavior–probe gap is localized to specific layers, and after instruction tuning the LM-head-decoded layer shifts about ten layers later than the probe-decoded layer.
AI.conclusion: Language models systematically encode more syntactic structure than their behavioral performance reveals. Behavioral evaluation alone underestimates their internal knowledge, while probing alone overestimates what they actually use in generation. The observed gaps and their layer localization suggest that decoding strongly favors surface heuristics over structural information, and that instruction tuning amplifies this preference by shifting effective decoding layers. A combined multi-level evaluation is therefore necessary for accurately characterizing syntactic competence and deployment in language models.

title: Multi-Task Learning by using Contextualized Word Representations for Syntactic Parsing of a Morphologically Rich Language
summary: We address the challenge of syntactic parsing for Urdu, a morphologically rich language, and present state-of-the-art results for both constituency and dependency parsing. This paper offers four major contributions: 1) the conversion of the CLE-UTB phrase structure treebank into a dependency treebank by developing language-specific head-word and phrase-to-dependency label mapping rules; 2) a novel sequence labeling scheme that transforms the parsing task into a unified representation; 3) the training of contextualized word representations on a large 220 million tokens Urdu corpus collected from the web; and 4) development of parsing framework using two learning paradigms, single-task and multi-task learning. Several post-processing rules are applied to improve the quality of the automatically converted dependency structure treebank. The proposed sequence labeling scheme enables the use of a shared architecture that learns the syntactic structures from both grammatical structures simultaneously and hence improves generalization. Experiments show that the multi-task learning setup significantly enhances parsing performance, achieving an F1 score of 91.39 for constituency parsing (an improvement of 3.29 points) and a labeled attachment score of 85.69 for dependency parsing (an improvement of 1.49 points). These results demonstrate that learning cross-task representations provides measurable benefits and advances the state of syntactic parsing for Urdu.

AI.tldr: The paper improves syntactic parsing for Urdu by converting an existing treebank, proposing a unified sequence-labeling parser, training Urdu-specific contextual embeddings, and showing multi-task learning yields state-of-the-art results for both constituency and dependency parsing.
AI.motivation: Urdu is morphologically rich and under-resourced for syntactic parsing, with separate treatments for constituency and dependency structures and limited language-specific tools. Existing treebanks and parsers do not fully exploit cross-task information or modern contextual representations, leading to suboptimal parsing accuracy. The authors aim to build better syntactic parsers for Urdu by leveraging task unification, large-scale Urdu data, and multi-task learning.
AI.method:
1) Convert the CLE-UTB phrase structure treebank into a dependency treebank using Urdu-specific head rules and label-mapping rules, followed by post-processing to correct systematic errors.
2) Design a novel sequence-labeling representation that encodes both constituency and dependency parsing decisions in a unified label sequence.
3) Train contextualized word representations on a 220M-token Urdu web corpus to capture rich morphology and context.
4) Develop a parsing framework with a shared neural architecture, evaluated in single-task and multi-task learning settings, where the model jointly learns constituency and dependency parsing from the unified sequence labels.
AI.result: The multi-task learning model using the unified sequence-labeling scheme and Urdu-specific contextual embeddings achieves state-of-the-art performance: F1 score of 91.39 for constituency parsing (a gain of 3.29 points over prior work) and labeled attachment score (LAS) of 85.69 for dependency parsing (a gain of 1.49 points). The automatically converted dependency treebank is of sufficient quality to support these improvements.
AI.conclusion: Unified sequence labeling combined with multi-task learning across constituency and dependency parsing, supported by large-scale Urdu contextual embeddings and a converted dependency treebank, substantially improves syntactic parsing for Urdu. Cross-task representation learning yields measurable accuracy gains and advances the state of the art for this morphologically rich, low-resource language.

title: MILO: Efficient Many-shot In-Context Learning with Block-wise Low-rank Compression
summary: Many-shot in-context learning (ICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to adapt to complex tasks by conditioning on thousands of demonstration examples, but this paradigm shifts the inference efficiency bottleneck to the key-value (KV) cache memory. Due to the linear scaling behavior of the KV cache, storing these intermediate tensors has become a paramount challenge for both online serving and on-device deployment. To address this issue, we propose a novel compression framework, termed MILO, that exploits the low-rank redundancy inherent in many-shot contexts. Specifically, MILO features a block-wise low-rank compression strategy that compresses the KV cache at the block granularity, where each block contains multiple many-shot examples. Furthermore, to handle the heterogeneous context density across different blocks, MILO dynamically allocates rank budgets based on the information entropy, preserving the fidelity of critical blocks while aggressively compressing redundant ones. Experimental results on Qwen2.5 models demonstrate that our method achieves up to 50% reduction in KV cache memory and 1.8x throughput improvement, with negligible performance degradation on classification and reasoning benchmarks, significantly outperforming prior baselines.

AI.tldr: Proposes MILO, a block-wise low-rank compression framework for KV cache in many-shot in-context learning, cutting memory by up to 50% and boosting throughput 1.8x with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Many-shot in-context learning requires conditioning LLMs on thousands of examples, causing the KV cache to grow linearly with context length, which creates a major memory and efficiency bottleneck for online serving and on-device deployment. Existing methods struggle to significantly reduce KV memory without harming performance, motivating a better compression scheme that exploits structural redundancy in long contexts.
AI.method: Introduce MILO, a KV-cache compression framework that leverages low-rank redundancy in many-shot contexts. It partitions the context into blocks, each containing multiple examples, and applies block-wise low-rank compression to the KV tensors. To account for varying information density, MILO dynamically allocates rank budgets to each block using an information-entropy-based criterion, assigning higher ranks to more informative blocks and lower ranks to redundant ones, thereby adaptively compressing the KV cache while preserving critical information.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5 models and many-shot ICL workloads, MILO reduces KV cache memory usage by up to 50% and increases throughput by up to 1.8x, while incurring only negligible performance degradation on classification and reasoning benchmarks. It also significantly outperforms previous KV cache compression baselines under comparable memory budgets.
AI.conclusion: Block-wise, entropy-aware low-rank compression of KV caches is an effective way to mitigate the memory and efficiency bottlenecks of many-shot ICL in LLMs. By adaptively allocating rank across context blocks, MILO attains substantial memory and throughput gains with minimal accuracy loss, making many-shot ICL more practical for both server-side and on-device deployment than prior compression approaches.

title: Cultural Divergence Preservation: Diagnosing Flattening and Caricature in LLM-Simulated Survey Populations
comment: Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Workshop on Pluralistic AI & NLP (PANDORA)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as synthetic survey respondents to estimate population response distributions. In cross-cultural survey simulation, evaluations should assess not only distributional fidelity within countries but also whether differences across countries are preserved. However, existing distance-based metrics such as Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) do not directly capture such cross-country differences. To address this limitation, we introduce Cultural Divergence Preservation (CDP), a reference-light diagnostic based on a one-time human calibration. CDP identifies reduced cross-country divergence as cultural flattening and increased divergence as cultural caricature. To evaluate CDP, we conduct experiments across four LLM backbones, three persona-based prompting methods, and two survey domains, the World Values Survey (WVS) and the Big Five Personality Test. The results reveal a systematic discrepancy between conventional fidelity metrics and CDP. Controlled experiments show that CDP changes monotonically as cross-country divergence is attenuated or amplified, while the corresponding changes in JSD remain relatively small. In our audit of real LLM generations, DeepPersona-Inspired prompting is frequently favored by conventional fidelity metrics but exhibits the strongest flattening in every model--domain block. CDP thus complements fidelity metrics by directly quantifying the attenuation or amplification of cross-country divergence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Cultural Divergence Preservation (CDP), a new metric to assess whether large language models preserve or distort cross-country differences when used as synthetic survey respondents.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLMs as synthetic survey respondents focus on how well they match response distributions within countries, but neglect whether cross-country differences are preserved. Distance-based metrics like Jensen–Shannon divergence cannot directly capture whether LLM outputs flatten or exaggerate cultural differences, which is critical in cross-cultural survey research.
AI.method: The authors propose CDP, a reference-light diagnostic that uses a one-time human calibration to measure how well LLM-generated survey responses preserve cross-country divergence. They define reductions in divergence as cultural flattening and increases as cultural caricature. They run experiments across four LLM backbones, three persona-based prompting strategies, and two survey domains (World Values Survey and Big Five Personality Test) to compare CDP against conventional fidelity metrics like JSD. They also run controlled experiments where they systematically attenuate or amplify cross-country divergence to test metric behavior.
AI.result: CDP responds monotonically and sensitively to controlled changes in cross-country divergence (attenuation or amplification), whereas JSD shows relatively small changes under the same manipulations. In audits of real LLM generations, DeepPersona-Inspired prompting often scores best on conventional fidelity metrics but shows the strongest cultural flattening according to CDP in every model–domain combination evaluated. This reveals a mismatch between standard fidelity metrics and actual preservation of cultural differences.
AI.conclusion: CDP effectively quantifies whether LLMs used as synthetic survey respondents preserve, flatten, or exaggerate cross-country differences, filling a gap left by standard distributional fidelity metrics. It shows that methods that appear strong under conventional metrics can still severely distort cultural divergence, so CDP should be used as a complementary diagnostic in cross-cultural survey simulations.

title: VietPrism: A large-scale Vietnamese speech and deepfake corpus with diverse dialects and code-switching
summary: Vietnamese speech research is constrained by resources that isolate automatic speech recognition from speaker, dialect, code-switching, and deepfake analysis. We introduce VietPrism, an open, multi-domain corpus that brings these dimensions together at scale: 993.4 hours and 403,941 bona fide utterances from 1,262 verified speakers across 8,388 real-world videos. To our knowledge, it is the first large-scale Vietnamese corpus to jointly provide transcripts, consistent speaker identities, five dialect groups, and naturally occurring Vietnamese--English code-switching, which constitutes nearly half of the corpus by duration. We further create over 3.1K hours of spoof speech with four open-source and commercial synthesis systems. Every spoof is conditioned on a verified speaker reference and paired with a transcript- and speaker-matched bona fide utterance, enabling unique controlled evaluation with reduced lexical and identity confounds. Zero-shot evaluation of five pretrained multilingual detectors reveals striking brittleness: EER greatly varies across detector--generator pairings, while recent multilingual detector DFA-1B degrades from 16.3% to 33.6% as speaker similarity increases. Dialect-stratified results expose further model-dependent disparities. By unifying natural linguistic diversity with controlled spoof generation, VietPrism provides a challenging foundation for Vietnamese speech modeling and trustworthy audio-deepfake detection.

AI.tldr: VietPrism is a large, open Vietnamese corpus unifying ASR, speaker, dialect, code-switching, and deepfake research, plus matched synthetic spoofs for rigorous deepfake detection evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing Vietnamese speech resources are scarce and fragmented: automatic speech recognition, speaker and dialect modeling, code-switching analysis, and deepfake detection are usually studied in isolation, with no single corpus that jointly supports these dimensions. This fragmentation limits robust modeling of real-world Vietnamese speech, especially in the presence of English code-switching and emerging audio-deepfake threats. The authors aim to create a unified, large-scale resource that reflects real linguistic diversity and enables controlled, fair evaluation of spoofing detectors.
AI.method: The authors construct VietPrism, an open multi-domain corpus collected from 8,388 real-world videos. They verify 1,262 speakers and label utterances with consistent speaker identities, five dialect groups, and transcripts, capturing naturally occurring Vietnamese–English code-switching. They then generate over 3.1K hours of spoofed audio using four open-source and commercial TTS/voice cloning systems. Each synthetic clip is conditioned on a verified speaker reference and is paired with a bona fide utterance that matches both transcript and speaker. Using this dataset, they perform zero-shot evaluation of five pretrained multilingual deepfake detectors, analyzing performance across detector–generator pairs, varying speaker similarity, and dialect strata.
AI.result: VietPrism comprises 993.4 hours and 403,941 bona fide utterances from 1,262 verified speakers, with nearly half of the duration containing natural Vietnamese–English code-switching and coverage of five dialect groups. The authors additionally generate more than 3.1K hours of synthetic (spoofed) speech, with strict one-to-one pairing between spoofed and bona fide utterances. Zero-shot tests of five multilingual deepfake detectors show high brittleness: equal error rates differ substantially across combinations of detector and spoof generator. For instance, the DFA-1B detector’s EER worsens from 16.3% to 33.6% as speaker similarity between spoof and bona fide audio increases. Dialect-stratified analysis further reveals model-dependent performance disparities across dialects.
AI.conclusion: VietPrism is presented as the first large-scale Vietnamese corpus that jointly offers transcripts, stable speaker identities, dialect labels, and extensive natural code-switching, along with tightly controlled spoofed counterparts. The dataset exposes serious robustness gaps in current multilingual deepfake detectors, including sensitivity to generator type, speaker similarity, and dialect, underscoring the difficulty of trustworthy audio-deepfake detection in realistic Vietnamese settings. By unifying diverse linguistic phenomena with controlled spoof generation, VietPrism establishes a challenging yet structured benchmark for future research in Vietnamese speech processing and secure deepfake detection.

title: Automated Regulatory Compliance Question Answering in Financial Services with Domain-Adapted Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Financial institutions operate under dense, frequently amended rulebooks, and answering a compliance question correctly requires not only fluency but verifiable grounding in the authoritative text. Large language models are attractive for this task, yet the models that firms can realistically deploy on-premise are compact ones, and compact models hallucinate obligations. We study whether a carefully domain-adapted retrieval-augmented generation pipeline closes that gap. Our retriever is built in three stages on top of LegalBERT: entailment tuning that recasts question--passage matching as premise--hypothesis reconstruction, contrastive tuning with in-batch negatives, and score-level fusion with BM25. Our generator is a compact model (2B--12B parameters) served under 4-bit quantization, either prompted or adapted with retrieval-aware fine-tuning (RAFT) through LoRA. On ObliQA, a question-answering benchmark built from the Abu Dhabi Global Market rulebooks, the staged retriever raises Recall@10 from 0.256 to 0.774 and outperforms BM25 (0.678) and E5-large-v2 (0.758), the strongest general-purpose dense encoder we tested. RAFT-LoRA then improves the composite RePASs answer-quality score for every model we could adapt, with the largest gain on the weakest one. However, the adapted models do not transfer to Australian case-law questions, and a closed-book model that receives no passages at all scores within 0.011 RePASs of the full pipeline while producing answers that cite nothing and misstate obligations. The retrieval gain is therefore measured directly, the generation gain is a gain in RePASs rather than demonstrated grounding, and grounding itself requires an evaluation protocol that RePASs does not provide.

AI.tldr: Domain-adapted retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with compact LLMs markedly improves retrieval and answer scores for regulatory compliance QA, but gains in measured answer quality do not guarantee true textual grounding, and models fail to generalize across legal domains.
AI.motivation: Financial institutions must answer nuanced compliance questions based on evolving, complex rulebooks, and on-premise deployment constraints limit them to compact LLMs that tend to hallucinate legal obligations. The authors aim to test whether a carefully engineered RAG pipeline—rather than just larger models—can deliver accurate, text-grounded answers in this high-stakes setting.
AI.method: They build a three-stage domain-adapted retriever on top of LegalBERT: (1) entailment-style tuning that reframes question–passage matching as a premise–hypothesis reconstruction task, (2) contrastive training with in-batch negatives to sharpen passage discrimination, and (3) score-level fusion of the dense LegalBERT retriever with the sparse BM25 retriever. For generation, they use small 2B–12B parameter models quantized to 4 bits, comparing plain prompting with retrieval-aware fine-tuning (RAFT) implemented via LoRA adapters. They evaluate on ObliQA, a question-answering benchmark derived from Abu Dhabi Global Market rulebooks, and also probe cross-domain transfer to Australian case-law questions, using the RePASs metric for answer quality and Recall@10 for retrieval.
AI.result: On the ObliQA benchmark, their staged retriever improves Recall@10 from 0.256 to 0.774 and outperforms both BM25 (0.678) and the strong general-purpose dense encoder E5-large-v2 (0.758). Applying RAFT-LoRA to the generators increases the RePASs answer-quality score for all adapted compact models, with the biggest relative improvements on the smallest/weaker models. However, these adapted generators show poor transfer to Australian case-law questions. Furthermore, a closed-book model without retrieval achieves a RePASs score within 0.011 of the full RAG pipeline while producing ungrounded, citation-free answers that misstate legal obligations.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specialized retrieval combined with retrieval-aware fine-tuning can substantially improve measured retrieval quality and benchmark answer scores for compact LLMs in regulatory QA, but current evaluation fails to capture whether answers are genuinely grounded in authoritative text. The small gap between closed-book and full RAG performance, plus lack of cross-domain transfer, highlights that improved metrics like RePASs may reward fluent but ungrounded responses; robust grounding in legal compliance contexts will require new evaluation protocols explicitly sensitive to citation correctness and obligation hallucinations.

title: Low-Cost Assays for Measuring Model Behavior Across Vendors and Releases
summary: Language models advise people, keep them company, and write software while they sleep. Measuring what they do is hard: behavior has to be sampled repeatedly across models, prompts and releases, most of it lives in unstructured text that has to be coded before it can be counted, and the result has to be legible and rigorous enough to meaningfully compare models and vendors. To address these constraints, we present a simple, cheap, scalable, and replicable model for studying model behavior. Each study is a frozen, public stimulus run identically on a cross-vendor panel, at a few dollars per model or less. Each reads its transcripts one of three ways, chosen by how much interpretation the behavior needs: exact match on a clamped reply, a codebook applied by LLM judges whose agreement with a human coder is reported per code, and an instrumented environment that records what an agent did independently of what it said. Run across four years of model releases from both frontier and open-source labs, these instruments find four things. Convergence: asked to pick a word, 27 of 44 models answer serendipity at least once in four tries. Resistance: a trailing "right?" moves endorsement by up to 32 points, and the sign flips from sycophantic to resistant as generations advance, keyed to the tag's surface form. House: whether a model holds a position under pressure tracks its generation, and how it holds tracks the lab that built it. Account: told to do something the documentation in their repository contradicts, some coding agents never went along silently and others always did, and the same model can change with the harness it runs in. Re-run on every release, batteries like these track how behavior is changing across vendors and over time.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a simple, scalable framework to systematically measure and compare language model behaviors across vendors and model generations using standardized behavioral ‘batteries’.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of language models are fragmented and difficult: behaviors must be sampled repeatedly across models, prompts, and time; outputs are unstructured text that need coding; and results must be rigorous enough for cross-model and cross-vendor comparison. The authors want a method that is cheap, replicable, and sensitive to behavioral changes over time and across labs.
AI.method: They design standardized, frozen ‘studies’ (stimulus batteries) run identically on a cross-vendor panel of models over multiple years. Each study operationalizes behavior in one of three coding regimes: (1) exact match on tightly constrained replies, (2) codebooks applied to free-form responses by LLM judges whose agreement with human coders is measured per code, and (3) instrumented environments that log agents’ concrete actions. They repeatedly re-run these batteries across successive model releases from various labs, including open-source and frontier models.
AI.result: Across four years of model releases, they uncover several behavioral patterns: (1) Convergence: many diverse models exhibit the same stereotyped response (e.g., 27/44 models answer “serendipity” at least once when asked to pick a word). (2) Resistance vs. sycophancy: subtle prompt tags like a trailing “right?” can shift endorsement rates by up to 32 points, and newer generations shift from sycophantic to resistant behavior depending on tag surface form. (3) House effects: a model’s willingness to maintain positions under pressure correlates with its generation and also systematically varies by lab. (4) Accountability: when coding instructions conflict with repository documentation, some agents always comply silently, some never do, and behavior can change depending on the run-time harness even for the same model.
AI.conclusion: The proposed behavioral batteries provide a cheap, scalable, and replicable way to track how language model behaviors change across vendors and over time. They show that model behavior converges in some surprising ways, evolves toward more resistance in certain conversational setups, exhibits systematic lab-specific ‘house styles,’ and is sensitive not just to model weights but also to deployment harnesses. Regular re-running of such batteries can yield a longitudinal, cross-vendor portrait of LM behavior.

title: Artificial Societies Benchmark: A Validation Framework for Synthetic Research
summary: A synthetic survey can reproduce the average answer while misrepresenting how people differ, how their answers relate to one another, or how they respond to changes in conditions. We introduce the Artificial Societies Benchmark to help researchers assess whether synthetic populations support their intended analyses. The framework combines eleven tests across internal, construct, and external validity, drawing on twenty human sources and comparing nine language models. It connects each research use to the evidence it requires and tests how results change with the information we supply about respondents. Importantly, strong performance in one domain does not establish fidelity in the others. Models often answer too consistently, compress response scales, and alter relationships between traits whilst richer profiles improve prediction for some models and worsen it for others. The resulting scorecard helps researchers identify which aspects of a synthetic population can support their analysis and where researchers need further human evidence.

AI.tldr: Introduces Artificial Societies Benchmark to evaluate whether synthetic survey populations generated by language models are valid for different research uses.
AI.motivation: Synthetic surveys from language models can match average responses but distort individual differences, relationships between answers, and responses to changing conditions; researchers lack a systematic way to test if such synthetic populations are valid for their specific analytic goals.
AI.method: Propose the Artificial Societies Benchmark consisting of 11 tests spanning internal, construct, and external validity. Use 20 human data sources as reference points and evaluate 9 language models under varying amounts of information provided about respondents. Map different research uses to specific required evidence and analyze how model performance changes with richer respondent profiles.
AI.result: Find that strong performance on one validity domain (e.g., matching means) does not guarantee fidelity in others (e.g., correlations, heterogeneity). Models tend to respond too consistently, compress response scales, and change relationships between traits. Adding richer profiles improves predictive performance for some models but degrades it for others. The benchmark yields a multi-dimensional scorecard per model.
AI.conclusion: Researchers cannot assume that synthetic survey populations are broadly valid just because they match certain metrics; instead, they should use a structured benchmark like Artificial Societies to determine which aspects of model-generated populations are trustworthy for their intended analyses and where additional human data are still necessary.

title: Scoring Both Directions: LLMs realize the MRS they cannot reliably parse
summary: The English Resource Grammar (ERG) is a hand-written computational grammar of English. Given a sentence, its processor, ACE, produces a formal meaning representation called Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS): a graph of the sentence's predicates and their arguments. The grammar is bidirectional and can also turn an MRS back into an English sentence. \citet{hajdik2019} used the ERG's treebank to build a benchmark for that generation task, MRS to text, and trained sequence-to-sequence models to solve it. The parsing task, text to MRS, can be tested on the same sentences. We reconstruct their 10K-sentence test split, and score two large language models, Claude Sonnet~4.5 and Claude Opus~5, in both directions against their trained systems and against ACE, with no task-specific training. Given an MRS and three examples, Opus writes the sentence at 76.3 BLEU, ten points above their system trained on 72k pairs (66.1 BLEU), and comparable to their system trained on a million extra pairs (77.2 BLEU). Sonnet scores 65.7 BLEU, and letting it choose among ACE's own candidate sentences lifts it to 69.6, while a pooled judge that keeps Opus's own sentence among the candidates adds 0.6 points (77.0 BLEU). In the parsing direction, however, the models fall far behind ACE: asked for the MRS of the same sentences, they reach 57.2 (Sonnet) and 65.5 (Opus) F$_1$ on the graph's predicates and arguments against 91.0 for ACE, and exact-match the gold on about 1\% of sentences. We characterize the failure modes for the parsing tasks, and conclude that a generation score alone does not show that models understand formal semantic representations.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates large language models on a formal semantic benchmark (ERG MRS) in both generation and parsing, finding that their strong generation performance does not translate into true understanding of formal meaning representations.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed that sequence-to-sequence models can generate English text from Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS) structures derived from the English Resource Grammar (ERG), but it was unclear whether strong generation performance reflects genuine understanding of formal semantic graphs, especially when compared to symbolic systems like ACE. The authors aim to test modern large language models on the same benchmark, in both MRS-to-text and text-to-MRS directions, to see how well they handle a linguistically precise semantic formalism without task-specific training.
AI.method: The authors reconstruct the 10K-sentence test split introduced by Hajdik et al. (2019) based on the ERG treebank. They then evaluate two large language models, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Claude Opus 5, on: (1) MRS-to-text generation, given an MRS plus three examples, and (2) text-to-MRS parsing, asking for the MRS for the same sentences. They compare the LLMs’ outputs to those of ACE (the ERG processor) and to sequence-to-sequence systems previously trained on 72k and 1M+ MRS–text pairs. They report BLEU scores for generation and F1 (on predicates and arguments) and exact-match rates for parsing, and analyze typical error patterns for the parsing task.
AI.result: In MRS-to-text generation, Claude Opus achieves 76.3 BLEU with only few-shot prompting, surpassing the previously trained 72k-pair system (66.1 BLEU) and approaching the 1M-pair system (77.2 BLEU). Claude Sonnet attains 65.7 BLEU, which rises to 69.6 BLEU when it is allowed to choose among ACE’s own candidate realizations. A pooled selection strategy that includes Opus’s own sentence as a candidate yields 77.0 BLEU. In contrast, in text-to-MRS parsing, both LLMs substantially underperform ACE: Sonnet and Opus reach 57.2 and 65.5 F1 respectively on predicate–argument graphs versus ACE’s 91.0, and they exactly match the gold MRS for only about 1% of sentences. The authors identify systematic failure modes in the LLMs’ MRS outputs, such as structural mismatches and semantic-role errors.
AI.conclusion: The experiments show that large language models can produce high-quality natural language realizations from formal semantic representations, rivaling or surpassing specialized neural generators when measured by BLEU. However, these models perform poorly at the inverse task of deriving precise MRS structures from text, lagging far behind a symbolic grammar-based system like ACE and rarely achieving exact matches. The authors conclude that strong generation performance from MRS does not imply that LLMs truly understand or faithfully manipulate formal semantic representations, and that evaluation based solely on surface-level generation metrics is insufficient evidence of deep semantic competence.

title: How Reproducible Are Evaluation Conclusions? A Self-Audit of LLM-Inferred Prompt Structure
comment: 13 pages. Previously submitted to TAE (Trust-AI-Eval), a NeurIPS 2026 workshop
summary: Evaluations of LLM systems routinely average over small prompt sets and report models as a ranked table. We ask how much confidence such a table deserves, using LLM-based prompt-structure inference as the case study: eight open model variants across five families and 8B to 675B parameters, caching disabled, 293 raw intermediate representations persisted. The measured phenomenon is unstable to begin with. Identical calls do not reliably recover identical structure, with mean node-set Jaccard from 0.39 to 0.96 and 72% of prompt-model cells never node-set-perfect. Auditing the evaluation weakens its conclusions further, and this is our main contribution. Under a joint cluster bootstrap over prompts, only the bottom of the ranking is firm: the two least reproducible models hold rank in 99% and 86% of replicates, the middle four in 27% to 48%, and the top two in 68% each, so the table identifies the worst model reliably but does not reliably identify the best. Two equally defensible rules for merging repeated campaigns change four of eight rows and move the study-wide headline by 7 percentage points. Checking the inferred structure against ground-truth annotations shows reproducibility cannot be read as accuracy. And four of the eight endpoints were withdrawn within ten weeks of measurement, so the study as specified can no longer be run. Small-sample LLM evaluations can therefore look far more definitive than their evidence supports. We recommend reporting rank stability, per-cell provenance, executed sensitivity comparisons, raw per-run outputs, and a measurement date alongside any ranking.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques common practices in evaluating LLMs using small prompt sets and simple rankings, showing that such rankings are often statistically unstable and misleading.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluations typically use small datasets and then present model performance as a clean ranked table, which gives a false sense of precision and confidence. The authors want to quantify how unreliable these rankings can be, using a concrete case study of LLM-based prompt-structure inference.
AI.method: They evaluate eight open LLM variants (five model families, 8B–675B parameters) on a prompt-structure inference task with caching disabled, persisting 293 intermediate representations. They measure reproducibility of model outputs across repeated identical calls using node-set Jaccard similarity, audit the evaluation with a joint cluster bootstrap over prompts to assess rank stability, compare different reasonable rules for merging repeated evaluation campaigns, and check correlation between reproducibility and accuracy against human-annotated ground truth.
AI.result: They find that the target phenomenon is intrinsically unstable: repeated identical calls to the same model often produce different inferred structures, with mean node-set Jaccard ranging from 0.39 to 0.96 and 72% of prompt–model pairs never producing identical node sets. Bootstrap analysis shows only the worst models are reliably ranked; middle models’ ranks are highly unstable, and even the top models’ ranks are far from certain. Alternative but reasonable choices for aggregating repeated runs change half the rows in the ranking and shift the main headline metric by 7 percentage points. Reproducibility does not reliably indicate accuracy, and many evaluated endpoints became unavailable shortly after measurement, undermining long-term replicability.
AI.conclusion: Small-sample LLM evaluations, especially when summarized as simple rankings, can appear much more decisive than the underlying evidence justifies. To mitigate this, the authors recommend that evaluation reports include rank stability analyses, detailed provenance for each cell in the results table, explicit sensitivity analyses to evaluation design choices, full raw per-run outputs, and clear measurement dates, so readers can better judge the robustness and durability of the reported rankings.

title: A Native-Reference Phone-Class Geometry for Second-Language Pronunciation Analysis
summary: Automatic speaking assessment systems can provide holistic proficiency scores, but often lack interpretable measures that characterize pronunciation quality. We propose a native-reference phone-class geometry for measuring second language (L2) pronunciation deviation without requiring pronunciation labels, read-aloud prompts, or matched recordings of the same text from native and L2 speakers. Given a native speech corpus, we average frame-level self-supervised representations for each context-dependent phone-class and use singular value decomposition (SVD) to derive a compact native-reference coordinate system. For each L2 utterance, we compute the corresponding averages and project them into the native-reference space. We then demonstrate that the distances between L2 and native-reference coordinates for matched phone-classes show consistent negative correlations with holistic speaking proficiency on the Dev subset of the Speak and Improve Corpus 2025 (Spearman's $ρ\!=\!-0.53$) and with pronunciation quality on the learner subset of the English Read by Japanese Students dataset ($ρ\!=\!-0.34$). These findings suggest that the proposed geometry captures acoustic-phonetic information relevant for proficiency rating while remaining applicable to spontaneous L2 speech without matched native recordings.

AI.tldr: They build a geometric, phone-based representation of speech from native self-supervised features and use distances in this space to quantify L2 pronunciation deviation, which correlates with proficiency and pronunciation scores.
AI.motivation: Existing automatic speaking assessment systems can output holistic proficiency scores but offer little interpretability about pronunciation quality and often rely on restrictive conditions like read prompts, pronunciation labels, or parallel native/L2 recordings. There is a need for a label-free, interpretable, phone-level measure of how L2 speech deviates from native pronunciation that can work on spontaneous speech.
AI.method: 1) Start from a native speech corpus and extract frame-level self-supervised speech representations. 2) Group frames by context-dependent phone-class and average them to obtain a prototype vector per phone-class. 3) Apply singular value decomposition (SVD) to these prototypes to derive a low-dimensional, native-reference coordinate system (a phone-class geometry). 4) For an L2 utterance, compute analogous phone-class averages from its self-supervised features and project them into the native-reference coordinate system. 5) Compute distances between the L2 phone-class coordinates and the corresponding native phone-class coordinates and analyze their relationship with human proficiency and pronunciation ratings.
AI.result: Distances between L2 and native phone-class coordinates correlate negatively with human assessments: on the Dev subset of the Speak and Improve Corpus 2025, the correlation with holistic speaking proficiency is Spearman’s ρ = -0.53, and on the learner subset of the English Read by Japanese Students dataset, the correlation with pronunciation quality is ρ = -0.34. Larger geometric deviations correspond to lower proficiency/pronunciation ratings, indicating that the geometry is informative about perceived quality.
AI.conclusion: A native-reference phone-class geometry derived from self-supervised speech representations can quantify L2 pronunciation deviation without requiring labels, read prompts, or parallel native/L2 recordings. Its distance-based measures correlate meaningfully with holistic speaking proficiency and pronunciation quality, suggesting it captures relevant acoustic-phonetic properties and is suitable for spontaneous L2 speech assessment.

title: The Gold in Bias: Maturing the AI Design Process through Verification
summary: Bias in AI systems is typically framed as a flaw to be minimized, yet it also serves as a critical indicator of underlying weaknesses in data, modeling assumptions, and system design. Existing approaches often treat bias as an isolated problem rather than as evidence that can strengthen verification and governance across the AI lifecycle. This paper aims to reconceptualize bias as a diagnostic tool that supports rigorous AI verification. We seek to develop a multidimensional framework to analyze bias, demonstrate how biases emerge in both Traditional and Generative AI, and provide a structured pathway for verification-driven mitigation. We present a multidimensional framework analyzing bias across four dimensions: origin sources, emergence points throughout the AI modeling lifecycle, technical and methodological causes, and validation approaches for detection and mitigation. Through a comprehensive typology spanning traditional and generative AI systems, we demonstrate how biases manifest and propagate across development stages. Our analysis encompasses 30 distinct bias types, 16 verification methods, and 20 countermeasures, providing an actionable roadmap for practitioners. We introduce a hierarchical evidence framework that distinguishes internal validity (mechanistic integrity of AI systems) from external validity (contextual reliability in deployment environments). The framework reveals how biases manifest and propagate across modeling stages, enabling systematic mapping between bias types, verification techniques, and effective countermeasures. The proposed evidence hierarchy clarifies how different verification strategies contribute to mechanistic integrity and contextual reliability. We advocate for ''Ethics by Design'' principles that integrate bias verification throughout the development lifecycle, enabling the construction of fairer, more robust, and trustworthy AI systems.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes bias in AI not just as a flaw to remove but as a diagnostic signal that can be systematically used to verify and govern AI systems across their lifecycle.
AI.motivation: Most current work treats bias in AI systems as an isolated ethical or technical defect to be minimized. This narrow view misses the opportunity to use bias as structured evidence about deeper issues in data, modeling assumptions, and system design. There is a need for a comprehensive, lifecycle-wide verification perspective in which bias helps reveal weaknesses and guide governance.
AI.method: The authors develop a multidimensional framework that analyzes bias along four axes: (1) origin sources, (2) emergence points across the AI modeling lifecycle, (3) technical and methodological causes, and (4) validation approaches for detection and mitigation. They construct a typology that covers both traditional and generative AI systems, cataloging bias types, verification methods, and countermeasures. Building on this, they define a hierarchical evidence framework distinguishing internal from external validity and map bias types to verification techniques and mitigations.
AI.result: The paper identifies and organizes 30 bias types, 16 verification methods, and 20 countermeasures into a comprehensive typology applicable to both traditional and generative AI. It shows how different biases arise and propagate through various development stages and how specific verification strategies and mitigations can be aligned with them. The hierarchical evidence framework clarifies which verification approaches support internal validity (mechanistic soundness) and which support external validity (reliability in context).
AI.conclusion: Bias should be systematically leveraged as a diagnostic tool within AI verification and governance, not treated solely as an undesirable byproduct. Using the proposed multidimensional and hierarchical evidence frameworks, practitioners can more rigorously detect, analyze, and mitigate bias throughout the AI lifecycle. Embedding “Ethics by Design” and bias verification into development processes can yield AI systems that are fairer, more robust, and more trustworthy in real-world deployment.

title: What, When, and How: Audio Description as Constrained Global Optimization
summary: Audio Description (AD) makes movies accessible to blind and visually impaired audiences by narrating visual information in gaps between dialogue. Existing automatic AD systems largely treat generation as a local video-to-text problem, assuming that the content to describe and its temporal location are already provided. Realistic AD instead requires coupled decisions about what visual information is narratively important, when it can be spoken without interfering with dialogue, and how it should be formulated to fit within the available time. We formalize AD generation as a constrained optimization problem over these three decisions. Our hybrid system uses large language models to propose and ground visual elements, estimate their salience to the narrative, and generate compressed realizations. A mixed-integer linear program then jointly selects and schedules descriptions across a scene subject to temporal constraints. When evaluated on REFRAMED, a benchmark for realistic AD of movies, our approach makes better decisions than prompted LLMs about what to describe and when to describe it, establishing a new SOTA on narrative QA and temporally grounded metrics. Ablations show that explicit temporal constraints drive gains in placement, while salience estimation controls how much narratively useful content is retained. Improvements are concentrated on temporal and narrative measures rather than n-gram overlap, although a significant gap to professional describers remains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a realistic, end-to-end framework for automatic movie audio description (AD) that jointly decides what to describe, when to speak, and how to phrase descriptions under timing constraints, achieving new state-of-the-art results on a movie AD benchmark.
AI.motivation: Current automatic AD systems assume that relevant visual content and its timing are pre-specified, reducing the task to local video-to-text generation. This is unrealistic for actual movie AD, where the system must simultaneously determine which visual events are narratively important, find time slots that do not clash with dialogue, and produce concise descriptions that fit into those slots. There is a need for a principled, globally optimized method that handles these coupled decisions together rather than in isolation.
AI.method: The authors formalize AD generation as a constrained optimization problem involving three coupled decisions: (1) selecting visual elements to describe, (2) deciding when they can be narrated without overlapping dialogue, and (3) compressing the linguistic realization to fit within temporal windows. Their hybrid system first uses large language models to: (a) identify and ground candidate visual elements, (b) estimate their narrative salience, and (c) generate short textual realizations. Then, a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation is applied to jointly select which descriptions to include and schedule them across the scene while respecting timing and non-overlap constraints.
AI.result: On the REFRAMED benchmark for realistic movie AD, the proposed approach outperforms prompted LLM baselines in choosing both what to describe and when to describe it. It achieves new state-of-the-art performance on narrative question answering and temporally grounded evaluation metrics. Ablation studies indicate that explicit temporal constraints significantly improve placement decisions, while the salience estimation module determines how much useful narrative content is preserved. The gains are particularly strong on temporal and narrative quality measures, with less improvement on surface-form n-gram overlap metrics.
AI.conclusion: Realistic automatic AD benefits from modeling the task as a global constrained optimization problem that couples content selection, temporal placement, and concise realization. The hybrid LLM-plus-MILP system yields more narratively appropriate and better-timed descriptions than purely prompt-based LLM approaches, establishing new state-of-the-art results on a challenging AD benchmark. Nonetheless, there remains a notable performance gap relative to professional human describers, indicating room for further advances in modeling narrative salience and temporal coordination.

title: AI-based detection of worsening heart failure from low-resolution telemonitoring data
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, under review for publication
summary: Objective: Heart failure (HF) presents a healthcare challenge due to its high comorbidity burden, aging patient population and frequent hospitalizations. Remote monitoring offers a promising approach to managing HF patients by early detection of health deterioration. Developing autonomous systems to detect signs of worsening in telemonitoring data is of interest to reduce the workload of healthcare personnel. Methods: We propose the TRACER model, a Transformer with Contrastive Event Representation, designed to predict timelines leading to rare hospitalization events in low-resolution and irregularly sampled telemonitoring data. TRACER incorporates time-aware embeddings for each biomarker, contrastive pre-training to enhance anomaly detection via representation learning, and independent binary classifiers for detection. We used measurement data containing remotely recorded biomarker sequences from 276 HF patients segmented into overlapping windows based on temporal rules, and labeled the windows based on the occurrence of HF relevant hospitalizations at the latter edge of the window. Results: TRACER was able to correctly predict 66.7% timelines leading up to HF hospitalizations in the highly imbalanced real-world dataset with an overestimation of 7.9%. Reformulating the training of TRACER as an event detection problem improved the predictive performance compared with training directly on forecasting windows, enabling more effective use of the limited hospitalization events. Conclusion: TRACER demonstrated superior performance in detecting signs of worsening status in real-world telemonitoring data compared to the other tested models. Significance: TRACER shows promise in identifying signs of clinical deterioration that allow for alerts to be generated to provide counteractive treatment in patients with HF.

AI.tldr: TRACER is a Transformer-based model that uses contrastive event representations to detect impending heart failure hospitalizations from sparse, irregular telemonitoring data, achieving improved early detection performance over baselines.
AI.motivation: Heart failure patients are at high risk of decompensation and rehospitalization, and continuous telemonitoring generates complex, low-resolution, irregular data that are hard for clinicians to manually interpret. There is a need for autonomous methods that can reliably detect early signs of worsening status to enable timely interventions and reduce clinical workload, especially given the rarity of hospitalization events and the imbalance in real-world datasets.
AI.method: The authors design TRACER, a Transformer architecture tailored for telemonitoring data with time-aware embeddings per biomarker to handle irregular sampling. They apply contrastive pre-training to learn discriminative event representations that enhance anomaly and deterioration signal detection. Patient biomarker time series from 276 heart failure patients are segmented into overlapping temporal windows; each window is labeled based on whether a heart failure–related hospitalization occurs at its end. Independent binary classifiers are trained on the learned representations, and the training is reformulated as an event detection problem rather than straightforward forecasting to better leverage the limited number of hospitalization events.
AI.result: On a highly imbalanced real-world telemonitoring dataset, TRACER correctly predicted 66.7% of the timelines leading to heart failure hospitalizations, with an overestimation of 7.9% (i.e., relatively low false positive rate given the imbalance). The event detection formulation of training improved predictive performance compared with directly forecasting over windows, indicating more efficient use of scarce hospitalization labels.
AI.conclusion: TRACER outperforms other evaluated models in detecting impending clinical deterioration in heart failure patients using real-world telemonitoring data. By leveraging time-aware embeddings and contrastive event representation learning, the model can more accurately identify timelines that precede hospitalization, suggesting potential for real-time alerting and earlier counteractive treatment to prevent or mitigate decompensation events.

title: Breaking the Environment Wall: Evolving LLM Agent Environments for Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: Many real-world tasks (e.g., office workflows, scientific experimentation) require LLM agents to interact repeatedly with their environments for context-dependent operations. However, such environments are often not agent-ready. First, information is often scattered and fragmented across the environment. Second, relevant evidence in the environment is often mixed with misleading information and conflicting versions. Third, environments evolve over time, introducing new noise and more challenging tasks. These challenges can substantially degrade performance for state-of-the-art AI agents (e.g., from 83.9% to 57.6%). To address these challenges, we propose Env-Rethink (a system with 27B post-trained model) that supports three main capabilities: (1) It adaptively builds Collection Maps (for organizing related files) and Event Logs (for contextualizing cross-data relationships) to supplement necessary context; (2) It further leverages the post-trained model (through offline trajectory learning) to identify underlying noise issues in the environment; (3) It ultimately evolves environments through virtual event histories that alter environmental states and evidence relationships, producing more tricky ones for further agent improvement. Experiments show that Env-Rethink can effectively improve downstream task performance (with over 15.1% rubric pass rate improvement across nine models on 30 tasks).

AI.tldr: Env-Rethink is a 27B post-trained system that restructures messy, evolving environments into organized, harder benchmarks so LLM agents can learn to handle noise and fragmented information, boosting task performance by 15%+ across models.
AI.motivation: Real-world environments like office workflows or scientific labs are not designed for LLM agents: information is scattered, mixed with misleading or conflicting evidence, and constantly changing. These issues significantly degrade the performance of current AI agents, so there is a need for a framework that can organize context, diagnose environmental noise, and systematically evolve the environment to better train and evaluate agents.
AI.method: Env-Rethink introduces a 27B post-trained model with three key capabilities: (1) It adaptively constructs Collection Maps that group related files and Event Logs that record cross-document relationships, enriching the context for agents; (2) It uses offline trajectory learning over past agent interactions to detect and characterize sources of environmental noise, such as misleading evidence or conflicting versions; (3) It ‘evolves’ the environment by generating virtual event histories that modify states and evidence relations, creating more challenging, noisy scenarios for continued agent training and evaluation.
AI.result: Across 30 tasks and nine different models, Env-Rethink leads to more than a 15.1% absolute improvement in rubric pass rate, demonstrating that reorganizing and evolving environments as proposed substantially improves downstream performance of LLM agents operating in complex, noisy settings.
AI.conclusion: By organizing fragmented information, identifying noise, and systematically evolving environments into more challenging but structured scenarios, Env-Rethink enables LLM agents to perform significantly better on context-dependent tasks in realistic, dynamic environments, suggesting a promising direction for making environments agent-ready rather than only making agents more capable.

title: A Training Criterion with Token-Level Tolerance to Transcription Ambiguity for Automatic Speech Recognition
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables; submitted to ICASSP 2027
summary: Automatic speech recognition is typically trained assuming that the reference transcript is the only valid labeling of an utterance, yet even nominally verbatim transcripts contain localized differences in pronunciation, spelling, or lexical realization that the acoustics do not uniquely determine. Omni-temporal Classification (OTC) tolerates such noise by adding wildcard paths to the connectionist temporal classification (CTC) alignment graph, but its word-level arcs are too coarse, since bypassing one unsupported token discards supervision for the whole word. We move wildcard arcs to token granularity so unsupported tokens can be bypassed while the rest of the word stays supervised, and we combine token- and word-level arcs as complementary escape paths. Across 19 languages and three corpora, token-level OTC improves over CTC on all 25 tasks. We also replace epoch-indexed relaxation of the wildcard weights with a predictive-entropy-indexed schedule, which performs comparably while reducing dependence on training length. Combining this schedule with the hybrid graph gives the lowest mean word error rate (WER) on every corpus and a 9.45% average relative WER reduction over CTC. Independent validator transcriptions show that token-level models place significantly more wildcard-bypass probability than CTC on disputed characters, indicating that token-level tolerance targets localized transcript ambiguity.

AI.tldr: Proposes a more fine-grained Omni-temporal Classification (OTC) for ASR by moving wildcards from word-level to token-level and combining both levels, yielding consistent WER improvements over CTC across many languages and corpora.
AI.motivation: Traditional CTC-based ASR assumes a single correct transcript, but real transcripts include localized ambiguities (pronunciation, spelling, lexical choice) that the acoustics do not uniquely determine. Existing OTC uses word-level wildcards that are too coarse, as skipping one token discards supervision for the entire word. The authors want a training objective that better tolerates localized transcript noise and ambiguity without sacrificing useful supervision.
AI.method: They modify OTC by (1) moving wildcard arcs from word-level to token-level so that only unsupported tokens can be bypassed while the rest of the word remains supervised, and (2) constructing a hybrid alignment graph that includes both token- and word-level wildcard arcs as complementary escape paths. They also replace the usual epoch-based schedule for relaxing wildcard weights with a schedule driven by predictive entropy, reducing sensitivity to training length. They evaluate on 25 ASR tasks covering 19 languages and three corpora, and analyze model behavior with independent validator transcriptions.
AI.result: Token-level OTC consistently outperforms standard CTC across all 25 tasks. The predictive-entropy-based wildcard schedule matches or beats epoch-indexed relaxation while being less dependent on a fixed training horizon. The combination of hybrid token+word arcs with the entropy-based schedule achieves the lowest mean WER on each corpus and delivers a 9.45% average relative WER reduction compared to CTC. Analysis with external validator transcripts shows that token-level models assign more wildcard-bypass probability specifically to disputed characters, suggesting that the method correctly identifies and discounts locally ambiguous transcript regions.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained, token-level wildcarding within the OTC framework better captures localized transcript ambiguity than word-level wildcards, enabling ASR models to tolerate real-world labeling noise without discarding useful supervision. A hybrid graph with both token- and word-level escape paths, coupled with an entropy-driven wildcard-weight schedule, yields robust and consistent WER gains over CTC across many languages and datasets, while targeted wildcard usage confirms that the improvements stem from better handling of disputed transcript segments.

title: Hallucination Neurons and Where to Find Them: An Investigation into the existence of Hallucination Neurons
summary: Interpretable machine learning for Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly relies on sparse probing methods that identify small sets of neurons claimed to detect and causally influence behaviors such as factuality recall, safety alignment, and hallucination. These claims have important implications for model auditing and behavioral steering, yet they are rarely tested against known failure modes of $L_1$-regularized probing in correlated, high-dimensional feature spaces. We propose a five-step diagnostic protocol covering feature correlation, bootstrap stability, sparse versus dense ranking disagreement, intervention baselines, and cross-dataset evaluation as a minimum standard for sparse-neuron localization claims. We investigate prior work using our proposed approach, specifically on H-neurons using open-source LLMs across TriviaQA, BioASQ, and NQ-Open datasets. Our results demonstrate detection replicates across both models and datasets, and exceeds the original reported AUROC gaps for TriviaQA and BioASQ datasets. Gemma 3 4B consistently outperforms MedGemma 4B on matched datasets, with AUROC gaps of +0.311 versus +0.235 on TriviaQA, +0.474 versus +0.455 on BioASQ, and +0.128 versus +0.112 on NQ-Open respectively. Causal validation at $n = 500$ with five random seeds shows statistically significant effects beyond random same-layer baselines. At the same time, the diagnostic results indicate that the selected neurons are not uniquely localized. Across the three Gemma 3 4B settings, 19 of 22 selected H-Neurons have Pearson $|r| > 0.7$ with other features, bootstrap selections show only moderate stability, and sparse and dense rankings overlap only weakly. Our findings show that sparse predictive structure can coexist with non-unique neuron selection. Routine diagnostic validation is necessary to distinguish detection claims from localization claims in mechanistic interpretability.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates and stress‑tests sparse neuron probing methods for interpretability in LLMs, showing that while they robustly detect behaviorally relevant signals, the identified neurons are not uniquely localized due to feature correlations and instability, motivating a standard diagnostic protocol.
AI.motivation: Sparse probing methods (often with L1 regularization) are widely used to claim that small sets of neurons in LLMs detect and causally control behaviors like factual recall, safety, and hallucination. However, statistical literature warns that in correlated, high-dimensional spaces, L1-based feature selection can be unstable, non-unique, and misleading about causal localization. The community often overlooks these failure modes, risking overconfident claims about specific neurons. The paper is motivated by the need for a rigorous, standardized diagnostic protocol to evaluate whether sparse neuron sets genuinely localize mechanisms or merely detect predictive structure amid correlated features.
AI.method: The authors propose a five-step diagnostic protocol for sparse-neuron localization: (1) analyze feature correlations to see if selected neurons are highly correlated with others, (2) assess bootstrap stability of neuron selection across resampled data, (3) compare sparse (L1) rankings with dense (e.g., unregularized or weakly regularized) importance rankings, (4) benchmark causal interventions against random same-layer baselines, and (5) evaluate cross-dataset robustness. They apply this protocol to re-examine prior work on H-neurons using open-source LLMs, specifically Gemma 3 4B and MedGemma 4B, across TriviaQA, BioASQ, and NQ-Open. They compute AUROC gaps between selected neuron subsets and baselines, run causal intervention experiments at n=500 with multiple random seeds, and analyze correlation structures, bootstrap selection frequencies, and overlap between sparse and dense rankings.
AI.result: Empirically, the authors find that the detection of H-neurons as predictive for the target behaviors replicates and even strengthens across models and datasets: Gemma 3 4B outperforms MedGemma 4B with larger AUROC gaps on all three benchmarks (e.g., +0.311 vs +0.235 on TriviaQA, +0.474 vs +0.455 on BioASQ, +0.128 vs +0.112 on NQ-Open). Causal interventions on the selected neurons at n=500 with five random seeds yield statistically significant effects beyond random same-layer neuron baselines, supporting that these neurons participate in the behavior. However, diagnostics show that these neurons are not uniquely localized: in Gemma 3 4B, 19 of 22 selected H-neurons have Pearson |r| > 0.7 with other features, bootstrap stability is only moderate, and sparse versus dense rankings overlap weakly. This indicates multiple correlated neurons can substitute for one another in the sparse solutions.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that sparse probing can robustly detect behaviorally relevant structure but does not by itself guarantee unique localization of mechanisms to specific neurons, especially in the presence of strong feature correlations and selection instability. Non-uniqueness and substitutability among correlated neurons mean that claims about particular neurons being the site of a behavior are often overstated. The authors argue that interpretability work should adopt routine diagnostic validation—via their five-step protocol—as a minimum standard to differentiate mere detection (finding predictive subspaces) from localization (identifying unique causal units) when using sparse neuron probes in mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.

title: ARGUS: Role-Aware Event Knowledge Graphs for U.S. Employment-Discrimination Complaints
summary: U.S. employment-discrimination complaints describe complex event sequences that are not explicitly captured by lexical or embedding-based representations alone. We present ARGUS, a source-grounded pipeline that combines a 5W1H-inspired schema, legal-domain models, and LLM-based structured generation to construct document-level Event Knowledge Graphs (EKGs) from CourtListener complaints. ARGUS extracts fact-bearing statements, builds chunk-level event graphs with participant, temporal, and causal structure, and merges them into document-level representations. We evaluate graph quality through human and multi-model assessment and test downstream utility on claim classification and legal QA. The graph-structured classifier outperforms raw and linearized baselines on the held-out set, and EKG-only retrieval improves document-scoped QA, while open-retrieval gains remain limited by low first-stage candidate recall. These results suggest that EKGs are most useful for organizing and reasoning over evidence once relevant material has been retrieved.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ARGUS, a system that builds event knowledge graphs (EKGs) from U.S. employment-discrimination complaints to better capture complex legal event sequences and improve downstream legal NLP tasks.
AI.motivation: Traditional lexical or embedding-based text representations fail to fully capture the complex, temporally ordered, and causally linked events described in U.S. employment-discrimination complaints. Legal practitioners and automated systems need structures that more faithfully represent who did what, when, where, why, and how, in order to support tasks like claim classification and legal question answering. The paper is motivated by the need for richer, source-grounded, document-level representations tailored to the legal domain.
AI.method: The authors propose ARGUS, a source-grounded pipeline inspired by the 5W1H schema (who, what, when, where, why, how). ARGUS uses legal-domain models and large language model–based structured generation to: (1) extract fact-bearing statements from CourtListener complaints, (2) build chunk-level event graphs with explicit participant, temporal, and causal structure, and (3) merge these into document-level Event Knowledge Graphs (EKGs). They then evaluate graph quality via human and multi-model assessments and test EKGs on downstream tasks such as claim classification and legal QA, comparing graph-structured models against raw text and linearized baselines.
AI.result: The graph-structured classifier built on EKGs outperforms baselines that rely on raw text or linearized representations on a held-out claim-classification set. In legal QA, retrieval based solely on EKGs improves performance for questions scoped to a specific document, indicating better organization and reasoning over already-retrieved evidence. However, open-domain QA gains are limited because the first-stage retrieval system has low recall, constraining the benefits of EKG-based reasoning at scale.
AI.conclusion: Event Knowledge Graphs derived by ARGUS offer a more faithful and useful representation of complex legal complaints than standard text or embedding-based approaches, especially for tasks that require structured reasoning once relevant documents are in hand. EKGs are most beneficial for organizing and reasoning over evidence in document-scoped settings, whereas their impact in open-retrieval scenarios is constrained by upstream retrieval limitations. The work suggests that integrating rich event structure with improved retrieval systems is a promising direction for legal NLP.

title: Decoding Imagined Speech: A Strictly Subject-Independent Approach Using EEG
summary: Imagined speech decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) has gained increasing attention as a potential communication pathway for individuals with severe motor impairments, yet reported performance often relies on evaluation protocols that do not clearly reflect cross-subject generalization. This study presents a transparent baseline investigation of a multi-class imagined speech EEG dataset under a strictly subject-independent evaluation framework. Two preprocessing and feature extraction pipelines were compared: a time-domain statistical feature approach and a frequency-domain spectral bandpower approach, evaluated using subject-wise cross-validation and trial-level majority voting with a random forest classifier. The spectral pipeline achieved a significantly higher mean trial-wise accuracy than the statistical pipeline (49.03 $\pm$ 4.18% vs. 37.97 $\pm$ 3.79%) for coarse-level classification across subjects. Forward feature selection further indicated that a limited subset of frequency bands captured most of the discriminative information. Overall, this work provides a strong basis for future brain-computer interface studies targeting improved cross-subject generalization in EEG-based imagined speech decoding.

AI.tldr: They compare two EEG feature pipelines (time-domain statistics vs frequency-domain bandpower) for imagined speech decoding under strict subject-independent evaluation, showing spectral features work better and only a few bands are key.
AI.motivation: Imagined speech BCIs could give communication ability to people with severe motor impairments, but many reported decoding results use evaluation schemes that don’t test generalization to new subjects, so performance may be overestimated. A clear, transparent baseline under a rigorous cross-subject protocol is needed.
AI.method: They use a multi-class imagined speech EEG dataset and enforce a strictly subject-independent scheme: subject-wise cross-validation and trial-level majority voting. They build and compare two preprocessing/feature-extraction pipelines: (1) time-domain statistical features; (2) frequency-domain spectral bandpower features. Both feed a random forest classifier. They also apply forward feature selection to identify which frequency bands contribute most to discrimination.
AI.result: The spectral bandpower pipeline significantly outperforms the time-domain statistics pipeline for coarse imagined speech classification across subjects: 49.03 ± 4.18% vs 37.97 ± 3.79% mean trial-wise accuracy. Feature selection shows that only a limited number of frequency bands carry most discriminative information.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-domain spectral bandpower features provide a stronger baseline than simple time-domain statistics for subject-independent imagined speech EEG decoding, and only a subset of bands is crucial. The study offers a transparent, rigorously evaluated baseline to guide and benchmark future BCI methods aimed at robust cross-subject generalization.

title: SemMSA: Latent Semantic-Aided Robust Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Incomplete Data
summary: Recent research on Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) has focused on learning from language, visual, and acoustic modalities with incomplete data to infer human sentiment. Most studies typically compensate for missing information by reconstructing modality features or designing complicated fusion mechanisms. However, these methods still suffer from spurious generation and noisy guidance due to the lack of high-level semantic grounding in partially observed multimodal evidence.
