To address these issues, we propose SemMSA, a latent semantic-aided framework that constructs rich sentiment-relevant semantics with LLMs, fully integrating with all modalities via anchor-free spectral alignment. It mainly consists of Cross-modal Semantic Refinement (CSR) and Cross-modal Spectral Alignment (CSA). Specifically, CSR first adaptively extracts visual and acoustic representations by corresponding adapters to form a unified multimodal prefix with language in the frozen LLM embedding space. It then iteratively produces continuous discriminative semantic states through a token-efficient latent refinement process without decoding explicit text. Next, CSA simultaneously aligns the refined semantics with all modalities by enhancing the dominant spectral component of their kernel Gram matrix. This captures global nonlinear dependencies among all representations without relying on a predefined anchor modality. In addition, an instance-level spectral separation constraint preserves cross-sample discriminability and mitigates representation collapse. Extensive experiments on SIMS, MOSI, and MOSEI benchmarks demonstrate that SemMSA achieves state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: A multimodal sentiment analysis framework (SemMSA) uses large language model-based latent semantics and spectral alignment to better handle missing or partial visual/acoustic data and achieves state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal sentiment analysis methods struggle with incomplete modalities and rely on reconstructing missing features or complex fusion. These still produce noisy or spurious signals due to lacking high-level semantic grounding across modalities.
AI.method: SemMSA introduces latent semantic guidance from LLMs and anchor-free spectral alignment. Cross-modal Semantic Refinement (CSR) maps visual and acoustic features via adapters into the frozen LLM embedding space, forming a unified multimodal prefix with text, then iteratively refines continuous semantic states without explicit decoding. Cross-modal Spectral Alignment (CSA) enhances the dominant spectral component of the kernel Gram matrix across modalities to align refined semantics with all modalities, capturing global nonlinear dependencies without a fixed anchor modality, and adds an instance-level spectral separation constraint to maintain cross-sample discriminability.
AI.result: On three standard MSA benchmarks (SIMS, MOSI, MOSEI), SemMSA outperforms previous methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance in sentiment prediction under incomplete multimodal settings.
AI.conclusion: Latent, LLM-derived semantic representations combined with anchor-free spectral alignment provide more robust and globally consistent multimodal fusion, alleviating issues from missing modalities and noisy guidance and improving sentiment prediction accuracy.

title: PUBG Ally: A Conversational Embodied Agent as an AI Teammate
summary: We introduce PUBG Ally, an embodied agent for PUBG: BATTLEGROUNDS that can reason, act autonomously, and play alongside players as a voice-enabled teammate. Building such a teammate requires combining two difficult capabilities: it must perceive and respond to a constantly changing game world under strict latency constraints while interacting naturally with players, keeping its speech synchronized with its actions. Ally therefore combines agentic tool use with real-time game control. A language-model agent uses a controlled interface to inspect game information, interpret player speech, maintain context, decide what to say, and issue high-level action choices that steer a faster control layer for movement, combat, and recovery. Because the player's and Ally's speech and actions continually shape each other and the course of the match, training requires data from actual gameplay. We therefore collect data across nearly 39k sessions in which real players play alongside Ally, recording gameplay, player speech, agent decisions, tool use, actions, and player feedback, and use these records for iterative training. To evaluate teammate quality, we use player feedback and preference comparisons to identify gaps between offline evaluations and player preferences, and iteratively refine the evaluation criteria. Deploying Ally in live service further requires low-latency on-device execution and safeguards for player-facing communication, which we address through model compression, context compaction, targeted safety training, runtime guardrails, and memory redaction. During the live service, we surveyed players in 141 countries. Among respondents whose play with Ally was confirmed in game records, positive responses exceeded negative responses by 25.1 percentage points when asked whether they would recommend Ally, with players describing Ally not only as a tool but also as a teammate or companion.

AI.tldr: PUBG Ally is a real-time, voice-enabled LLM-based teammate for PUBG that jointly reasons, talks, and acts in game, trained and refined from large-scale real-player interactions and feedback.
AI.motivation: Most LLM-based agents either reason with tools in relatively slow, turn-based settings or control game characters without natural language teamwork. Creating a believable in-game teammate for a fast-paced battle royale requires tightly coupling language interaction, decision making, and low-latency control, while also satisfying safety, performance, and player-experience constraints in a live commercial title.
AI.method: The authors design a two-layer embodied agent, PUBG Ally. A top language-model agent uses a controlled tool interface to read game state, interpret player speech, track context and memory, choose high-level strategies, and generate synchronized dialogue plus high-level commands. A lower control layer translates these decisions into fast, fine-grained game actions for movement, combat, and recovery. They deploy Ally to real players, logging ~39k sessions of gameplay, speech, tool calls, and feedback, and iteratively train and refine both behavior and evaluation metrics based on preference data and alignment between offline metrics and live player preferences. For deployment, they apply model compression, context reduction, specialized safety training, runtime guardrails, and automated redaction of sensitive memory content to enable on-device, low-latency, safe interactions.
AI.result: They successfully deploy Ally as a live, voice-enabled teammate in PUBG: BATTLEGROUNDS, used across 141 countries. The system operates under strict latency constraints while jointly handling perception, reasoning, tool use, dialogue, and continuous control. Survey data from players whose Ally usage was confirmed in logs shows that positive sentiment (willingness to recommend Ally) exceeds negative by 25.1 percentage points, and qualitative feedback indicates that players often view Ally as a teammate or companion rather than just a tool.
AI.conclusion: It is feasible to deploy a real-time, LLM-driven, voice-enabled game teammate at scale in a complex commercial title by combining agentic tool use with a specialized control layer and by training iteratively on large volumes of real gameplay interactions. Aligning evaluations with real player preferences and implementing strong optimization and safety measures are critical for both technical performance and positive player experience, and the resulting system can be perceived as a genuine teammate, not merely an assistive interface.

title: JevOut: Natural Context Can Flip Decision Models
comment: 32 pages, 5 figures, 23 tables. Homepage: https://xzx34.github.io/jevout/ ; Code: https://github.com/xzx34/JevOut
summary: Dedicated decision models such as Jev map unstructured language to probability distributions over finite choices, allowing their outputs to directly route requests, select tools, and trigger actions. Yet real-world inputs rarely arrive in isolation: they come with background details and surrounding context. We find that short additions that fit naturally into this context can nevertheless redirect an otherwise correct decision, even when the correct answer remains unchanged. To study this behavior, we fix a wrong target option for each initially correct item and use the model's option probabilities to refine fluent context additions while preserving the source, question, choices, and gold answer. Within 64 accepted target evaluations, the optimizer identifies contexts that redirect Jev on 312 of 508 initially correct decisions (61.4%); in 229 cases, Jev assigns at least 0.7 probability to the fixed wrong option. Across seven datasets, three additional decision systems show targeted flip rates of 64.9%-73.2% on decisions they initially answer correctly. Taken together, these results expose a pronounced fragility in current decision models: short, ordinary-looking context can shift a correct choice to a high-confidence wrong one. Because these models turn language directly into downstream choices, this sensitivity raises concerns about treating their probability outputs as reliable decision interfaces.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that decision models that map language directly to discrete choices are highly fragile: small, natural-looking pieces of added context can push them from a correct to a high-confidence wrong decision.
AI.motivation: Decision models like Jev are increasingly used to turn natural language into concrete actions, tool selections, and routing decisions based on probability over a finite set of options. In practice, inputs to these systems are embedded in rich context rather than presented as isolated questions. If small, plausible modifications to surrounding context can reliably distort these models’ choices, then using their probabilities as trustworthy decision interfaces is risky. The authors want to quantify and understand how vulnerable such models are to subtle, context-based perturbations that keep the core task unchanged but shift the model’s choice.
AI.method: The authors take decision models (including Jev) that output probability distributions over a fixed set of options. For items they initially answer correctly, they artificially fix a specific wrong ‘target’ option. Then they use an optimization procedure that iteratively constructs short, fluent context additions around the original input while leaving the source text, question, answer choices, and gold label unchanged. The optimizer uses the model’s option probabilities as a signal: it searches for context snippets that increase the model’s probability on the pre-chosen wrong option until the model flips its decision. They run this procedure across multiple datasets and on several different decision systems, measuring how often and how strongly the decisions can be redirected.
AI.result: For the Jev model, within 64 accepted target evaluations, the optimization procedure finds contextual additions that flip 312 out of 508 initially correct decisions (61.4%). In 229 of these cases, Jev assigns at least 0.7 probability to the fixed wrong option, indicating high-confidence errors. Across seven datasets and three additional decision systems, targeted flip rates on initially correct decisions range from 64.9% to 73.2%. Thus, short, natural context is frequently sufficient to push these systems from the correct answer to a confidently wrong one.
AI.conclusion: Current decision models that map language directly to discrete choices are highly sensitive to small, natural contextual changes: seemingly benign added sentences can systematically redirect correct decisions to targeted, high-confidence mistakes without altering the underlying question or true answer. This fragility suggests that their probability outputs should not be treated as robust, reliable decision interfaces for routing, tool selection, or action triggering, and it highlights the need for improved robustness and defenses against such context-induced failures.

title: A Risk-Adaptive and Evidence-Constrained Framework for Generative AI Feedback in Programming Education
summary: Generative artificial intelligence can turn learning analytics into personalized support, but feedback systems must decide when to intervene, which evidence to use, and how much assistance to provide. We developed a risk-adaptive, evidence-constrained framework for introductory programming using 2993 failed-submission states from 215 students. Student-disjoint models predicted persistent failure and related outcomes; four matched feedback conditions were generated for 136 cases; and calibrated risk informed capacity-limited intervention policies. The validation-selected logistic regression model achieved a test precision-recall area under the curve of 0.550 and a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve of 0.681. Broader student histories improved prediction of unmodified resubmission. After standardized repair and evidence gating, 519 of 544 newly generated messages contained all required components. A fixed-threshold sequential policy selected 17.8% of eligible test states and captured 25.2% of observed persistent failures. These findings support an evidence-gated progressive assistance strategy: calibrated risk guides intervention timing, recorded evidence constrains feedback content, and assistance progresses from self-checks to localized hints when warranted. The framework connects prediction, decision-making, and grounded generation while keeping their evaluation outcomes distinct.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a risk-adaptive, evidence-gated feedback framework for introductory programming that uses predictive models to decide when and how to generate generative-AI-based feedback, linking prediction, decision, and content generation while evaluating each separately.
AI.motivation: Generative AI can enhance learning analytics by providing personalized feedback, but practical deployment requires principled answers to three questions: when to intervene, what evidence to base feedback on, and how much help to provide. Existing systems often blur prediction, decision-making, and feedback generation, making it hard to ensure that feedback is timely, appropriately targeted, and grounded in observable student behavior. The authors aim to build a framework that coordinates these elements and to demonstrate its feasibility and performance in an introductory programming context.
AI.method: The authors collected 2993 failed code-submission states from 215 students in an introductory programming course. They trained student-disjoint predictive models to estimate the risk of persistent failure and related outcomes, and then selected a logistic regression model based on validation performance. Using 136 cases, they generated four matched feedback conditions that varied in assistance level. They designed intervention policies that used calibrated risk scores and capacity limits to determine when to intervene. They then standardized feedback message structure, applied evidence gating so that feedback content had to be supported by recorded data, and evaluated model performance (PR-AUC, ROC-AUC), feedback completeness (presence of all required components), and policy coverage (fraction of states and failures captured).
AI.result: The chosen logistic regression model achieved a precision-recall AUC of 0.550 and ROC-AUC of 0.681 on test data. Including broader student histories improved prediction of whether students would resubmit without modification. After applying standardized repair and evidence gating, 519 of 544 newly generated feedback messages contained all mandated components, indicating high structural completeness and grounding. A fixed-threshold sequential intervention policy acted on 17.8% of eligible test states while capturing 25.2% of persistent failures, indicating selective but effective targeting. These results show that risk scores can meaningfully guide intervention timing and that evidence-gated generative feedback can be both feasible and structurally reliable.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that an evidence-gated, risk-adaptive framework can effectively coordinate prediction, intervention decisions, and generative feedback in programming education. Calibrated risk estimates are suitable for controlling when to intervene; recorded, verifiable evidence can constrain what feedback is allowed to say; and assistance can escalate progressively from self-check prompts to focused hints when justified by predicted risk. The framework demonstrates a way to integrate learning analytics and generative AI while keeping the evaluation of prediction quality, decision policy performance, and feedback generation separate, supporting more accountable and interpretable educational AI systems.

title: When Can Agents Forget Their Reasoning? ICLR for Long-Horizon Agent Context Compression
summary: Long horizon language model agents continually accumulate reasoning history, increasing context length and inference cost even after earlier decisions have been executed and observed. Unlike static Chain of Thought compression, removing historical reasoning can change future actions and the resulting interaction trajectory. We study when such reasoning can be safely forgotten. We propose Interaction Aware Compression for Long Horizon Reasoning (ICLR), a training free online method that ranks reasoning blocks using frozen proxy entropy while preserving actions, tool calls, and observations. On 260 WorkBuddyBench tasks, ICLR improves average reward from 0.699 to 0.718, while reducing input, output, and cache read tokens by 25.5%, 14.4%, and 33.3%, respectively. Ablations reveal trajectory amplification, where local reasoning deletion produces nonlinear changes in total computation by altering subsequent interaction. Representation probing, activation patching, and controlled trajectory analyses further suggest that historical reasoning becomes more replaceable once task relevant derived state has been reliably externalized into code, files, tool outputs, or environmental feedback. These results characterize agent reasoning as dynamic working state rather than permanent interaction history.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method for safely deleting parts of an LLM agent’s past reasoning to reduce context length and computation, without hurting—and sometimes improving—long-horizon task performance.
AI.motivation: In long-horizon tasks, LLM agents generate extensive chains of reasoning and tool interactions over many steps. All this history is usually kept in the context, which grows unbounded, raising inference cost and latency. Simple chain-of-thought compression may not work because deleting earlier reasoning can alter later actions and the overall interaction trajectory. There is a need to understand when past reasoning is no longer functionally necessary and can be forgotten without degrading the agent’s performance.
AI.method: They introduce Interaction Aware Compression for Long Horizon Reasoning (ICLR), a training-free, online compression method. ICLR segments the agent’s past reasoning into blocks and ranks them using a frozen proxy-entropy measure to estimate their importance, while always preserving actions, tool calls, and observations. Reasoning blocks deemed less critical are removed from the context. They then evaluate this on the WorkBuddyBench benchmark and perform ablation and analysis using trajectory amplification studies, representation probing, and activation patching to understand how deleting reasoning influences future interaction and internal representations.
AI.result: On 260 WorkBuddyBench tasks, ICLR increases average reward from 0.699 to 0.718 while significantly reducing token usage: input tokens by 25.5%, output tokens by 14.4%, and cache read tokens by 33.3%. Ablation experiments reveal a trajectory amplification effect, where small local deletions of reasoning can nonlinearly alter total computation and behavior by changing subsequent interactions. Probing and controlled analyses show that once key task state has been externalized (e.g., into code, files, tool outputs, or environment feedback), the internal reasoning that led to it is more safely removable.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that for long-horizon LLM agents, much of the historical chain-of-thought functions as transient working memory rather than essential long-term history. By selectively forgetting reasoning that has already been externalized into stable artifacts or observations, agents can reduce context length and computation while maintaining or even improving performance. This reframes agent reasoning as dynamic working state and suggests that context management should focus on preserving externalized task state and high-entropy reasoning, rather than storing full interaction transcripts.

title: Ontology-Mediated Neurosymbolic Constraint Acquisition from Multiple Stakeholders
comment: Accepted for KG-NeSy Workshop, co-located with ISWC 2026
summary: Neurosymbolic research typically assumes a pre-existing symbolic specification, leaving the upstream challenge of acquiring and formalizing requirements and constraints largely unaddressed. We present an architecture that fills this gap by using an OWL configuration ontology to mediate between neural constraint sources and downstream consumers. In this framework, LLM assistants elicit soft stakeholder preferences, while hardware specifications define hard physical and engineering limits. The ontology unifies these heterogeneous inputs, leverages description logic to identify unsatisfiability, and generates symbolic explanations that enable LLMs to interactively renegotiate terms with users. Any remaining conflicts are resolved downstream via priority-based relaxation. We illustrate our approach on a microgrid use case from the FLEXI project and argue its generalizability to multi-stakeholder domains where constraint acquisition is distributed across human and automated sources of unequal authority.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an ontology-centered architecture that connects neural constraint sources (like LLM assistants) with symbolic reasoning for requirement acquisition and conflict resolution, illustrated in a microgrid case study.
AI.motivation: Most neurosymbolic systems assume that a clean, formal symbolic specification of constraints already exists, but in practice gathering and formalizing requirements from different stakeholders and physical limits is messy and underexplored. The authors want to close this gap by providing a principled way to acquire, unify, and reason over heterogeneous constraints coming from humans, LLMs, and hardware specifications.
AI.method: They design an architecture where an OWL configuration ontology serves as the central schema. LLM-based assistants interact with stakeholders to elicit soft preferences, while hardware and engineering specs provide hard constraints. These heterogeneous inputs are encoded in the ontology. Description logic reasoning is then used to check satisfiability, detect conflicts, and derive symbolic explanations. LLMs use these explanations in an interactive loop to renegotiate requirements with users. Remaining conflicts that cannot be resolved at this stage are handled later using priority-based relaxation mechanisms.
AI.result: The authors implement the architecture in a microgrid scenario from the FLEXI project, demonstrating that their ontology and reasoning pipeline can integrate human preferences and physical constraints, detect inconsistencies, and support iterative renegotiation. The case study suggests that the approach can manage distributed constraint acquisition across different sources and authority levels.
AI.conclusion: An OWL-based configuration ontology coupled with LLM assistants and description-logic reasoning can operationalize the upstream phase of requirement and constraint acquisition in neurosymbolic systems. The proposed framework not only detects and explains inconsistencies but also enables interactive renegotiation and downstream conflict relaxation, and is argued to generalize to multi-stakeholder domains beyond the showcased microgrid use case.

title: Qwen-Planner-Agent: A Closed-Loop AI-for-AI Framework for Real-World Mobile Planner Agents
summary: The rapid progression of large language models is extending AI from passive content generation into the active workflows of engineering and scientific discovery. This shift raises a compelling question: can AI be both the object of development and an active participant in building next-generation AI systems? We explore this question by building Qwen-Planner-Agent within a closed-loop AI-for-AI framework for scalable development and iterative improvement. Mobile planning offers a demanding test of this approach: complex, long-horizon tasks challenge agent reliability, while costly real-device interaction limits development scalability. The framework connects data production, model training, and deployment through a shared action-feedback-verification contract. (i) AI for Data builds a human-gated agentic data flywheel in which specialized agents construct tasks, collect interaction trajectories, curate and balance training data, and use training feedback to guide subsequent data generation. (ii) AI for Training combines a supervised planning cold start with hybrid-environment online agentic reinforcement learning, where we introduce Competence-Aware Reward-and-Advantage Engineering (CARE) to reduce reasoning and tool-use costs while preserving task performance. (iii) AI drives model--harness co-evolution through an execution-evidence-driven loop that orchestrates memory, skills, and tools at runtime and feeds structured action feedback and preserved failure traces back into coordinated model and harness adaptation. Qwen-Planner-Agent achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated models and systems on MobilePA-Bench, improving over its base model across tool use, memory, skills, and sub-agent coordination. Further evaluations of our model show improvements across non-mobile agentic benchmarks while largely preserving general capabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Qwen-Planner-Agent, an AI agent developed within a closed-loop AI-for-AI framework that uses AI to generate data, train models, and co-evolve the runtime harness, achieving state-of-the-art performance on a mobile planning benchmark and improving general agentic capabilities.
AI.motivation: As large language models move from passive generation to active roles in engineering and scientific workflows, there is a need for scalable, iterative methods where AI both develops and improves next-generation AI systems. Mobile planning is a challenging testbed because tasks are complex and long-horizon, and real-device interaction is expensive, making conventional data collection and training pipelines hard to scale.
AI.method: The authors build Qwen-Planner-Agent within a closed-loop AI-for-AI framework that tightly couples data generation, training, and deployment via an action-feedback-verification contract. (i) AI for Data: a human-gated agentic data flywheel where specialized AI agents generate tasks, collect trajectories, and curate/balance data using training feedback. (ii) AI for Training: start with supervised planning, then apply hybrid-environment online agentic reinforcement learning augmented by Competence-Aware Reward-and-Advantage Engineering (CARE) to lower reasoning and tool-use costs without harming task success. (iii) AI for Deployment: co-evolve the model and runtime harness through an execution-evidence-driven loop that manages memory, skills, and tools and feeds structured feedback and failure traces back into model and harness updates.
AI.result: Qwen-Planner-Agent attains the best overall performance on MobilePA-Bench among all evaluated models and systems, outperforming its base model in tool usage, memory handling, skill execution, and sub-agent coordination. It also delivers improvements across other non-mobile agentic benchmarks while largely maintaining its original broad capabilities.
AI.conclusion: A closed-loop AI-for-AI framework, where AI systems help generate data, guide training, and co-evolve deployment harnesses, can effectively build stronger agentic LLMs. The proposed Qwen-Planner-Agent demonstrates that this approach scales to complex mobile planning tasks and transfers to other agent benchmarks, suggesting a promising direction for automated, iterative AI system development.

title: Who Holds the Pen? Let Specifications, Not Agents, Sign Off
summary: Large language model agents increasingly combine generation, decision-making, execution, and self-evaluation within a single agentic loop. Although they operate under external specifications such as task instructions, guidelines, output schemas, and reusable skills, these specifications typically remain context for the same model that acts and declares completion, leaving no independent specification authority boundary. We identify two resulting gaps. The understanding--execution gap arises when a requirement is understood but not satisfied in execution; the state--authority gap arises when an agent's interpretation or completion claim does not establish the required state. On SkillsBench, using only agent-visible prompts, workspace information, and injected skill specifications, we extract 509 source-grounded task directions. Across seven models, only 79.6%--86.4% are satisfied, while completion-claim rates exceed official evaluator pass rates by 28.7--37.9 percentage points. We therefore separate agent proposals from authoritative state. Agents may plan, act, and request completion, but only admissible evidence from qualified providers may establish specification-governed state. SpecHarness operationalizes this principle by compiling visible specifications into source-linked obligations and governing execution and finalization through versioned obligation state. Verifiable requirements are mediated or validated at runtime, while ambiguous or subjective requirements remain advisory. Experiments on guideline-following and artifact-generation tasks show that specifications can serve not merely as behavioral guidance, but as authority over compliant execution and completion.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies reliability gaps in current LLM agents and introduces SpecHarness, a framework that treats specifications as an independent source of authority over whether tasks are truly completed, separating agent behavior from authoritative task state.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents both interpret task specifications and judge their own completion, which leads to mismatches between what is required and what is executed, and to agents overclaiming success. There is no independent, authoritative mechanism that turns specs into enforceable obligations and verifies that the required state is actually achieved. The authors want to formalize and enforce the role of specifications so that agent behavior and task completion can be evaluated and governed more robustly.
AI.method: 1) Empirically analyze LLM agents on SkillsBench using only information visible to the agent (prompts, workspace info, injected skill specs) and automatically extract 509 source-grounded task directions. 2) Measure how often models satisfy these directions versus how often they claim completion across seven LLMs, revealing execution and authority gaps. 3) Propose a new paradigm where specifications are compiled into explicit, versioned obligations that govern execution and completion. 4) Implement this paradigm as SpecHarness, which (a) converts visible specs into source-linked obligations, (b) maintains an obligation state machine, and (c) mediates or validates verifiable requirements at runtime via qualified evidence providers while treating ambiguous/subjective requirements as advisory. 5) Evaluate the framework on guideline-following and artifact-generation tasks to show improved alignment between specifications and authoritative completion.
AI.result: Empirically, the authors find that although models satisfy only about 79.6%–86.4% of the extracted task directions, they claim completion far more often, with completion-claim rates exceeding official evaluator pass rates by 28.7–37.9 percentage points. This confirms both an understanding–execution gap and a state–authority gap. With SpecHarness, specifications are turned into enforceable obligations whose satisfaction is determined via admissible evidence, leading to more faithful adherence to requirements and more accurate determinations of task completion on the tested tasks.
AI.conclusion: The work shows that treating specifications merely as instructions within an LLM’s context is insufficient for reliable, trustworthy agent behavior. By separating agent proposals from authoritative task state and compiling specifications into obligation-governed execution via SpecHarness, systems can ensure that verifiable requirements are checked by independent mechanisms and that completion is not determined solely by the agent’s self-report. Specifications can thus function as an authority over execution and completion, reducing overclaiming and improving compliance on complex tasks.

title: Neuro-symbolic AI for Industrial Configuration
comment: Accepted at the Industrial Track at the NeSy Conference 2026
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance on a wide range of generative tasks. Yet their probabilistic nature makes them, in isolation, fundamentally unsuited for industrial product configuration, where outputs must be syntactically valid, semantically consistent with a knowledge base of hundreds of features and rules, and producible by an existing manufacturing chain. We argue that Neuro-symbolic (NeSy) AI methods lay out a promising path towards industrial-grade configurators that are reliable by design, explainable, and trustworthy. This paper describes a taxonomy of three NeSy integration strategies, namely hybrid inference, hybrid fine-tuning, and hybrid training, exploring their usage in the configuration domain. We report our effort to operationalize NeSy concepts in an industrial configuration copilot and derive a set of practical design choices for deploying trustworthy AI in engineering environments. We close with a discussion of open research challenges we consider most pressing, in particular how to scale NeSy methods from small academic demonstrators to the size of industrial configurators.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and analyzes neuro-symbolic integration strategies to make large language model–based industrial product configurators reliable, explainable, and scalable to real-world engineering settings.
AI.motivation: Pure LLMs are probabilistic and thus unreliable for industrial product configuration, where every configuration must strictly obey complex syntactic constraints, engineering rules, and manufacturability requirements encoded in large knowledge bases. Industry needs AI configurators that are correct-by-construction, traceable, and trustworthy, which current LLM-only approaches do not guarantee.
AI.method: The authors introduce a taxonomy of three neuro-symbolic integration strategies tailored to configuration systems: (1) hybrid inference, where LLMs and symbolic solvers or rule engines are composed at inference time; (2) hybrid fine-tuning, where LLMs are adapted using data or feedback generated from symbolic knowledge; and (3) hybrid training, where symbolic constraints are incorporated directly into the model’s learning objective. They examine how each strategy can be applied to configuration tasks and describe their implementation experience in an industrial configuration copilot.
AI.result: They operationalize these neuro-symbolic strategies in a real industrial configuration copilot, identifying what worked and what failed in practice. From this, they distill concrete design choices and architectural patterns that make AI-assisted configuration more reliable and usable in engineering workflows.
AI.conclusion: Neuro-symbolic AI is a promising route to build industrial-grade configuration copilots that are reliable, explainable, and aligned with complex engineering constraints. However, substantial open challenges remain, particularly around scaling NeSy methods from small academic prototypes to large, real-world configurators with hundreds of features and rules. The paper highlights these challenges and calls for further research on scalability, integration, and robustness in industrial settings.

title: ENDOPROMPT: Victim-Side Pseudo-References for Utility Degradation
summary: Prompt injection can degrade benign task performance without eliciting harmful content. Yet many attack objectives depend on task labels or predefined target responses. We present ENDOPROMPT, a white-box method that learns utility-degrading prefixes from unlabeled instructions. Its generator takes the request text as input. Clean victim continuations serve as pseudo-references: local search identifies prefixes that reduce continuation likelihood, and preference fitting on comparisons within the same instruction, followed by reward refinement, distills this signal into a generator. At deployment, the generator produces one prefix per request without further victim-side search. Across four instruction-tuned models and the complete splits of seven benign benchmarks, ENDOPROMPT yields a mean utility change of -26.8 percentage points; 27 of 28 cells are negative. Failure analysis reveals output expansion and prefix reuse; the controls do not establish a degradation advantage from request matching. Victim-derived supervision can reveal utility weaknesses without benchmark feedback or prescribed failure responses. The code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ENDOPROMPT, a white-box method for automatically generating adversarial text prefixes that reliably degrade the task performance of instruction-tuned language models on benign tasks, without needing labeled data, benchmark scores, or explicit harmful targets.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt injection attacks often aim to elicit specific harmful content or follow label-dependent targets, and they usually require supervision such as task labels, predefined target responses, or benchmark feedback. However, real-world adversaries may want to generally reduce the utility of models on benign tasks, and defenders need tools to uncover such vulnerabilities without relying on labeled benchmarks or hand-crafted failure modes. The authors are motivated to design an attack that can (i) systematically degrade benign task performance, (ii) use only unlabeled instructions and model behavior, and (iii) generalize across models and datasets, thereby exposing structural weaknesses in instruction-tuned LMs.
AI.method: The authors propose ENDOPROMPT, a white-box attack that learns adversarial prefixes using only access to the victim model’s logits. For each benign instruction, they use the model’s clean continuation as a pseudo-reference. They then apply a local search procedure over candidate prefixes, looking for tokens that lower the likelihood of this reference continuation, effectively identifying text that steers the model away from its preferred answer. From multiple such comparisons for the same instruction, they perform preference learning (preference fitting) to train a generator that maps instructions to harmful prefixes. A subsequent reward refinement step further distills the signal about which prefixes are most utility-degrading. At test time, the trained generator takes each new instruction as input and outputs an adversarial prefix in a single forward pass; no additional search over the victim model is required during deployment.
AI.result: Evaluated on four different instruction-tuned language models and seven benign benchmark datasets (using all splits), ENDOPROMPT achieves a mean performance drop of 26.8 percentage points in task utility, with 27 out of 28 model–dataset combinations showing negative utility changes. The analysis highlights two notable phenomena: (1) the attacks often cause responses to become unnecessarily long or expanded, and (2) the learned prefixes exhibit reuse patterns, meaning similar or repeated adversarial prefixes are effective across different inputs. Control experiments, in which prefixes are not tailored to requests, indicate that simple request matching alone does not explain the degradation, suggesting the method is learning genuinely more damaging perturbations than naive baselines.
AI.conclusion: ENDOPROMPT demonstrates that it is possible to learn powerful, generalized prompt-injection-style prefixes that significantly degrade language model performance on benign tasks using only victim-derived supervision—specifically, the model’s own clean continuations—without labels, benchmark feedback, or explicit harmful targets. This shows that instruction-tuned models harbor exploitable weaknesses that can be surfaced purely through white-box access and preference-based training, and that targeted request-conditioned adversarial prefixes can be generated efficiently at inference time. The work suggests that stronger robustness and better defenses against such utility-degrading prompt injections are necessary, and that evaluation frameworks should consider these label-free, utility-oriented attacks.

title: Augur: A Synthetic Decision Lab for Rehearsing Reactions to Product and Policy Changes
summary:
Before a product or policy change ships, the question that matters is how people will react to it. Augur rehearses that reaction offline: it builds a typed knowledge graph from the change documents, populates a grounded persona market, simulates the interaction, and returns an auditable decision memo recommending one of five actions. We assemble Gold-50, fifty real product and policy episodes whose real-world outcome is known, adjudicated against the public record, and score the five-way release verdict against it.
  Our central finding is methodological and negative: most of the measured gap between frontier cloud models and open-weight models we fine-tune and serve offline is attributable to an under-specified evaluation, not a difference in capability. We show this three ways. First, the prompt envelope alone can dominate the score: holding weights, cases and scorer fixed, one system -- a LoRA-SFT adapter on Qwen3-32B -- swings from 0% to 73%. Second, in a matched 2x2 ablation, defining the decision taxonomy in the prompt -- with no model change -- lifts every frontier model by +24 to +34pp; under the under-specified prompt, Qwen3-32B LoRA-SFT served offline beats all three frontier models (paired McNemar, Holm-corrected), and once the prompt is fair no significant difference from any of them is detected. Third, agreement with the distillation teacher rises without accuracy following, and the full pipeline amplifies a systematic "over-doom" bias rather than improving the verdict. Separately, we validate the reaction layer on its own terms: blind judges across four model families find the synthetic reaction recovers 67-90% of the concerns the public actually raised, and a pre-registered ablation locates its value -- largest where the decision is hardest, redundant near ceiling. The pipeline that regenerates every number and figure here is available from the authors.

AI.tldr: Augur is a system that simulates public reaction to product and policy changes using a knowledge graph, persona market, and LLM-based decision memo; the paper finds that apparent performance gaps between frontier and fine-tuned open models mostly come from under-specified evaluation prompts, not true capability differences.
AI.motivation: Organizations need a way to anticipate how people will react to product or policy changes before launch, ideally in a systematic, auditable way. Current LLM-based evaluation setups suggest large gaps between frontier and open-weight models, but it's unclear how much of this is real versus an artifact of the evaluation design. The paper aims to (1) build a pipeline (Augur) to rehearse user reactions offline and (2) rigorously test whether observed model performance differences are genuine or driven by evaluation underspecification.
AI.method: The authors build Augur, a pipeline that: (1) parses product/policy change documents into a typed knowledge graph; (2) constructs a grounded market of personas; (3) simulates their reactions via LLMs; and (4) produces an auditable decision memo recommending one of five release actions. They assemble Gold-50, a set of 50 real historical product/policy episodes with known outcomes. They then run a series of controlled ablations: varying only the prompt envelope; performing a matched 2x2 ablation on prompt taxonomy vs. model; comparing offline fine-tuned Qwen3-32B LoRA-SFT against frontier cloud models; and measuring how agreement with a distillation teacher tracks (or fails to track) accuracy. They also conduct blind-judge evaluations across four model families to assess how well synthetic reactions recover real-world public concerns, and a preregistered ablation to see in which difficulty regimes the reaction layer adds value.
AI.result: 1) Prompt design has a huge impact on measured performance: for the same Qwen3-32B LoRA-SFT model, changing only the prompt envelope moves accuracy from 0% to 73% on the five-way verdict task. 2) Explicitly defining the decision taxonomy in the prompt boosts every frontier model's performance by +24–34 percentage points, and under the weaker, under-specified prompt, the offline Qwen3-32B LoRA-SFT outperforms all tested frontier models; with the fair, well-specified prompt, no significant performance differences remain. 3) Greater agreement with a distillation teacher model does not imply higher accuracy, and the full Augur pipeline tends to amplify a systematic "over-doom" bias in decisions rather than correcting it. 4) When evaluated on its own, the reaction-simulation layer recovers 67–90% of real public concerns according to blind judges, with the biggest benefits on harder decisions and little added value when performance is near ceiling. The authors release a reproducible pipeline for all reported numbers and figures.
AI.conclusion: The perceived superiority of frontier LLMs over fine-tuned open-weight models in this safety/release decision task is largely an artifact of under-specified evaluation prompts rather than genuine capability differences. Careful prompt and taxonomy specification can erase these apparent gaps and reveal that open models, when fine-tuned and evaluated fairly, perform comparably. At the same time, multi-stage pipelines like Augur can introduce systematic biases (e.g., over-pessimism) if not carefully designed. Nonetheless, the reaction-simulation component is validated as a useful tool for anticipating public concerns, especially in challenging, non-trivial cases, and the fully reproducible setup supports transparent methodological scrutiny.

title: Advancing Model Research in AgentX: Long-Horizon Autonomy for Industrial Recommender Systems
comment: Technical report. 37 pages, 11 figures, 13 tables, including appendices
summary: Sustaining industrial recommendation research requires using the results of one experiment to decide what to investigate next. We present AgentX-Model, the next generation of AgentX's model research framework, which connects proposal development and model experimentation within sandboxes defined by business inputs and prediction tasks. AgentX-Model adopts a dual-agent architecture comprising a Research Agent and a Model Agent. The Research Agent develops independently reviewed proposals from papers and experimental findings, while the Model Agent conducts multi-round investigations and returns code, measurements, and unresolved questions. Using the returned results, the Research Agent selects a starting implementation and formulates the next research question, allowing subsequent experiments to build on earlier findings. We organize this continuing research around four actions: Reproduce, Follow-up, Composition, and Diagnose. The first three actions drive routine research, while Diagnose acquires the evidence needed to choose a repair, including for issues raised by business feedback and online evaluation, such as prediction bias measured by PCOC. Across the production evaluation, 560 of 636 completed model-changing experiments recorded AUC above their business baselines. As research continued, some experiments recorded AUC above every comparable ancestor in their lineages. The five latest online A/B evaluations across different business settings reported gains including 10-15% in acquisition efficiency, 15-20% in target-segment advertising spend, and 0.3-0.8% in watch time; the watch-time model used approximately 10% fewer FLOPs and parameters. A dependency-aware historical-replay benchmark further evaluates research allocation, with initial results showing no consistent efficiency gain from more complex scheduling when agents already analyze and select concrete candidates.

AI.tldr: AgentX-Model is a dual-agent research framework that continuously improves industrial recommender models by structuring how experiments are proposed, run, and iterated within business-constrained sandboxes.
AI.motivation: Industrial recommendation systems need a systematic way to use the outcome of each experiment to decide what to test next, aligning model research with concrete business goals and constraints. Existing ad hoc research processes make it hard to reproduce results, build on prior work, and integrate offline metrics with online business feedback such as bias or efficiency concerns.
AI.method: The authors design AgentX-Model, a dual-agent architecture with a Research Agent and a Model Agent operating inside sandboxes defined by business inputs and prediction tasks. The Research Agent reads papers and past experiments, writes independently reviewed research proposals, selects starting implementations, and formulates the next research questions. The Model Agent executes multi-round model investigations, producing code, metrics, and unresolved issues. Research is structured into four actions—Reproduce, Follow-up, Composition, and Diagnose—that guide how new experiments are derived from previous ones and from business/online feedback. They evaluate the framework with large-scale production experiments, online A/B tests across multiple business settings, and a dependency-aware historical replay benchmark of research allocation strategies.
AI.result: In production, 560 of 636 completed experiments that changed models achieved higher AUC than their business baselines, and some experiments surpassed all comparable ancestors in their lineages. Five recent online A/B tests across different products showed substantial gains: 10–15% improvement in acquisition efficiency, 15–20% improvement in advertising spend allocation for target segments, and 0.3–0.8% increase in watch time, while the improved watch-time model required about 10% fewer FLOPs and parameters. The historical-replay benchmark showed that, once agents already analyze and choose concrete candidates, adding more complex scheduling policies gave no consistent efficiency improvements in how research effort was allocated.
AI.conclusion: A structured, agent-based research framework can make industrial recommender-system experimentation more effective and business-aligned. By tightly coupling proposal generation, experiment execution, and iteration under four core actions, AgentX-Model yields frequent offline AUC improvements and meaningful online business gains while sometimes even reducing computational cost. Additionally, advanced scheduling of experiments appears less important once intelligent agents are already curating and selecting candidate experiments, suggesting that future gains may come more from better proposal/diagnosis mechanisms than from more complex scheduling heuristics.

title: Synthetic Hospital: An Open, Verifiable, Physician-Validated Longitudinal EHR Benchmark
summary: Frontier language models are rarely used in clinical workflows because the realistic, longitudinal benchmarks needed to develop them are scarce. Real electronic health record (EHR) data cannot be openly shared due to privacy, ethics or data use issues and it does not contain verifiable ground truth since the chart records only reflect what clinicians documented. We introduce Synthetic Hospital, an open, fully synthetic, fact-grounded longitudinal EHR benchmark that resolves the open sharing and verifiable ground truth barriers. Built entirely from public medical-education material with no protected health information, it comprises 1,268 longitudinal patients and 5,602 encounters, where every diagnosis, finding, and temporal relation is grounded in standard ontologies (ICD-10-CM, SNOMED CT, LOINC) and with a complete provenance chain back to its source medical education material. Synthetic Hospital is served through a simulated hospital record system that mirrors real EHR infrastructure (standard interoperability APIs, role-based access and function-calling interface). In a blinded review, physicians distinguished its records from real patient charts at near-chance rates (53\%). Across 10 frontier and open models, none approaches ceiling: the best model reconstructs a patient's longitudinal problem list with a severity-weighted F1 of 0.73, level with the mean of seven physicians on a matched subset but well below the best of them (0.89), and misses roughly half of clinically relevant findings when summarizing a chart. Overall, these results highlight that Synthetic Hospital is a difficult and realistic test of clinical AI performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Synthetic Hospital, a fully synthetic, realistic longitudinal EHR benchmark built from public medical-education materials to evaluate clinical AI models while avoiding privacy issues and enabling verifiable ground truth.
AI.motivation: Clinical foundation and frontier language models need realistic, longitudinal electronic health record benchmarks to guide development and evaluation, but real EHRs cannot be openly shared due to privacy and legal constraints, and they lack verifiable ground truth because documentation is incomplete and biased. There is a gap for an open, sharable, clinically realistic benchmark with explicit ground truth and full provenance that can rigorously test clinical AI systems, especially on complex longitudinal reasoning tasks.
AI.method: The authors construct Synthetic Hospital, a fully synthetic EHR corpus generated solely from publicly available medical-education materials (e.g., teaching cases, textbooks, question banks). They transform these into 1,268 synthetic patients and 5,602 encounters with longitudinal trajectories. Every diagnosis, clinical finding, lab, and temporal relation is linked to standard medical ontologies (ICD-10-CM, SNOMED CT, LOINC) and traced back via a full provenance chain to source educational content. They deploy the data through a simulated hospital record system that mimics real EHR infrastructure, including standard interoperability APIs, role-based access, and function-calling. They then perform a blinded physician Turing-test–style assessment of realism and benchmark 10 state-of-the-art open and frontier language models on tasks such as reconstructing longitudinal problem lists and summarizing charts, comparing model performance against physicians.
AI.result: Physicians in a blinded review could distinguish Synthetic Hospital records from real patient charts only at near-chance levels (53%), indicating high realism of the synthetic data. When evaluated on the benchmark, none of the 10 tested language models approached ceiling performance. The best model achieved a severity-weighted F1 of 0.73 for reconstructing a patient's longitudinal problem list—comparable to the mean performance of seven physicians on a matched subset but substantially below the best physician score of 0.89. In chart summarization tasks, the best models still missed about half of clinically relevant findings, revealing substantial performance gaps. These findings demonstrate that Synthetic Hospital is both challenging and discriminative for current clinical AI systems.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic Hospital provides an open, privacy-safe, fact-grounded longitudinal EHR benchmark that closely resembles real clinical data while offering verifiable ground truth and full provenance. The difficulty of the benchmark and the performance gap between current language models and top physicians show that frontier models are not yet ready to match expert clinical reasoning on realistic longitudinal tasks. The resource can serve as a standardized, sharable platform for stress-testing and improving clinical AI models, as well as for developing tools and infrastructure that interact with EHR-like systems via modern APIs and role-based access controls.

title: How does Adversarial Influence Scale in Multi-Agent Systems?
summary: Multi-agent deliberation can improve performance, but what happens when some agents do not act in good faith? In practice, an agent may be deceptive and work to subvert the group, whether through its own objectives or external instruction. We study how susceptibility to deception scales as groups increase in size and deceivers become more prevalent. It is not the number of agents in the group that matters, but the proportion of deceivers. We observe that the defection rate, how often initially correct agents switch to an incorrect final answer, rises linearly with this proportion. Whereas humans in comparable conformity studies are reliably swayed only when misleading confederates form a majority, LLM agents defect regularly even when deceivers remain a minority. Susceptibility also depends on which models are interacting, especially on the honest agent side. Unexpectedly, allowing deceivers to coordinate privately can make them less effective. Altogether, our results show that adding more agents is therefore not a sufficient defense, because the adversary can simply scale with the group.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how vulnerable multi-agent LLM systems are to deceptive agents and finds that susceptibility to deception scales with the proportion of deceivers, not the number of agents, with LLMs being more easily swayed than humans in classic conformity experiments.
AI.motivation: As multi-agent LLM systems become more common for deliberation and decision-making, there is concern about what happens when some agents are deceptive or adversarial. Understanding how group size and the prevalence of deceivers affect system robustness is crucial for building secure and reliable multi-agent AI systems.
AI.method: The authors construct multi-agent deliberation settings where some agents are designated as deceivers with incentives or instructions to push incorrect answers. They vary group size and the proportion of deceptive agents, compare different LLMs in honest and deceptive roles, and test the effect of allowing deceivers to coordinate privately. They measure defection rate: how often initially-correct honest agents are persuaded to adopt an incorrect final answer.
AI.result: The defection rate increases approximately linearly with the proportion of deceptive agents, and depends strongly on which LLMs are used, especially for honest agents. Unlike humans in classic conformity experiments, LLM agents often defect even when deceivers are a minority. Surprisingly, letting deceptive agents coordinate privately can reduce their overall effectiveness at causing defection.
AI.conclusion: Robustness to deception in multi-agent LLM systems is determined more by the fraction of deceptive agents than by absolute group size. Simply adding more agents does not reliably improve security, since adversaries can scale their presence with the group. Model choice and interaction design matter, and naive multi-agent scaling is not a sufficient defense against coordinated deception.

title: Style, Not Self: Surface Cues Explain Zero-Shot Code Attribution by Large Language Models
summary: If a language model can recognize code it wrote, it may favor that code as a judge, and instances of one model monitoring each other could collude. We test this zero-shot on current commercial models. Five LLMs generate solutions to MBPP, HumanEval, and DS-1000, seven more to MBPP, and models act as evaluators in four tasks: picking their own solution from a pair, judging whether a single solution is their own, identifying which of two solutions a named model wrote, and judging quality blind. In the single-solution task, balanced accuracy is 49-58% for all 15 model-benchmark combinations, while raw accuracy (38-67%) mostly reflects how readily a model claims authorship. In the pairwise task, accuracy across 14 evaluator-opponent combinations correlates at r=0.93 with how often the evaluator's solution is longer. Attribution to a named model succeeds on some pairs and is consistently inverted on others. A rule-based normalization that strips docstrings, comments, type hints, and local names preserves Pass@1 and leaves ten of twelve re-tested results at chance; the other two follow a length difference it leaves, although a trained classifier still separates most normalized pairs. Claude Haiku's self-preference also disappears. We recommend reporting balanced accuracy, heuristic baselines, and label consistency.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether current large language models can recognize, and thereby preferentially favor, their own code, posing risks of collusion and biased evaluation.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used both to generate and to evaluate code, there is a risk they could recognize their own outputs and systematically favor them, undermining benchmark validity, model comparisons, and multi-agent setups where models supervise each other. The authors want to empirically test how strong this self-recognition and self-preference effect is in modern commercial models, and whether simple defenses can remove it.
AI.method: The authors run zero-shot experiments on several commercial LLMs. First, five models generate code solutions to three benchmarks (MBPP, HumanEval, DS-1000) and seven more models generate solutions to MBPP. Then models are used as evaluators in four tasks: (1) from a pair of solutions, pick which one is their own; (2) given a single solution, decide if they wrote it; (3) given two solutions and a model name, identify which solution the named model wrote; (4) judge solution quality without being told about authorship. They measure raw and balanced accuracy, analyze biases like always claiming authorship and length-correlated choices, and examine how often models invert attributions. They also apply a rule-based normalization to the code (removing docstrings, comments, type hints, local variable names) and re-test, and additionally train a classifier on normalized code pairs to see whether subtle stylistic signals remain.
AI.result: In single-solution self-recognition, balanced accuracy stays near chance (49–58%) across 15 model–benchmark combinations; raw accuracy varies widely (38–67%) but mostly tracks how often a model simply says a solution is its own. In pairwise self-identification, accuracy across 14 evaluator–opponent combinations is strongly correlated (r=0.93) with which solution is longer, indicating a heuristic bias rather than true self-recognition. Attribution to a named model shows mixed behavior: some pairs are correctly attributed, while others are systematically misattributed (inverted). After rule-based normalization, Pass@1 performance is unchanged, and ten of twelve re-tested settings drop to chance-level recognition; in the remaining two, residual performance matches remaining length differences. Nonetheless, a trained classifier can still distinguish most normalized pairs, indicating that subtle stylistic signals persist. For at least one model, Claude Haiku, the previous self-preference effect disappears after normalization.
AI.conclusion: Current commercial LLMs show little genuine ability to recognize their own generated code; apparent self-preference is largely driven by trivial heuristics like code length and an overall bias toward claiming authorship. Simple rule-based code normalization can effectively remove detectable self-signals for practical purposes without harming task performance, though machine-learned classifiers can still find residual style features. To ensure reliable evaluation and mitigate risks of collusion or biased judging, the authors recommend that future work report balanced accuracy (not just raw accuracy), include heuristic baselines such as length-based rules, and check label consistency across conditions.

title: NNV3: Expanding Neural Network Verification to New Architectures and Domains
summary: We present NNV3, the latest version of the Neural Network Verification (NNV) tool, a MATLAB framework for formal verification of deep learning models and learning-enabled cyber-physical systems. Building on the set-based reachability foundation of NNV 1.0 (FFNNs, CNNs, NNCS) and NNV 2.0 (RNNs, SSNNs, neural ODEs), NNV3 introduces new members of the Star-set family: ModelStar for verifying networks under weight perturbation, VolumeStar for video and 3D volumetric inputs, and GraphStar for graph neural networks. A conformal-inference-based probabilistic reachability mode complements sound analysis for problems where deterministic verification is intractable, while FairNNV certifies counterfactual and individual fairness properties over continuous input regions. NNV3 introduces new benchmarks for malware detection, graph-based power-system models, medical imaging, variable-length time series data, and action recognition. NNV3 also incorporates tutorials and developer guides through a unified documentation site. This paper details these major updates, demonstrating NNV's maturation into a comprehensive, robust, and accessible verification tool for a diverse range of AI systems.

AI.tldr: NNV3 is an expanded MATLAB-based tool for formally verifying a wide variety of neural networks and AI-enabled cyber-physical systems, with new set representations, probabilistic reachability, fairness certification, and broad benchmarks and documentation.
AI.motivation: As neural networks are increasingly deployed in safety- and mission-critical systems, there is a growing need for rigorous, scalable verification tools that can handle diverse architectures (e.g., CNNs, RNNs, GNNs, neural ODEs), input types (images, videos, graphs, time series), and properties (robustness, fairness). Previous versions of NNV provided strong foundations but were limited in supported models, input modalities, and types of uncertainties, and lacked comprehensive benchmarks and user support. NNV3 aims to address these gaps and move toward a mature, practical verification framework that practitioners can apply to real-world AI systems.
AI.method: NNV3 extends the Star-set based reachability analysis framework by introducing new Star variants tailored to different verification scenarios: ModelStar for capturing weight perturbations, VolumeStar for high-dimensional inputs such as videos and 3D volumetric data, and GraphStar for graph neural networks. It combines exact/sound reachability with a new probabilistic reachability mode based on conformal inference to cope with intractable deterministic verification tasks. Additionally, it incorporates a FairNNV module for certifying counterfactual and individual fairness over continuous input regions. The tool is packaged with new benchmarks across multiple application domains and enhanced with unified documentation, tutorials, and developer guides.
AI.result: The paper reports that NNV3 can verify properties of a much broader class of models and applications than previous versions, including networks with weight uncertainty, GNNs, models processing videos and 3D data, and systems using variable-length time series and action recognition. It can provide both sound guarantees and probabilistic certificates where exact verification is infeasible. The new benchmarks demonstrate NNV3’s applicability to malware detection, power systems modeled as graphs, medical imaging, and other realistic tasks. Usability is improved through comprehensive documentation and examples.
AI.conclusion: NNV3 represents a significant maturation of the NNV tool into a comprehensive verification framework for modern AI systems. By expanding its set-based representations, adding probabilistic reachability and fairness certification, and supplying diverse benchmarks and documentation, NNV3 positions itself as a robust, accessible platform for formal analysis of deep learning models and learning-enabled cyber-physical systems across many architectures and domains.

title: SciWalker: Synthesizing Scientific Coding Problems with Operator Graphs and Execution Feedback
summary: Improving the scientific coding capabilities of large language models (LLMs) requires high-quality training data. However, such data remain scarce because manually authoring realistic problems is costly and time-consuming, while systematically covering diverse scientific domains and algorithmic combinations remains challenging. To address this, we introduce SciWalker, a framework for synthesizing scientific coding problems through operator-chain sampling and execution feedback. The framework combines scientific library interfaces with operation modes to instantiate operators, organizes them into operator graphs, and samples operator chains as computational workflow cues. Guided by these cues, we adopt LLMs to generate scientifically grounded problem statements, reference solutions, and tests, with failed generations iteratively repaired using execution feedback. By combining structured workflow composition with verification and quality review, SciWalker enables scalable task generation while promoting scientific grounding, computational diversity, and executability. Using this framework, we construct 8,178 high-quality problems spanning 5 scientific domains and 32 subdomains. To evaluate their training utility, we conduct reinforcement learning on Qwen3.5-9B using the GSPO algorithm. This training improves SciCode subproblem accuracy by 9.9 percentage points, from 29.3% to 39.2%, with gains across scientific code generation, code repair, and reasoning benchmarks. The code for SciWalker is available at https://github.com/lichenx1/SciWalker.

AI.tldr: SciWalker is a framework for automatically generating large-scale, high-quality scientific coding problems to improve LLMs’ scientific coding skills.
AI.motivation: High-quality, realistic, and diverse scientific coding datasets are scarce because manual creation is expensive and does not scale well across many domains and algorithmic patterns. The authors want a scalable, systematic way to synthesize such problems so LLMs can be better trained for scientific programming.
AI.method: They design SciWalker, which (1) uses scientific libraries and their operation modes to define operators; (2) composes these into operator graphs and samples operator chains as abstract computational workflows; (3) conditions an LLM on these chains to generate problem statements, reference solutions, and tests; and (4) iteratively repairs failed generations through execution feedback and verification, ensuring executability and quality. The final result is a curated dataset of scientific coding tasks created via this structured workflow plus quality review.
AI.result: Using SciWalker, they generate 8,178 scientific coding problems across 5 domains and 32 subdomains. Training the Qwen3.5-9B model with reinforcement learning (GSPO) on this data increases its SciCode subproblem accuracy by 9.9 percentage points (from 29.3% to 39.2%), and yields improvements on scientific code generation, code repair, and reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: SciWalker provides a scalable, execution-verified method to synthesize diverse, scientifically grounded coding tasks, and the resulting data significantly improves an LLM’s performance on scientific programming benchmarks, indicating the framework’s effectiveness and utility for training scientific coding models.

title: Self-Play Pretraining with Zero Data
comment: AC, KD, and MYL contributed equally; authors are listed alphabetically
summary: Advances in language modeling have been driven by scaling pretraining on ever more data. Yet, the training data is still largely curated on the model's behalf. A more general approach to pretraining would let the model learn to generate the data most useful for its own improvement. This would provide an effectively unbounded source of training data, limited by compute rather than human knowledge. We introduce Self-Play Pretraining with Zero Data, an initial proof-of-concept towards realizing this vision. Our procedure casts synthetic data generation as a search over the space of all computable structure, taking inspiration from Solomonoff induction. Starting from random initialization, two models learn in tandem: a generator proposes programs interpreted by a universal Turing machine, generating byte sequences, while a learner autoregressively predicts these byte sequences. The learner is trained with standard cross-entropy, while the generator is trained with reinforcement learning to produce sequences at the frontier of the learner's capabilities, yielding an adaptive curriculum. A universal Turing machine gives us a search space over all computable data-generating processes, imposing little domain-specific structure, and self-play searches over this space for useful training data. We test whether zero-shot performance on natural data improves predictably with self-play compute; this is a clean test of transfer since neither generator nor learner is trained on natural data. Across several natural datasets, zero-shot loss exhibits predictable scaling in compute. The models also exhibit in-context learning, and discover recognizable mathematical sequences during training.

AI.tldr: They propose a self-play pretraining scheme where a generator model creates synthetic programs/data and a learner model trains on them, showing that language-model-like abilities can emerge without any human-curated training data.
AI.motivation: Current large language models rely on massive, human-curated corpora. This is inherently limited and domain-biased, and it requires continuous data collection and cleaning. The authors want a more general, scalable way to obtain training data, ideally one that uses compute instead of human data as the main resource. They explore whether a model can bootstrap its own training data from scratch and still transfer to natural tasks.
AI.method: They design a self-play framework with two models starting from random initialization. A generator proposes programs that are executed by a universal Turing machine to yield byte sequences. A learner model is trained autoregressively, via cross-entropy, to predict these sequences. The generator is trained with reinforcement learning to produce sequences that are challenging but learnable for the learner—i.e., that sit at the frontier of its abilities—thus creating an adaptive curriculum. By using a universal Turing machine as the data-generating substrate, the search space in principle covers all computable processes. They then measure zero-shot performance of the resulting learner on various natural datasets, none of which were seen during training, as a function of compute spent in self-play.
AI.result: They find that zero-shot loss on several natural datasets improves in a predictable way as more compute is devoted to self-play, even though the models were never trained directly on natural data. The learner exhibits in-context learning behaviors, and the system discovers familiar mathematical sequences during training, indicating that it uncovers meaningful structure. The scaling of zero-shot performance with compute suggests reliable transfer from synthetic, self-generated data to real-world tasks.
AI.conclusion: Self-play pretraining on purely synthetic data, generated via a search over computable processes using a universal Turing machine, can yield models that transfer to natural datasets and show in-context learning. The results support the feasibility of using compute-driven, self-generated training curricula instead of massive human-curated corpora, providing an early proof-of-concept for a more general and potentially unbounded pretraining paradigm.
